Solovej, *The Ionization Conjecture in Hartree-Fock Theory*, arXiv:math-ph/0012026); the full Schrödinger problem remains open because available total-energy asymptotics do not control the required order-one difference. The problem is surveyed in M. Lewin (2025), *Some open mathematical problems concerning charged quantum particles*, DOI:10.5802/crphys.249.
solved_when: A rigorous proof of a Z-independent constant C bounding the difference \(E_Z(Z-1)-E_Z(Z)\) for neutral atoms with the full electron–electron interaction; no specific constant value is required.
why: It would place the bounded energy scale of outer-electron chemistry on a rigorous many-body foundation, explaining why atomic chemistry operates in a fixed energy window regardless of nuclear charge.
key_works: J. P. Solovej (2003), *The Ionization Conjecture in Hartree-Fock Theory*, [arXiv:math-ph/0012026](https://arxiv.org/abs/math-ph/0012026); M. Lewin (2025), *Some open mathematical problems concerning charged quantum particles*, [DOI:10.5802/crphys.249](https://doi.org/10.5802/crphys.249).

title: Uniform outer-electron radius bound
open: In a neutral atom of nuclear charge \(Z\), is there a radius beyond which only a fixed number \(m>0\) of electrons reside, with a bound that does not grow with \(Z\) but carries the appropriate dependence on \(m\) — proved for the full interacting many-body theory?
status: The corresponding Hartree–Fock ionization-radius results are proved (J. P. Solovej, 2003, *The Ionization Conjecture in Hartree-Fock Theory*, arXiv:math-ph/0012026); comparable control of the exact many-electron density tail remains a decades-old open problem.
solved_when: A \(Z\)-independent upper bound on the outer radius \(R_m(Z)\), with correct dependence on \(m\), is established for the exact interacting neutral atom.
why: Such a bound explains why chemically relevant valence length scales stay fixed rather than shrinking as the atomic core grows.
key_works: J. P. Solovej (2003), *The Ionization Conjecture in Hartree-Fock Theory*, [arXiv:math-ph/0012026](https://arxiv.org/abs/math-ph/0012026).

title: Sharp three-dimensional Lieb–Thirring kinetic constant
open: What is the sharp fermionic kinetic-energy constant in three dimensions — equivalently, the sharp Lieb–Thirring spectral constant at \(\gamma=1\)? In particular, determine whether the semiclassical value is optimal.
status: Open since the 1970s. The semiclassical constant was proved for shifted Coulomb Hamiltonians in 2025 (Corso and T. Ried, *On a Variational Problem Related to the Cwikel–Lieb–Rozenblum and Lieb–Thirring Inequalities*, [DOI:10.1007/s00220-024-05216-y](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00220-024-05216-y); Corso, T. Weidl and Z. Zeng, *Lieb–Thirring inequalities for the shifted Coulomb Hamiltonian*, [DOI:10.4171/JST/574](https://doi.org/10.4171/JST/574)), but arbitrary admissible potentials remain unresolved.
solved_when: The optimal three-dimensional Lieb–Thirring constant at \(\gamma=1\) is determined, settling whether it equals the semiclassical value.
why: It sharpens electronic kinetic-energy lower bounds and quantitative stability estimates for matter.
key_works: T. C. Corso and T. Ried (2025), *On a Variational Problem Related to the Cwikel–Lieb–Rozenblum and Lieb–Thirring Inequalities*, [DOI:10.1007/s00220-024-05216-y](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00220-024-05216-y); Corso, T. Weidl and Z. Zeng (2025), *Lieb–Thirring inequalities for the shifted Coulomb Hamiltonian*, [DOI:10.4171/JST/574](https://doi.org/10.4171/JST/574).

title: Hohenberg–Kohn mapping for the physical total current
open: Do the particle density and the physical total current of a ground state together determine the scalar and vector potentials, up to gauge, under precisely specified ground-state assumptions — or is there a counterexample revealing what additional information the mapping requires?
status: The standard uniqueness argument for the paramagnetic current fails, and proposed arguments based on the total current have known defects. The question for the physical current remains open following the 2021 analysis of Diener’s construction by A. Laestadius, M. Penz and E. I. Tellgren, *Revisiting density-functional theory of the total current density*, [DOI:10.1088/1361-648X/abf784](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-648X/abf784).
solved_when: A proof that density and physical total current uniquely determine the potentials modulo gauge under stated ground-state assumptions, or an explicit counterexample identifying the missing information.
why: A positive result would place current-density-functional theory on rigorous footing, enabling reliable density-functional descriptions of magnetic response and molecular currents; a counterexample would clarify what data must supplement them.
key_works: A. Laestadius, M. Penz and E. I. Tellgren (2021), *Revisiting density-functional theory of the total current density*, [DOI:10.1088/1361-648X/abf784](https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-648X/abf784).

title: Generic coupled-cluster singles-and-doubles root counts
open: How many isolated complex solutions do the coupled-cluster singles-and-doubles (CCSD) amplitude equations generically admit as the numbers of electrons and orbitals vary? A usable formula should distinguish arbitrary algebraic systems from the physically relevant case of two-body Hamiltonians.
status: Algebraic geometry currently provides only bounds and special cases; the Grassmannian CCS degree is solved, but arbitrary-size CCSD root counts are not (F. M. Faulstich, B. Sturmfels and S. Sverrisdóttir (2025), *Algebraic Varieties in Quantum Chemistry*, [DOI:10.1007/s10208-024-09657-8](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-024-09657-8)).
solved_when: A closed-form (or otherwise effectively computable) formula for the generic number of isolated complex CCSD amplitude solutions is derived, valid for arbitrary electron and orbital counts, with the arbitrary algebraic case and the two-body Hamiltonian case treated separately.
why: It would quantify the multiplicity of CCSD solutions, directly determining the completeness requirements of continuation and homotopy-tracking algorithms used to locate all amplitude roots.
key_works: F. M. Faulstich, B. Sturmfels and S. Sverrisdóttir (2025), *Algebraic Varieties in Quantum Chemistry*, [DOI:10.1007/s10208-024-09657-8](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10208-024-09657-8).

title: Computable coupled-cluster truncation error certificates
open: Can we attach rigorous, computationally evaluable error bars to the energies produced by practical truncated coupled-cluster methods — and include tests that detect when the assumptions underlying the certificate fail?
status: Recent analysis (Hassan, Maday, and Wang, 2023, arXiv:2311.00637) proves local well-posedness and a posteriori estimates for the discrete coupled cluster equations under structural assumptions; inexpensively evaluating the stability constants and missing-correlation bounds for difficult molecules remains open.
solved_when: A certificate is given that, for practical truncated coupled-cluster energies, yields a rigorous a posteriori error bound evaluable at reasonable cost, together with tests detecting failure of its structural assumptions; inexpensively evaluating the stability constants and missing-correlation bounds for difficult molecules remains the concrete barrier.
why: It separates convergence of the amplitude solver from actual chemical accuracy of the computed energy, telling users when a "converged" coupled-cluster result can actually be trusted.
key_works: M. Hassan, Y. Maday and Y. Wang (2023), *Analysis of the Single Reference Coupled Cluster Method for Electronic Structure Calculations: The Discrete Coupled Cluster Equations*, [arXiv:2311.00637](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.00637).

title: Guaranteed numerical errors for nonconvex Kohn–Sham calculations
open: Can we compute guaranteed error bounds on the energy for Kohn–Sham calculations when the density functional is nonconvex? Such bounds must account for both discretization and the self-consistency iteration, and must say whether a computed solution is merely a local stationary point or the global minimum.
status: Guaranteed bounds were obtained for periodic Kohn–Sham equations with convex density functionals in 2025 (A. Bordignon et al., *Fully Guaranteed and Computable Error Bounds on the Energy for Periodic Kohn–Sham Equations with Convex Density Functionals*, [DOI:10.1137/25M1735676](https://doi.org/10.1137/25M1735676)), but many practical exchange-correlation approximations violate that central convexity hypothesis.
solved_when: A computable bound is available for nonconvex Kohn–Sham functionals that certifies the energy error from discretization and self-consistency together, and that distinguishes local stationary states from the global minimum.
why: It would make numerical phase orderings and energy differences testable independently of functional approximation error.
key_works: A. Bordignon et al. (2025), *Fully Guaranteed and Computable Error Bounds on the Energy for Periodic Kohn–Sham Equations with Convex Density Functionals*, [DOI:10.1137/25M1735676](https://doi.org/10.1137/25M1735676).

title: Selecting the physical branch of self-consistent Green’s functions
open: When a self-consistent GF2 or GW calculation converges to several distinct Green's-function solutions, what principle decides which branch is the physical equilibrium state? A satisfactory answer must give criteria that select the physical branch and, at the same time, distinguish genuinely metastable states from spurious artifacts of the diagrammatic truncation.
status: Multiple solutions to the self-consistent equations are documented. Pokhilko and Zgid's 2025 homotopy continuation method tracks branches of the Dyson equation fully self-consistently, with applications including NdNiO₂ [DOI:10.1063/5.0288359], but it does not resolve the question of universal physical branch selection.
solved_when: A usable criterion (or set of criteria) exists that identifies the physical equilibrium solution among the multiple branches of the self-consistent Dyson equation in GF2/GW, and reliably separates true metastability from truncation-induced artifacts.
why: Without such a criterion, a merely converged numerical solution can be dressed with an unjustified thermodynamic interpretation, undermining the physical meaning of self-consistent simulations.
key_works: P. Pokhilko and D. Zgid (2025), *Homotopy continuation method for solving Dyson equation fully self-consistently: Theory and application to NdNiO2*, [DOI:10.1063/5.0288359](https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0288359).

title: Quantitative microscopic prediction of chiral spin selectivity
open: Can a microscopic theory predict the magnitude, sign, and temperature dependence of chiral-induced spin selectivity (CISS) directly from molecular structure and contact geometry? Such a theory must succeed without resorting to artificially inflated spin–orbit coupling as a fitting parameter.
status: Competing mechanisms each reproduce subsets of CISS experiments. A 2025 ab initio Hubbard-model parametrization by D. K. A. Phan Huu et al. (2025), *Ab initio parametrization of a generalized Hubbard model in a molecule displaying chirality-induced spin selectivity* ([DOI:10.1038/s43246-025-00821-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43246-025-00821-3)), demonstrates consequential electron–vibration effects, but a transferable quantitative theory remains unresolved.
solved_when: Quantitative, transferable predictions of spin-polarization magnitude, sign, and temperature dependence are obtained from molecular structure and contacts alone, with no artificially large spin–orbit coupling, and these predictions agree with CISS experiments.
why: It would enable the rational design of chiral spin filters and of spin-dependent chemical reactions, replacing empirical tuning with predictive design.
key_works: D. K. A. Phan Huu et al. (2025), *Ab initio parametrization of a generalized Hubbard model in a molecule displaying chirality-induced spin selectivity*, [DOI:10.1038/s43246-025-00821-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43246-025-00821-3).

title: Separating molecular and contact contributions to CISS
open: Can a single CISS device be instrumented so that the spin filtering intrinsic to the chiral molecule is measured separately from the spin selectivity of the electrode–molecule contact? Formally, this requires independent quantification of both contributions in the same device, with controls for current direction, magnetization, molecular handedness, and nonlinear voltage response.
status: Direction-dependent magnetic conductive AFM supplied evidence against a purely interfacial interpretation in one 2025 geometry (J. A. Albro et al. (2025), *Measurement Platform to Probe the Mechanism of Chiral-Induced Spin Selectivity through Direction-Dependent Magnetic Conductive Atomic Force Microscopy*, [DOI:10.1021/acsnano.5c04980](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.5c04980)). A general decomposition across contacts and molecular families remains open.
solved_when: A single-device experiment reports intrinsic molecular spin filtering and electrode-interface selectivity as independently measured quantities, with the controls above (current direction, magnetization, handedness, nonlinear voltage response) demonstrated.
why: It identifies which chemical modifications affect spin transport through the molecule itself and which merely affect spin injection at the interface, guiding rational molecular design for CISS devices.
key_works: J. A. Albro et al. (2025), *Measurement Platform to Probe the Mechanism of Chiral-Induced Spin Selectivity through Direction-Dependent Magnetic Conductive Atomic Force Microscopy*, [DOI:10.1021/acsnano.5c04980](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsnano.5c04980).

title: Bright, stable emitters with inverted singlet–triplet gaps
open: Can an organic emitter whose lowest singlet lies below its triplet (an inverted singlet–triplet gap) be built to work in a real device, combining strong light absorption, fast triplet harvesting, and operational stability?
status: Inverted-gap examples exist, but the strongest computational lead comes from a 2026 search that screened 118,081 aza-hydrocarbons and proposed 34 candidates with oscillator strengths of at least 0.01 (R. Mahaan and Z. Shuai (2026), *Cost-Effective Digital Discovery of Aza-Hydrocarbons via Isomerization for Inverted Singlet–Triplet Emitters*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.jpclett.6c01031](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpclett.6c01031)); their predicted advantages still require experimental realization.
solved_when: A molecule with an experimentally verified inverted singlet–triplet gap demonstrates appreciable oscillator strength (at least 0.01), rapid triplet harvesting, and stable operation in a device context.
why: Inverted gaps could cut exciton residence times and thereby reduce OLED efficiency losses such as roll-off.
key_works: R. Mahaan and Z. Shuai (2026), *Cost-Effective Digital Discovery of Aza-Hydrocarbons via Isomerization for Inverted Singlet–Triplet Emitters*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.jpclett.6c01031](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpclett.6c01031).

title: Directly resolving the charge-density oscillation of correlation-driven migration
open: Can we directly observe the coherent oscillation of electronic charge density that correlation-driven migration predicts, in a way that rules out nuclear motion and incoherent electron populations as alternative explanations? Formally, the goal is an experiment that selectively ionizes a molecule and resolves the predicted quantum beating of the charge density while excluding these competing mechanisms.
status: Correlation-driven charge-migration signatures in adenine were reported in 2021 (E. P. Månsson et al., *Real-time observation of a correlation-driven sub 3 fs charge migration in ionised adenine*, [DOI:10.1038/s42004-021-00510-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42004-021-00510-5)), but direct observation of the predicted quantum beating remains elusive; a 2025 study (C. Guiot du Doignon et al., *Correlation-driven charge migration triggered by infrared multi-photon ionization*, [DOI:10.1039/D5SC02374B](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5SC02374B)) proposed infrared multi-photon preparation combined with X-ray probing to achieve it.
solved_when: A direct observation of the predicted charge-density quantum beating is reported, with control measurements sufficient to exclude nuclear motion and incoherent populations as the source of the signal — e.g., via the infrared-preparation, X-ray-probing scheme recently proposed.
why: It would establish whether electron correlation alone can relocate chemically meaningful charge on sub-3-fs timescales, before the nuclei have time to respond.
key_works: E. P. Månsson et al. (2021), *Real-time observation of a correlation-driven sub 3 fs charge migration in ionised adenine*, [DOI:10.1038/s42004-021-00510-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42004-021-00510-5); C. Guiot du Doignon et al. (2025), *Correlation-driven charge migration triggered by infrared multi-photon ionization*, [DOI:10.1039/D5SC02374B](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5SC02374B).

title: Direct observation of waveform-controlled Kolbe branching
open: Can we watch a Kolbe electrolysis happen inside a single polarity cycle — measuring the interfacial pH, the radical populations, and how much radical converts to carbocation as the waveform swings? A quantitative, cycle-resolved account of these intermediates and fluxes would explain how dimerization, substitution, and overoxidation products emerge under waveform control.
status: The 2023 waveform study by Hioki et al. proposed local-pH effects as the mechanism behind waveform-controlled Kolbe coupling. Cycle-resolved intermediate and product balances remain the experimental test of that mechanism.
solved_when: Interfacial pH, radical populations, and radical-to-carbocation conversion are measured within individual polarity cycles, and these measurements quantitatively explain the observed dimerization, substitution, and overoxidation product balances.
why: A cycle-resolved mechanism would make waveform selection transferable across substrates and reactors, rather than empirically tuned case by case.
key_works: Y. Hioki et al. (2023), *Overcoming the limitations of Kolbe coupling with waveform-controlled electrosynthesis*, [DOI:10.1126/science.adf4762](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adf4762).

title: Enantioselective capture of unbound electrogenerated carbocations
open: Can a freely diffusing tertiary carbocation, generated electrochemically at an electrode, be trapped with predictable enantioselectivity by a chiral external nucleophile before it rearranges or is captured by solvent — without resorting to covalently attached chiral auxiliaries?
status: A 2024 method by Q. Lin et al. (*Enantioselective SN1-type reaction via electrochemically generated chiral α-Imino carbocation intermediate*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-024-50945-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-50945-2)) controls chiral α-imino carbocations using primary-amine catalysis; freely diffusing tertiary carbocations present a distinct, unresolved selectivity problem.
solved_when: A demonstrated experimental protocol achieves enantioselective capture of an unbound, non-catalyst-bound tertiary carbocation generated electrochemically, with predictable stereochemical outcome ahead of rearrangement or solvent capture.
why: It would enable asymmetric substitutions at sterically crowded carbon centers starting from readily oxidizable feedstocks, expanding enantioselective electrosynthesis beyond catalyst-stabilized intermediates.
key_works: Q. Lin et al. (2024), *Enantioselective SN1-type reaction via electrochemically generated chiral α-Imino carbocation intermediate*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-024-50945-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-50945-2).

title: C–B axial chirality that survives Lewis-base coordination
open: Can a boron Lewis acid be built whose C–B axial chirality survives the actual conditions of use — repeated association and dissociation of a Lewis-base donor — while the acid remains strongly Lewis acidic?
status: Doan et al. showed in 2025 that Lewis-base binding can accelerate triarylborane atropisomerization from decades to minutes; the stability of the free borane therefore leaves the question of stability across a catalytic cycle unresolved (T.-H. Doan et al. (2025), *Atropisomerism in Triarylboranes: Lewis Base Assisted Rotation at C−B Stereogenic Axis in Asymmetrical Boron Lewis Acids*, [DOI:10.1002/ange.202421931](https://doi.org/10.1002/ange.202421931)).
solved_when: An axially chiral boron Lewis acid is designed that retains its configuration through repeated cycles of donor binding and release without measurable loss of Lewis acidity.
why: It would make C–B atropisomers usable as persistent asymmetric Lewis-acid catalysts rather than species whose chirality is only stable when idle.
key_works: T.-H. Doan et al. (2025), *Atropisomerism in Triarylboranes: Lewis Base Assisted Rotation at C−B Stereogenic Axis in Asymmetrical Boron Lewis Acids*, [DOI:10.1002/ange.202421931](https://doi.org/10.1002/ange.202421931).

title: Direct asymmetric NH transfer to dialkyl sulfoxides
open: Can racemic dialkyl sulfoxides be converted directly into enantioenriched, unprotected NH-sulfoximines via catalytic NH transfer coupled with in situ racemization of the sulfoxide? In formal terms, this asks for a dynamic kinetic resolution in which the substituents at sulfur are both alkyl groups.
status: Fan et al.'s 2025 iron/photoredox resolution performs well for many aryl–alkyl sulfoxides; the single tested dialkyl substrate gave 29% yield and racemic product [F.-X. Fan, H. Xu, S.-X. Tang, Y. Dang and F. Wang (2025), *Iron-catalysed stereoselective NH transfer enables dynamic kinetic resolution of sulfoxides*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-56860-4].
solved_when: A catalytic NH-transfer method converts a racemic dialkyl sulfoxide into an unprotected NH-sulfoximine in non-racemic, synthetically useful enantioenrichment and materially improved yield over the 29% racemic outcome currently on record.
why: It would furnish compact sulfur stereocenters without requiring chiral starting materials, opening a direct route to enantioenriched dialkyl sulfoximine building blocks.
key_works: F.-X. Fan, H. Xu, S.-X. Tang, Y. Dang and F. Wang (2025), *Iron-catalysed stereoselective NH transfer enables dynamic kinetic resolution of sulfoxides*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-56860-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-56860-4).

title: The dark racemization pathway in iron-catalyzed sulfoxide imidation
open: What nonphotochemical pathway racemizes sulfoxides in the iron/aminating-reagent system? A satisfying answer would distinguish the roles of electron transfer, sulfur substitution, and iron–aminyl chemistry, including the part played by the base.
status: Dark racemization requiring iron, ligand, and aminating reagent was observed in 2025 (F.-X. Fan et al., *Iron-catalysed stereoselective NH transfer enables dynamic kinetic resolution of sulfoxides*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-56860-4); the additional pathway and the base contribution remain unresolved.
solved_when: A mechanistically assigned dark racemization pathway is established, distinguishing electron transfer, sulfur substitution, and iron–aminyl chemistry and clarifying the base's contribution.
why: Resolving the pathway would enable simpler dynamic resolutions and suppress unwanted stereochemical erosion.
key_works: F.-X. Fan et al. (2025), *Iron-catalysed stereoselective NH transfer enables dynamic kinetic resolution of sulfoxides*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-56860-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-56860-4).

title: Quantitative stereochemical proteome maps for sulfonimidoyl fluorides
open: Can we map, across a native proteome, how a matched pair of sulfur enantiomers differs in which residues they occupy and how fast they react — with hydrolysis and nonspecific binding measured separately rather than lumped into the signal?
status: Buffer-phase stereospecific transformations and chirality-dependent protein ligation were demonstrated in 2024–2025 (H.-S. Huang et al. (2025), *Enantioselective Synthesis of Chiral Sulfonimidoyl Fluorides Facilitates Stereospecific SuFEx Click Chemistry*, [DOI:10.1002/anie.202415873](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202415873)); quantitative proteome-wide stereochemical reactivity maps remain open.
solved_when: A quantitative proteome-wide dataset exists giving residue occupancy and reaction kinetics for matched sulfur-enantiomer pairs, with separate quantification of hydrolysis and nonspecific binding.
why: Such maps connect sulfur configuration directly to selective covalent recognition, turning stereochemistry from a synthetic curiosity into a predictive variable for covalent ligand design.
key_works: H.-S. Huang et al. (2025), *Enantioselective Synthesis of Chiral Sulfonimidoyl Fluorides Facilitates Stereospecific SuFEx Click Chemistry*, [DOI:10.1002/anie.202415873](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202415873).

title: Long heparan-sulfate chains with independently programmed epimers and sulfates
open: Can we synthesize long heparan-sulfate chains in which every uronate epimer and every N-, 2-O-, 3-O-, and 6-O-sulfation site is independently specified? Formally, the goal is a route that sets each of these modification sites at will and preserves the intended pattern through synthesis and purification.
status: A 2023 platform produced all 64 N-/2-O-/6-O-sulfation patterns on a fixed tetrasaccharide framework [L. Wang et al. (2023), *Efficient platform for synthesizing comprehensive heparan sulfate oligosaccharide libraries for decoding glycosaminoglycan–protein interactions*, DOI:10.1038/s41557-023-01248-4]. Long-chain epimer and 3-O-sulfate programming remain outside that comprehensive library.
solved_when: A synthetic method yields long heparan-sulfate chains whose complete epimerization and sulfation pattern (all N-, 2-O-, 3-O-, and 6-O-sites) is prescribed in advance and confirmed intact after synthesis and purification.
why: Such chains would enable causal tests of long-range sulfation domains, probing how extended sulfation patterns control glycosaminoglycan–protein interactions rather than local motifs alone.
key_works: L. Wang et al. (2023), *Efficient platform for synthesizing comprehensive heparan sulfate oligosaccharide libraries for decoding glycosaminoglycan–protein interactions*, [DOI:10.1038/s41557-023-01248-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-023-01248-4).

title: Complete native heparan-sulfate chain sequencing
open: Can we determine the full sequence of a single native heparan-sulfate chain — its ordered sugars, uronate epimers, and sulfation sites — rather than just short fragments? Formally, the goal is a complete reconstruction that retains fragment provenance across long domains and correctly captures rare 3-O-sulfated motifs.
status: The 2020 SIMMS² method of R. L. Miller et al. (2020) (*Shotgun ion mobility mass spectrometry sequencing of heparan sulfate saccharides*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-020-15284-y) used 36 synthetic di- to decasaccharide standards and sequenced natural hexasaccharides; complete native-chain reconstruction remains beyond that fragment-level result.
solved_when: An individual native chain's complete sequence is recovered end to end, with ordered sugars, uronate epimers, and sulfation sites assigned while preserving fragment provenance across long domains and rare 3-O-sulfated motifs.
why: It would make the proposed heparan-sulfate sequence code directly readable, turning a hypothesized regulatory language into observable sequence data.
key_works: R. L. Miller et al. (2020), *Shotgun ion mobility mass spectrometry sequencing of heparan sulfate saccharides*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-020-15284-y](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-15284-y).

title: Unbiased quantitative inventories of heparan-sulfate 3-O-sulfation
open: Can we measure how abundant native 3-O-sulfated heparan-sulfate motifs really are, with recovery calibrated across the diverse neighboring sulfate patterns and epimers? In formal terms, the goal is a quantitative inventory in which apparent abundances are corrected for losses and biases in release, enrichment, and ionization, so that true rarity can be distinguished from analytical undersampling.
status: Cationic-peptide enrichment followed by HILIC–cyclic-ion-mobility MS improved detection of 3-O-sulfated motifs in 2025 [E. Mernie et al. (2025), *Untangling Heparan Sulfate 3-O-Sulfation Using a Novel Offline Cationic-Peptide Affinity Enrichment, Followed by HILIC-cIM-MS*, DOI:10.1021/acs.analchem.4c05019]. However, absolute motif abundances still require recovery and selectivity corrections, so truly quantitative inventories remain out of reach.
solved_when: A method delivers absolute abundances of native 3-O-sulfated motifs with calibrated recovery and selectivity corrections across neighboring sulfate patterns and epimers, such that measured abundances are directly comparable rather than confounded by differential release, enrichment, or ionization.
why: It enables reliable comparison of rare but functionally important sulfation events across samples, which current uncorrected measurements cannot distinguish from analytical artifacts.
key_works: E. Mernie et al. (2025), *Untangling Heparan Sulfate 3-O-Sulfation Using a Novel Offline Cationic-Peptide Affinity Enrichment, Followed by HILIC-cIM-MS*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.analchem.4c05019](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.analchem.4c05019).

title: Native sialic-acid O-acetyl maps before migration
open: Can we measure the native distribution of O-acetyl groups across the C7, C8, and C9 positions of sialic acid side chains as it exists in the living sample, without the measurement itself scrambling it? Formally, this requires recovering the original biological C7/C8/C9 O-acetyl distribution while separately quantifying any migration induced during quenching, extraction, digestion, and analysis.
status: Reversible pH-dependent migration of the O-acetyl group within the sialic acid side chain was established in 2021 (Y. Ji et al., *Reversible O-Acetyl Migration within the Sialic Acid Side Chain and Its Influence on Protein Recognition*, [DOI:10.1021/acschembio.0c00998](https://doi.org/10.1021/acschembio.0c00998)), and positional and linkage assignment by ion-mobility MS followed in 2023 (G. M. Vos et al., *Sialic acid O-acetylation patterns and glycosidic linkage type determination by ion mobility-mass spectrometry*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-023-42575-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-42575-x)). Preservation of the original biological distribution remains a separate, unmet requirement.
solved_when: An experimental workflow yields the native C7/C8/C9 O-acetyl distribution together with a separate quantification of migration occurring during quenching, extraction, digestion, and analysis.
why: Without it, analytical rearrangement of the O-acetyl positions can masquerade as biological regulation, corrupting interpretation of sialic-acid-mediated recognition events.
key_works: Y. Ji et al. (2021), *Reversible O-Acetyl Migration within the Sialic Acid Side Chain and Its Influence on Protein Recognition*, [DOI:10.1021/acschembio.0c00998](https://doi.org/10.1021/acschembio.0c00998); G. M. Vos et al. (2023), *Sialic acid O-acetylation patterns and glycosidic linkage type determination by ion mobility-mass spectrometry*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-023-42575-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-42575-x).

title: Complete enzymatic release of structurally diverse O-glycans
open: Can we find enzymatic means to release intact mucin-type O-glycans across all eight cores and their common extensions from native proteins, without stripping informative terminal modifications? Formally, the target is a release workflow whose specificity spans the full core diversity while leaving sialylation and other terminal chemistry untouched.
status: The 2025 POGases broadened release to cores 1, 2 and 3 and selected sialylated structures (L. Zhou et al. (2025), *Dual functional POGases from bacteria encompassing broader O-glycanase and adhesin activities*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-57143-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-57143-8)). Native substrates remained harder than denatured ones; combined core coverage and accessibility remain unresolved.
solved_when: Intact O-glycans from all eight mucin-type cores and common extensions can be released from native (not denatured) protein substrates with terminal modifications preserved.
why: It removes the structural bias currently introduced before instrumental analysis, so downstream measurements reflect the glycan population as it exists rather than as the release chemistry allows.
key_works: L. Zhou et al. (2025), *Dual functional POGases from bacteria encompassing broader O-glycanase and adhesin activities*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-57143-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-57143-8).

title: Are wybutosine derivatives yW-72 and yW-86 glycoRNA attachment sites?
open: Do the wybutosine derivatives yW-72 and yW-86 carry covalently attached N-glycans in native glycoRNA? A satisfying answer requires direct proof of the linkage and its bond structure, ruling out indirect release or co-enrichment of glycans.
status: Xie et al. (2024) established acp³U as an attachment site for N-glycans in glycoRNA (DOI:10.1016/j.cell.2024.07.044). Their experiments also recovered carboxyl-containing yW derivatives, but direct linkage proof equivalent to that obtained for acp³U remains missing.
solved_when: The presence or absence of covalent N-glycans on native yW-72 and yW-86 is demonstrated with direct linkage evidence establishing the bond structure, and indirect release or co-enrichment is excluded.
why: A second confirmed attachment chemistry would show that RNA glycosylation is not limited to a single modification, reshaping how glycoRNA linkages are sought and characterized.
key_works: Xie et al. (2024), *The modified RNA base acp3U is an attachment site for N-glycans in glycoRNA*, [DOI:10.1016/j.cell.2024.07.044](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2024.07.044).

title: The enzyme that amidates acp³U before RNA N-glycosylation
open: Which enzyme converts the carboxyl group of acp³U into the carboxamide that RNA N-glycosylation requires, and can that conversion be reconstituted in vitro? Alternatively, is there a different route altogether by which the glycan linkage forms at this base?
status: The 2024 acp³U study explicitly proposes an unidentified amidating enzyme upstream of oligosaccharyltransferase; known genetic and transport dependencies do not identify that activity (Xie et al. (2024), *The modified RNA base acp3U is an attachment site for N-glycans in glycoRNA*, [DOI:10.1016/j.cell.2024.07.044](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2024.07.044)).
solved_when: The amidating enzyme acting on acp³U upstream of the oligosaccharyltransferase step is identified and its activity reconstituted, or an alternative linkage-forming route is experimentally established in its place.
why: It closes a missing chemical step in glycoRNA biosynthesis, without which the mechanism by which N-glycans attach to RNA remains incomplete.
key_works: Xie et al. (2024), *The modified RNA base acp3U is an attachment site for N-glycans in glycoRNA*, [DOI:10.1016/j.cell.2024.07.044](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2024.07.044).

title: Preventing delayed Cr(VI) rebound after reductive remediation
open: Can we predict, and ultimately prevent, the delayed regeneration of Cr(VI) as Cr–Fe hydroxide precipitates age toward goethite in the presence of manganese, oxygen, and shifting pH? The goal is an engineering strategy for reductive chromium remediation that stays effective through mineral transformation, not just at the moment of treatment.
status: A 2025 study by S. Xie et al. (2025) found approximately tenfold higher Cr(VI) release following mineral transformation of CrxFe1-x(OH)3 in the presence of Mn(II), identifying an overlooked process in the reoccurrence of Cr(VI) in reduced chromite ore processing residue (DOI:10.1016/j.envpol.2025.126327); long-term control across residue compositions remains open.
solved_when: A quantitative framework predicts Cr(VI) release during aging of CrxFe1-x(OH)3 across realistic residue compositions, and a demonstrated prevention method suppresses the roughly tenfold Cr(VI) release enhancement observed under the 2025 study's transformation conditions, holding reduced chromium immobilized over the long term.
why: Without control of this pathway, "successfully" reduced chromium residues can re-release toxic Cr(VI) years later, undermining the permanence of in-situ immobilization and the sites declared remediated.
key_works: S. Xie et al. (2025), *Enhanced oxidation of Cr(III) with the mineral transformation of CrxFe1-x(OH)3 in the presence of Mn(II): overlooked process during the reoccurrence of Cr(VI) in reduced chromite ore processing residue*, [DOI:10.1016/j.envpol.2025.126327](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.envpol.2025.126327).

title: Decoupling cement dispersion from hydrate-nucleation retardation
open: Can we design polymeric cement dispersants that reduce water demand without also delaying setting — that is, can the dispersion function be decoupled from retardation of hydrate nucleation? A satisfactory answer would let us predict a candidate dispersant's separate effects on tricalcium silicate dissolution, calcium-silicate-hydrate nucleation, and portlandite precipitation, including conditions near saturation.
status: Vohburger et al. (2025) showed that four polymers inhibited hydrate nucleation without measurable inhibition of dissolution under the undersaturated conditions tested; behavior near saturation and in mixed-clinker systems remains unresolved.
solved_when: A dispersant (or dispersant design rule) is demonstrated that lowers water demand while producing no unwanted setting delay, with quantitative predictions — validated experimentally — of its separate effects on dissolution, C–S–H nucleation, and portlandite precipitation under near-saturation conditions and with mixed clinkers.
why: It preserves early-age strength development while cutting the mixing water required, the central trade-off limiting modern concrete formulation.
key_works: A. Vohburger et al. (2025), *Influence of Polymeric Dispersants on the Dissolution Rate of Tricalcium Silicate and the Nucleation of Calcium-Silicate-Hydrate and Portlandite*, [DOI:10.1002/chem.202500207](https://doi.org/10.1002/chem.202500207).

title: Distinguishing dissolution-driven and rearrangement-driven cement creep
open: Which microscopic mechanism — stress-assisted dissolution and reprecipitation, sliding of hydrates, or continuing hydration — actually drives creep in cement paste, and can their individual contributions be separated and predicted as functions of humidity and mix composition?
status: The microscopic origin of cement creep remains debated. A 2025 study (J. Wang et al., *Does the hydration process of supplementary cementitious materials affect the aging creep of blended cement paste?*, [DOI:10.1016/j.cemconres.2025.107826](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cemconres.2025.107826)) found that continued fly-ash reaction increases creep while foil-like C-A-S-H in slag blends inhibits it; quantitative separation of the mechanisms remains open.
solved_when: A quantitative framework is available that decomposes the total creep into dissolution/reprecipitation, hydrate sliding, and continuing-hydration contributions, with verified predictions of each term's dependence on humidity and cement composition.
why: It would connect hydrate chemistry directly to long-term structural deformation, allowing blends to be designed for reduced creep rather than treating it as an empirical bulk property.
key_works: J. Wang et al. (2025), *Does the hydration process of supplementary cementitious materials affect the aging creep of blended cement paste?*, [DOI:10.1016/j.cemconres.2025.107826](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cemconres.2025.107826).

title: Predicting steel passivity after alkali-activated binder carbonation
open: Can we predict when embedded steel loses its passive film in alkali-activated binders as their pore solutions and hydrate assemblages evolve under carbonation, chloride exposure, and leaching? In formal terms, the goal is a model that tracks pH-buffering and chloride-binding chemistry well enough to forecast depassivation in these systems.
status: A 2025 calcined-clay/slag study by S. D. C. Gomes et al. (*Shrinkage and carbonation of alkali-activated calcined clay-ground granulated blast furnace slag (GGBFS) concrete*, [DOI:10.1016/j.cemconres.2025.107899](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cemconres.2025.107899)) observed no corrosion after the carbonation front reached the steel, consistent with retained high pH; conventional carbonation-front criteria therefore lack universal transferability.
solved_when: A chemically grounded criterion exists that correctly predicts steel passivity or depassivation as a function of the evolving pore-solution composition and hydrates during coupled carbonation, chloride exposure, and leaching, including cases where carbonation does not cause depassivation.
why: It would give chemically valid durability and service-life criteria for reinforced low-carbon concrete made with alternative binders, replacing front-based rules that fail to transfer.
key_works: S. D. C. Gomes et al. (2025), *Shrinkage and carbonation of alkali-activated calcined clay-ground granulated blast furnace slag (GGBFS) concrete*, [DOI:10.1016/j.cemconres.2025.107899](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cemconres.2025.107899).

title: Pair-specific RO₂ accretion branching beyond small radicals
open: Do self-reaction kinetics carry over to cross-reactions? The goal is to measure absolute rate constants and accretion-product yields for reactions between unlike, multifunctional peroxy (RO₂) radicals, and test whether rules derived from self-reactions predict these cross-reactions.
status: A 2025 study of small β-hydroxy RO₂ radicals (S. E. Murphy et al., 2025, *Accretion product formation in the self- and cross-reactions of small β-hydroxy peroxy radicals*, [DOI:10.1039/D5EA00106D](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5EA00106D)) measured accretion-channel rate constants spanning approximately \(4.7\times10^{-13}\) to \(8.0\times10^{-16}\) cm³ molecule⁻¹ s⁻¹. Complex atmospheric radicals remain inadequately covered.
solved_when: Absolute rate constants and accretion yields are measured for unlike multifunctional RO₂ pairs spanning the range relevant to complex atmospheric radicals, with a demonstrated test of whether self-reaction rules predict the cross-reaction outcomes.
why: Accretion branching controls the formation of low-volatility products and hence particle growth, ultimately influencing growth to cloud-condensation-nucleus sizes.
key_works: S. E. Murphy et al. (2025), *Accretion product formation in the self- and cross-reactions of small β-hydroxy peroxy radicals*, [DOI:10.1039/D5EA00106D](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5EA00106D).

title: Surface accretion of RO₂ on freshly nucleated particles
open: Can peroxy radicals (RO₂) actually accrete onto the surfaces of freshly nucleated sulfuric-acid/base nanoparticles, and how does that pathway compete with desorption and gas-phase reaction? The goal is a direct experimental test of RO₂ surface accretion at these nanoparticle interfaces under atmospherically relevant conditions.
status: A 2026 computational study (G. Hasan, T. Kurtén, I. Neefjes and J. Elm, *Can Accretion Products Be Formed at the Interface of Freshly Nucleated Particles?*, [DOI:10.1021/acsomega.5c13316](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsomega.5c13316)) identified rapid candidate pathways; particle-size-resolved experimental confirmation and demonstration of atmospheric-flux relevance remain missing.
solved_when: Peroxy-radical accretion at sulfuric-acid/base nanoparticle interfaces is directly measured in a particle-size-resolved experiment, quantifying its competition with desorption and gas-phase reaction and establishing its relevance to atmospheric fluxes.
why: A positive result would explain how organic material grows on particles immediately after nucleation, a critical early step in the survival of newly nucleated clusters.
key_works: G. Hasan, T. Kurtén, I. Neefjes and J. Elm (2026), *Can Accretion Products Be Formed at the Interface of Freshly Nucleated Particles?*, [DOI:10.1021/acsomega.5c13316](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsomega.5c13316).

title: Isomer-resolved organic-nitrate hydrolysis in concentrated aerosol
open: How do individual monoterpene-derived organic nitrate isomers hydrolyze, and what competing reactions do they undergo, inside concentrated aerosol particles where water activity is low? Specifically, what are the isomer-resolved hydrolysis rates as functions of acidity, ionic strength, and organic-matrix composition?
status: Seven synthesized standards studied in 2021 showed strongly structure-dependent minute-to-hour lifetimes, with some secondary nitrates resistant under neutral conditions (Y. Wang et al. 2021, *Synthesis and Hydrolysis of Atmospherically Relevant Monoterpene-Derived Organic Nitrates*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.est.1c05310](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.1c05310)). Actual aerosol matrices remain insufficiently characterized.
solved_when: Hydrolysis and competing reaction rates have been measured for individual monoterpene-nitrate isomers in low-water-activity aerosol, across varied acidity, ionic strength, and organic matrices, and real aerosol matrices are sufficiently characterized to place these laboratory kinetics in atmospheric context.
why: The isomer-resolved rates determine whether aerosol-phase organic nitrates act as a sink or recycle nitrogen oxides to the atmosphere, directly affecting models of NOx cycling and secondary organic aerosol.
key_works: Y. Wang et al. (2021), *Synthesis and Hydrolysis of Atmospherically Relevant Monoterpene-Derived Organic Nitrates*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.est.1c05310](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.1c05310).

title: Origin of unequal nitrate-aerosol yields from the two phellandrenes
open: Why do the two phellandrene isomers produce such different amounts of nitrate-derived aerosol when their gas-phase chemistry looks nearly the same — what particle-phase pathways account for the gap? Formally, identify the condensed-phase reactions that explain the α- versus β-phellandrene nitrate-oxidation yield difference, with resolved products closing both the carbon and nitrate balances.
status: A 2025 chamber study (S. Harb et al., *Highly oxygenated molecules (HOMs) and secondary organic aerosol (SOA) formation from the oxidation of α- and β-phellandrenes by NO3 radicals*, [DOI:10.5194/acp-25-11003-2025](https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-25-11003-2025)) found maximum aerosol yields near 35% and 60% for α- and β-phellandrene, respectively, despite similarities in the measured gas chemistry. The condensed-phase explanation remains incomplete.
solved_when: A mechanistic account of particle-phase pathways is identified that explains the divergence between the observed maximum aerosol yields of roughly 35% (α-phellandrene) and 60% (β-phellandrene), with resolved products closing the carbon and nitrate balances.
why: It determines how terpene structural differences should be represented in regional aerosol models, where getting the isomer dependence wrong would misstate secondary organic aerosol formation from vegetation emissions.
key_works: S. Harb et al. (2025), *Highly oxygenated molecules (HOMs) and secondary organic aerosol (SOA) formation from the oxidation of α- and β-phellandrenes by NO3 radicals*, [DOI:10.5194/acp-25-11003-2025](https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-25-11003-2025).

title: Reactive-solute control of aqueous HPMTF sulfur branching
open: Do the solutes actually present in marine clouds change how hydroperoxymethyl thioformate reacts in the aqueous phase and how its sulfur branches among products? Formally, the goal is to determine HPMTF's aqueous reaction mechanisms and product branching under realistic cloud-solute conditions, closing both the sulfur and carbon balances.
status: A 2024 laboratory experiment (C. M. Jernigan et al. 2024, *Sulfate and Carbonyl Sulfide Production in Aqueous Reactions of Hydroperoxymethyl Thioformate*, [DOI:10.1021/acsestair.3c00098](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsestair.3c00098)) found sulfate consistent with unit yield and carbonyl sulfide below 1.2%, but in effect under solute-free conditions; 2025 field observations (D. B. Kilgour et al. 2025, [DOI:10.5194/acp-25-1931-2025](https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-25-1931-2025)) confirmed substantial cloud removal of DMS oxidation products in the eastern North Atlantic marine boundary layer. Whether realistic solutes alter the mechanisms and branching remains unresolved.
solved_when: HPMTF aqueous reactions have been characterized in the presence of realistic cloud solutes, with product yields reported and full closed sulfur and carbon balances, resolving whether solute-dependent chemistry alters the branching seen in pure water (sulfate consistent with unit yield; carbonyl sulfide below 1.2%).
why: The outcome directly links marine dimethyl sulfide oxidation to atmospheric sulfate aerosol and carbonyl sulfide budgets, and constrains how much cloud processing limits SO2 and OCS production.
key_works: C. M. Jernigan et al. (2024), *Sulfate and Carbonyl Sulfide Production in Aqueous Reactions of Hydroperoxymethyl Thioformate*, [DOI:10.1021/acsestair.3c00098](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsestair.3c00098); D. B. Kilgour et al. (2025), *Cloud processing of dimethyl sulfide (DMS) oxidation products limits sulfur dioxide (SO2) and carbonyl sulfide (OCS) production in the eastern North Atlantic marine boundary layer*, [DOI:10.5194/acp-25-1931-2025](https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-25-1931-2025).

title: Chemical origin of nitryl chloride emitted during automotive braking
open: Where does the chlorine in nitryl chloride emitted during automotive braking come from, and what chemistry produces it? Specifically, identify the chloride sources and reaction sequences that generate braking-associated ClNO₂, distinguishing new tribochemical formation from the release of pre-existing material.
status: HONO, ClNO₂ and N₂O₅ were detected during braking in 2025 (M. E. Cooke et al., *Emissions of Nitrous Acid, Nitryl Chloride, and Dinitrogen Pentoxide Associated with Automotive Braking*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.est.4c13202](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.4c13202)). Precursor inventories and a closed nitryl-chloride production mechanism remain unresolved.
solved_when: The chloride sources feeding braking-associated ClNO₂ are identified and a closed, validated production mechanism is established that accounts for the observed emissions of HONO, ClNO₂, and N₂O₅ during braking.
why: It reveals reactive gas emissions that particle-mass-based emission inventories currently omit, a prerequisite for chemically complete non-exhaust vehicle emission accounting.
key_works: M. E. Cooke et al. (2025), *Emissions of Nitrous Acid, Nitryl Chloride, and Dinitrogen Pentoxide Associated with Automotive Braking*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.est.4c13202](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.4c13202).

title: Identity of the mid-polarity Pacific iron-binding ligand group
open: What are the unidentified mid-polarity iron-binding compounds detected along the Pacific GP15 transect, and how do they behave chemically? A satisfying answer would isolate these putative siderophores and establish their structures, binding affinities, and degradation pathways.
status: A 2025 survey (Li, Babcock-Adams, McIlvin and Repeta, *Distribution and Cycling of Siderophores in the Eastern North and Tropical Pacific Oceans*, DOI:10.1029/2024GL113874) found unresolved putative siderophores in upper-mesopelagic tropical waters, but coelution prevented confident molecular-ion and formula assignments.
solved_when: The mid-polarity iron-binding ligand group is isolated from GP15 samples with confident molecular-ion and formula assignments, and its structures, iron-binding affinities, and degradation pathways are determined.
why: Converts a recurrent oceanographic signal into an interpretable transport mechanism for subsurface iron cycling and nutrient limitation.
key_works: J. Li, L. Babcock-Adams, M. R. McIlvin and D. J. Repeta (2025), *Distribution and Cycling of Siderophores in the Eastern North and Tropical Pacific Oceans*, [DOI:10.1029/2024GL113874](https://doi.org/10.1029/2024GL113874).

title: Identity of non-cobalamin cobalt-binding ligands in the surface ocean
open: What chemical compounds bind cobalt strongly in the surface ocean besides the cobalamins, and where do they come from biologically? A complete answer should identify these non-cobalamin ligands, their cobalt oxidation states, and the organisms or processes that produce them.
status: A 2025 North Pacific study (J. Park et al., *Efficient cobalamin uptake and cycling contribute to the lack of cobalamins in the surface cobalt-binding ligand pool in the North Pacific*, DOI:10.1002/lol2.70019) measured approximately 31–87 pM dissolved cobalt without detecting cobalamin-related compounds in the corresponding strong-ligand pool; the remaining ligand structures are unknown.
solved_when: The dominant strong cobalt-binding ligands in the surface ocean are structurally identified (including the oxidation state of bound cobalt), and at least their principal biological sources are established.
why: Without knowing the ligand identities, we cannot explain how scarce dissolved cobalt is stabilized against scavenging or how it is exchanged among marine microbes that compete for it.
key_works: J. Park et al. (2025), *Efficient cobalamin uptake and cycling contribute to the lack of cobalamins in the surface cobalt-binding ligand pool in the North Pacific*, [DOI:10.1002/lol2.70019](https://doi.org/10.1002/lol2.70019).

title: Mechanisms converting dimethylmercury into monomethylmercury at depth
open: By what mechanisms is dimethylmercury converted to monomethylmercury in waters below the strongly illuminated surface layer, and how fast do these pathways proceed? The goal is direct, pathway-specific measurements of these conversion reactions at depth, obtained independently of fitting concentration profiles.
status: A 2024 study of a highly productive upwelling system (H. M. Adams, X. Cui, C. H. Lamborg and A. T. Schartup, *Dimethylmercury as a Source of Monomethylmercury in a Highly Productive Upwelling System*, DOI:10.1021/acs.est.4c01112) inferred a net dimethylmercury loss of \(2.0\pm1.1\%\) per day from field profiles and mass-budget modeling; direct pathway-specific field rates remain unresolved.
solved_when: Conversion pathways below the surface layer are identified and their in-situ rates directly measured, without reliance on concentration-profile fitting or mass-budget modeling.
why: It would explain how monomethylmercury — the form that bioaccumulates in marine food webs — is produced away from its immediate primary formation sites.
key_works: H. M. Adams, X. Cui, C. H. Lamborg and A. T. Schartup (2024), *Dimethylmercury as a Source of Monomethylmercury in a Highly Productive Upwelling System*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.est.4c01112](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.est.4c01112).

title: Chemical evolution and self-limiting growth of ZDDP tribofilms
open: Can we predict how zinc dialkyldithiophosphate (ZDDP) tribofilms evolve chemically and physically — phosphate-chain chemistry, film growth, and film removal — under realistic, changing contact stresses, and identify the chemical feedbacks that cause growth to self-limit at a finite thickness?
status: A 2023 study (L. Fang et al., *What stress components drive mechanochemistry? A study of ZDDP tribofilm formation*, [DOI:10.1039/D2FD00123C](https://doi.org/10.1039/D2FD00123C)) separated shear-promoted growth from compression-induced inhibition, but a complete growth–conversion–removal network for service contacts remains missing.
solved_when: A model exists that captures the coupled growth–conversion–removal network under varying stress histories and reproduces the observed self-limiting film thickness for service-relevant contacts.
why: It would let engines maintain wear protection while consuming less additive, and enable wear-lifetime prediction from contact histories.
key_works: L. Fang et al. (2023), *What stress components drive mechanochemistry? A study of ZDDP tribofilm formation*, [DOI:10.1039/D2FD00123C](https://doi.org/10.1039/D2FD00123C).

title: Native structure of soluble methane monooxygenase intermediate Q
open: What is the true structure of intermediate Q in soluble methane monooxygenase — is its diiron core open or diamond? A determination must fix the Fe–O connectivity, the protonation state, and the Fe–Fe distance, consistently reconciling vibrational, X-ray, and magnetic spectra measured on the same intermediate population.
status: The question has been debated for over 30 years. A 2021 QM/MM study by C. E. Schulz et al. (*Structure–Spectroscopy Correlations for Intermediate Q of Soluble Methane Monooxygenase: Insights from QM/MM Calculations*, [DOI:10.1021/jacs.1c01180](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.1c01180)) favors an open core, but complete experimental discrimination from diamond-core assignments remains unresolved.
solved_when: A single structural assignment for Q is established that simultaneously explains the vibrational, X-ray, and magnetic spectroscopic data from the same intermediate population, resolving the open-core versus diamond-core dispute.
why: It would reveal how a biological diiron center achieves the activation of methane at ambient conditions, a reaction central to understanding and potentially engineering alkane-oxidizing enzymes.
key_works: C. E. Schulz et al. (2021), *Structure–Spectroscopy Correlations for Intermediate Q of Soluble Methane Monooxygenase: Insights from QM/MM Calculations*, [DOI:10.1021/jacs.1c01180](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.1c01180).

title: Substrate coordination in catalytically active methyl-coenzyme M reductase
open: How does the methyl-SCoM substrate bind at the active Ni(I) site of methyl-coenzyme M reductase as the C–S bond is cleaved? In formal terms, which coordination mode — nickel–sulfonate binding or a sulfur-coordinated alternative — persists in the catalytically active enzyme through the cleavage step?
status: A 2021 study by A. Patwardhan et al. supports nickel–sulfonate binding ([DOI:10.1021/jacs.1c01086](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.1c01086)), and 2025 atomic structures by M.-C. Müller et al. add constraints ([DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-63387-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-63387-1)); however, a native active-state trajectory from substrate to radical remains missing.
solved_when: The coordination geometry of methyl-SCoM at the active Ni(I) center is experimentally determined through the C–S cleavage step, clearly discriminating nickel–sulfonate binding from sulfur-coordinated alternatives.
why: It fixes the geometry that enables methane formation and its reversal, and thereby constrains the mechanism of biological methane production and anaerobic methane oxidation.
key_works: A. Patwardhan et al. (2021), *Nickel–Sulfonate Mode of Substrate Binding for Forward and Reverse Reactions of Methyl-SCoM Reductase Suggest a Radical Mechanism Involving Long-Range Electron Transfer*, [DOI:10.1021/jacs.1c01086](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.1c01086); M.-C. Müller et al. (2025), [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-63387-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-63387-1).

title: Functions of the unusual modifications in methane-oxidizing MCR
open: What does each unusual post-translational modification in methane-oxidizing methyl-coenzyme M reductase (MCR) actually do? Formally, the aim is to assign the causal effect of individual modifications on methane activation, cofactor stability, and catalytic directionality through controlled modification states and kinetic measurements.
status: Atomic-resolution structures of ANME-2c/2d MCR published in 2025 (M.-C. Müller et al., *Nat. Commun.*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-63387-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-63387-1)) revealed extensive post-translational modifications, but the individual chemical functions of these modifications remain unassigned.
solved_when: Each modification identified in the atomic-resolution ANME-2c/2d MCR structures has an experimentally assigned causal role in methane activation, cofactor stability, or directionality, demonstrated via controlled modification states and kinetics.
why: It identifies the maturation functions required when transferring the methane-oxidation machinery into other hosts, a prerequisite for synthetic deployment of anaerobic methanotrophy.
key_works: M.-C. Müller et al. (2025), *Atomic resolution structures of the methane-activating enzyme in anaerobic methanotrophy reveal extensive post-translational modifications*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-63387-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-63387-1).

title: Electron accounting during ACS thioester release
open: Determine whether native acetyl-CoA release uses oxidation-triggered nickel chemistry, tracking the transferred electron through enzyme reset.
status: One-electron oxidation accelerated thioester elimination approximately 1,800-fold in a 2025 model [S. Nath, L. Griego and L. M. Mirica (2025), *The mechanism of acetyl-CoA synthase through the lens of a nickel model system*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-60163-z]. The corresponding native oxidation sequence remains unverified.
solved_when: The native oxidation sequence is experimentally verified (or ruled out), with the transferred electron followed through enzyme reset; success would be signalled by native thioester elimination showing the same oxidation-triggered acceleration seen in the model.
why: Discriminates mechanisms with different electron-donor and cofactor requirements.
key_works: S. Nath, L. Griego and L. M. Mirica (2025), *The mechanism of acetyl-CoA synthase through the lens of a nickel model system*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-60163-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-60163-z).

title: Carrier of the 6614 Å diffuse interstellar band
open: What molecule in the interstellar medium gives rise to the diffuse interstellar band at 6614 Å? A successful identification must reproduce not only the band's laboratory wavelength but also its substructure and the way its profile changes with environment, under a chemically plausible route to formation and survival in interstellar space.
status: The carrier remains unassigned. A 2025 oblate-top fit (C. Bhatt et al. 2025, *The EDIBLES Survey IX*, [DOI:10.1021/acsearthspacechem.4c00238](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsearthspacechem.4c00238)) suggests roughly 54 carbon atoms under that model, but competing geometric interpretations remain possible; see also H. MacIsaac et al. 2022, [DOI:10.1051/0004-6361/202142225](https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202142225).
solved_when: A specific carrier molecule is identified whose laboratory spectrum matches the 6614 Å band in wavelength and substructure, and whose behavior accounts for the observed environmental profile variations, with a viable mechanism for interstellar formation and survival.
why: It would identify a major molecular population hidden from rotational surveys, opening a window into carbon chemistry in diffuse clouds.
key_works: C. Bhatt et al. (2025), *The EDIBLES Survey IX: Simulations of the λ6614 DIB Profile Variations: A Surprising Connection with CH⁺*, [DOI:10.1021/acsearthspacechem.4c00238](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsearthspacechem.4c00238); H. MacIsaac et al. (2022), [DOI:10.1051/0004-6361/202142225](https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202142225).

title: Carrier of the 6379 Å diffuse interstellar band
open: What molecule absorbs the 6379 Å diffuse interstellar band? An answer must account for the band's rotational substructure and how its excitation changes, and must break the degeneracy between linear and approximately spherical carrier geometries.
status: A 2022 contour analysis by H. MacIsaac et al. yields geometry-dependent rotational constants; the spherical interpretation implies roughly 77–114 carbons, and no molecular formula is securely assigned.
solved_when: A specific molecular carrier is securely assigned, with the assignment reproducing the observed rotational substructure and excitation behavior, and resolving whether the geometry is linear or approximately spherical (the latter implying roughly 77–114 carbons).
why: It separates chemical families that produce nearly identical astronomical band profiles, turning a spectral fingerprint into a tool for identifying interstellar molecule classes.
key_works: H. MacIsaac et al. (2022), *The EDIBLES survey V: Line profile variations in the λλ5797, 6379, and 6614 diffuse interstellar bands as a tool to constrain carrier sizes*, [DOI:10.1051/0004-6361/202142225](https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202142225); [arXiv:2203.01803](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.01803).

title: First identified optical transitions of neutral lawrencium
open: Can any optical transition of neutral lawrencium be observed and spectroscopically assigned, so that its level structure can be measured and used to test the predicted relativistic valence configurations of the final actinide element?
status: The 2026 search scanned approximately 800 cm⁻¹ around each of two predicted strong transitions without detecting either. The experiment demonstrated efficient evaporation and sufficient sensitivity, leaving the transition locations or excitation assumptions unresolved (E. Rickert et al. (2026), "Progress toward identifying atomic transitions in lawrencium," [DOI: 10.1140/epjd/s10053-026-01198-9](https://doi.org/10.1140/epjd/s10053-026-01198-9)).
solved_when: A neutral-lawrencium optical transition is detected and its assignment established, with the resulting level structure compared against the predicted relativistic valence configurations.
why: It supplies direct electronic-level evidence for the final actinide, anchoring tests of relativistic orbital ordering in the heaviest elements.
key_works: E. Rickert et al. (2026), “Progress toward identifying atomic transitions in lawrencium,” [DOI: 10.1140/epjd/s10053-026-01198-9](https://doi.org/10.1140/epjd/s10053-026-01198-9).

title: Radium-223 chelation that survives tracer-level dilution in serum
open: Can we build a molecular chelate that holds radium-223 in a form suitable for targeted delivery — that is, a Ra(II) complex that stays intact after dilution into serum at tracer concentration? The problem is to demonstrate, over the intended delivery interval and in every analytical fraction, that the complex survives without relying on excess free ligand to recapture dissociated radium.
status: A 2026 screen (Southwell, Gumiela et al., DOI: 10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c04877) achieved quantitative room-temperature labeling with 14 of 17 chelators, but even macropa dissociated within one hour at higher dilution; apparently favorable size-exclusion results could conceal free radium.
solved_when: A molecular Ra(II) chelate is shown to remain intact after tracer-level dilution into serum, with analysis that distinguishes intact complex from free radium in every fraction and rules out artifacts (e.g., apparently favorable size-exclusion results concealing free radium), over the intended delivery interval and without excess free ligand recapturing dissociated radium.
why: It would enable targeted radium delivery beyond radium's natural bone-seeking behavior, controlling off-target alpha dose in nuclear medicine.
key_works: J. W. Southwell, M. Gumiela et al. (2026), “Synthesis, Characterization, and Evaluation of Chelators for Radium-223,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c04877](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c04877).

title: Does a transient cyclic astatinane protect ortho-substituted aryl–At bonds?
open: Does an ortho benzyl-alcohol group protect aryl–astatine bonds by forming a transient cyclic astatinane intermediate when the astatine is oxidized? The goal is to detect or rule out this intramolecular arylalkoxyastatinane and to quantify how much it contributes to the observed resistance of the C–At bond to cleavage.
status: In 2025, ortho alcohols were shown to improve resistance of aryl–At compounds to both chemical and microsomal oxidation (Fouinneteau, Maingueneau, Galland, Perrio, and Guérard, "Ortho-functionalization of a 211At-labeled aryl compound provides stabilization of the C-At bond against oxidative dehalogenation," DOI: 10.1038/s41598-025-01162-4). However, the hypothesized cyclic intermediate could not be observed, and steric shielding alone failed to explain the chemical-oxidation results.
solved_when: The proposed cyclic intermediate is either directly observed or conclusively excluded, and its contribution to suppressed C–At oxidative cleavage is quantified.
why: It would convert an effective stabilization motif into a transferable mechanism for designing metabolically robust astatine radiolabels.
key_works: R. Fouinneteau, C. Maingueneau, N. Galland, C. Perrio, and F. Guérard (2025), “Ortho-functionalization of a 211At-labeled aryl compound provides stabilization of the C-At bond against oxidative dehalogenation,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41598-025-01162-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-01162-4).

title: Unidentified cleavage products of lead–TCMC thiourea bioconjugates
open: What radioactive metabolites form when the thiourea linker in Pb–TCMC bioconjugates breaks down, and what serum components drive that cleavage? In particular, distinguish experimentally between cleavage of the linker itself and loss of the radiometal from the chelator.
status: A 2025/2026 study by B. L. McNeil et al. (2026; online 2025), "Is Thiourea the Weak Link? An Investigation of the In Vitro and In Vivo Destabilization of [203Pb]- and [212Pb]Pb2+ Thiourea-Based Bioconjugates" [DOI: 10.1021/acsbiomedchemau.5c00224](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsbiomedchemau.5c00224), found similar degradation products for FAPI and CycMSH conjugates, and showed that amide replacements improved stability. Attempts to identify the products using nonradioactive lead and LC–MS hit sensitivity limits, leaving the products' identities and formation mechanisms unresolved.
solved_when: The degradation products of Pb–TCMC thiourea conjugates are identified (including the serum components responsible and the formation mechanism), clearly separating linker cleavage from radiometal loss from the intact chelator.
why: Without this, intact metal chelation can be mistaken for an intact targeting molecule, corrupting interpretation of biodistribution and stability data for these radiopharmaceuticals.
key_works: B. L. McNeil et al. (2026; online 2025), “Is Thiourea the Weak Link? An Investigation of the In Vitro and In Vivo Destabilization of [203Pb]- and [212Pb]Pb2+ Thiourea-Based Bioconjugates,” [DOI: 10.1021/acsbiomedchemau.5c00224](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsbiomedchemau.5c00224).

title: Competitive-ligand boundary for loss of protactinium’s mono-oxo bond
open: Where exactly, in composition space, does the persistent mono-oxo bond of protactinium(V) give way to non-oxo species when chloride, fluoride, and other acidic media compete for the metal? A solution would map the species fractions of mono-oxo versus non-oxo Pa(V) complexes across the full composition boundary.
status: A 2026 study established a roughly 1.83 Å Pa–O bond persisting even in highly acidic chloride solution (M. Maloubier et al. (2026; online 2025), "Persistent Mono-Oxo Bonding with Protactinium(V) Revealed in Highly Acidic Chloride Solutions," DOI: 10.1002/anie.202518403). Its persistence with competing ligands remains unresolved; acidity alone does not provide the missing speciation rule.
solved_when: The boundary in mixed chloride/fluoride and other competing acidic media is determined compositionally, with measured species fractions of mono-oxo and non-oxo Pa(V) complexes on either side of it.
why: It would make protactinium chemistry predictable across changes of medium, replacing the observation that acidity alone does not govern speciation with an actual rule.
key_works: M. Maloubier et al. (2026; online 2025), “Persistent Mono-Oxo Bonding with Protactinium(V) Revealed in Highly Acidic Chloride Solutions,” [DOI: 10.1002/anie.202518403](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202518403).

title: Resolving inverse trans influence in a Pa(V) solution complex
open: Can the trans and cis Pa–Cl distances in the protactinium(V) mono-oxo chloride complex be measured apart experimentally, rather than inferred from a fitted calculated geometry? In other words, can the predicted inverse trans influence — a shortening of the Pa–Cl bond trans to the oxo group — be confirmed by direct observation?
status: The 2026 analysis (M. Maloubier et al. 2026; online 2025, “Persistent Mono-Oxo Bonding with Protactinium(V) Revealed in Highly Acidic Chloride Solutions,” DOI: 10.1002/anie.202518403) predicts trans-bond shortening of 0.04–0.08 Å; that difference falls within the EXAFS uncertainty and has not been resolved experimentally.
solved_when: An experimental method resolves the trans vs. cis Pa–Cl distance difference independently of any fitted calculated geometry, at a precision sufficient to distinguish the predicted 0.04–0.08 Å trans-bond shortening, which currently lies within the EXAFS uncertainty.
why: It would test a directional-bonding prediction for an exceptionally data-poor actinide, and demonstrate a route to resolving small structural differences without imposing the answer through the model.
key_works: M. Maloubier et al. (2026; online 2025), “Persistent Mono-Oxo Bonding with Protactinium(V) Revealed in Highly Acidic Chloride Solutions,” [DOI: 10.1002/anie.202518403](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202518403).

title: Isolation of a molecular promethium(II) complex
open: Can a molecular complex of divalent promethium, Pm(II), be isolated as a stable compound? The target is a complex whose metal-centered reduction and coordination geometry are established independently, ruling out ligand-radical alternatives.
status: Anderson-Sanchez's 2024 dissertation identifies Pm as the missing radioactive member of the molecular divalent-lanthanide series. The 2024 aqueous Pm–diglycolamide structure establishes Pm(III), leaving divalent isolation as a distinct target.
solved_when: A molecular Pm(II) complex is isolated and characterized, with evidence demonstrating that the reduction is metal-centered and determining the coordination geometry, to the exclusion of ligand-radical interpretations.
why: It supplies a missing test of how electronic configuration and ligand symmetry control lanthanide reduction, completing the molecular divalent-lanthanide series with its sole radioactive member.
key_works: L. M. Anderson-Sanchez (2024), “Understanding the Role of Steric Factors in the Successful Isolation of Low Oxidation State Lanthanide and Actinide Complexes,” [doctoral dissertation](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/0nz1t51t); D. M. Driscoll et al. (2024), “Observation of a promethium complex in solution,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41586-024-07267-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07267-6).

title: Site-resolved explanation of flerovium’s two adsorption populations
open: What causes flerovium atoms to split into two distinct adsorption populations when they land on gold? A site-resolved account is needed that quantifies the separate contributions of weak terrace adsorption, surface diffusion, and trapping at rare active sites, using characterized surfaces and independently testable kinetic predictions.
status: A 2022 study by A. Yakushev et al. (“On the adsorption and reactivity of element 114, flerovium,” DOI: 10.3389/fchem.2022.976635) reconciled contrasting adsorption observations using inhomogeneous surfaces and a proposed two-stage mechanism, but experimental discrimination of the individual adsorption states remains unresolved.
solved_when: An experiment on characterized gold surfaces separately identifies each adsorption state — terrace adsorption, diffusion-mediated transport, and trapping at active sites — with quantified contributions to flerovium deposition that pass independent kinetic tests.
why: It would separate flerovium's intrinsic chemical reactivity from artifacts of the detector's microscopic surface structure, which is essential for drawing any conclusion about the element itself.
key_works: A. Yakushev et al. (2022), “On the adsorption and reactivity of element 114, flerovium,” [DOI: 10.3389/fchem.2022.976635](https://doi.org/10.3389/fchem.2022.976635).

title: Direct chemical-form verification of chromatographed nihonium and moscovium
open: Are the superheavy atoms of nihonium and moscovium, after gas-chromatographic transport and adsorption, actually deposited as neutral atoms, as ions, or as compounds formed with trace impurities? A direct, mass-sensitive determination of the adsorbed species' molecular identity — connected explicitly to the measured chromatogram — would settle the question.
status: The 2024 gas-chromatography experiment measured adsorption-enthalpy magnitudes near 58 and 54 kJ/mol and supported atomic assignments only computationally (A. Yakushev et al. 2024, [DOI: 10.3389/fchem.2024.1474820](https://doi.org/10.3389/fchem.2024.1474820)). A stronger proposed test is direct mass-sensitive identification, a technique developed for other heavy elements in 2025 (F. H. Garcia et al. 2025, [DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpca.5c02098](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpca.5c02098)), which has not yet been applied to Nh/Mc.
solved_when: The chemical form (atom, ion, or impurity compound) of the transported and adsorbed Nh/Mc species is directly verified, and the measured chromatogram is shown to follow from that identified species rather than from a computationally assumed atomic identity.
why: It would make the apparent relativistic reactivity trends in these elements independent of any assumed chemical identity, so conclusions about relativistic effects rest on measured species rather than model assignments.
key_works: A. Yakushev et al. (2024), “Manifestation of relativistic effects in the chemical properties of nihonium and moscovium revealed by gas chromatography studies,” [DOI: 10.3389/fchem.2024.1474820](https://doi.org/10.3389/fchem.2024.1474820); F. H. Garcia et al. (2025), “Atom-at-a-Time Radioactive Molecule Identification: Looking toward Studies of Superheavy Elements,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.jpca.5c02098](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpca.5c02098).

title: Does oxygen-bound seaborgium hexaisocarbonyl exist as a metastable molecule?
open: Can a seaborgium center bind six carbon monoxide ligands through their oxygen ends — Sg(OC)₆ — and survive as a metastable molecule? Formally, is the oxygen-bound isomer a genuine local minimum on the potential-energy surface once electron correlation, spin–orbit coupling, and vibrational effects are fully included, and if so, how long does it live before isomerizing to the carbon-bound form?
status: A 2023 Dirac–Fock/Breit–Gaunt study by G. L. Malli ("Relativistic and magnetic Breit effects for the reaction Sg + 6CO → Sg(CO)6 and Sg(OC)6: Prediction of the existence and atomization energy of the isomer Sg(OC)6," DOI: 10.1063/5.0152081) predicted the existence of the oxygen-bound isomer while finding Sg(CO)₆ to be more stable. The study reports an optimized octahedral structure and a favorable atomization energy, but leaves the question of kinetic survival unresolved.
