solved_when: A quantum-chemical treatment including correlation, spin–orbit, and vibrational effects either rules out Sg(OC)₆ as a local minimum or establishes its metastability, together with an estimate of its isomerization lifetime and, if viable, a distinguishing experimental signature.
why: It probes whether unusual ligand connectivity can persist at the relativistic edge of coordination chemistry, where superheavy elements defy trends extrapolated from their lighter homologues.
key_works: G. L. Malli (2023), “Relativistic and magnetic Breit effects for the reaction Sg + 6CO → Sg(CO)6 and Sg(OC)6: Prediction of the existence and atomization energy of the isomer Sg(OC)6,” [DOI: 10.1063/5.0152081](https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0152081).

title: Complete ligand identities of native nonpertechnetate tank-waste species
open: What chemical species actually carry the "nonpertechnetate" technetium in untreated alkaline Hanford tank waste — that is, what ligands coordinate each low-valent technetium fraction and what are their molecular structures? A complete answer should also quantify how sample handling and processing alter these species before measurement.
status: Measurements on AN-102 waste identified Tc(I) carbonyl and Tc(IV) species in 2020 [S. Chatterjee et al. (2020), "Identification and Quantification of Technetium Species in Hanford Waste Tank AN-102," DOI: 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c02864], and a 2024 study of AP-105/AP-107 waste added Tc(VI) [R. M. Asmussen et al. (2024), "The simultaneous removal of technetium and iodine from Hanford tank waste," DOI: 10.1016/j.cej.2024.151449]. Beyond these oxidation-state assignments, positive identification of the resin-interacting and unretained species remains incomplete.
solved_when: The coordination ligands and molecular structures of the low-valent technetium fractions in untreated tank waste are assigned, and the transformations introduced by sample processing are quantified — including positive identification of both the resin-interacting and the unretained species, beyond mere oxidation-state assignments.
why: It enables treatment of the technetium species that escape pertechnetate-specific capture in the waste-processing flowsheet.
key_works: S. Chatterjee et al. (2020), “Identification and Quantification of Technetium Species in Hanford Waste Tank AN-102,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.analchem.0c02864](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.analchem.0c02864); R. M. Asmussen et al. (2024), “The simultaneous removal of technetium and iodine from Hanford tank waste,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.cej.2024.151449](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cej.2024.151449).

title: AmSel selectivity through repeated accumulation of TODGA degradation products
open: Can Am/Cm selectivity in the AmSel process be predicted and sustained as the TODGA solvent is reused and its degradation products accumulate? The goal is a quantitative account of which fragments build up over repeated cycles and how each contributes to metal binding and stripping behavior.
status: A 2025 study by Vacas-Arquero, Sánchez-García, and Galán examined individual and combined TODGA degradation products and adjustments to stripping conditions in the AmSel process [DOI: 10.1016/j.pnucene.2025.105677](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pnucene.2025.105677). Long-run closure of degradation, regeneration, and selectivity remains a proposed systems extension.
solved_when: A model validated against measurement predicts Am/Cm separation over repeated solvent reuse cycles, including the accumulated concentrations of each TODGA degradation fragment and each fragment's individual metal-binding contribution.
why: It would make extractant radiation resistance meaningful over a full process lifetime rather than a single-cycle property, turning degradation chemistry into a controllable system parameter.
key_works: P. Vacas-Arquero, I. Sánchez-García, and H. Galán (2025), “Influence of the accumulation of TODGA degradation compounds in the separation of Americium from Curium by the AmSel process,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.pnucene.2025.105677](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.pnucene.2025.105677).

title: Predicting methyl-iodide capture by chemically aged silver mordenite
open: Can the breakthrough performance of silver mordenite for methyl-iodide capture be predicted from the measured populations of metallic silver, exchanged Ag(I), and nitrate species present after a given NOₓ/moisture exposure history? A successful theory would map each chemical state to its iodine-capture contribution and aggregate these into a state-to-breakthrough prediction.
status: A 2020 study (A. I. Wiechert et al., DOI: 10.1021/acsami.0c15456) identified oxidation and inward silver migration upon aging, with nitrates carrying up to 95% of capacity in well-aged samples. A 2024 study (H. Goettsche et al., DOI: 10.1007/s10450-024-00473-8) adds moisture and storage effects. Prospective state-to-breakthrough prediction remains open.
solved_when: A validated model predicts breakthrough curves for methyl iodide on chemically aged silver mordenite directly from quantified populations of metallic silver, exchanged Ag(I), and nitrate species arising from specified NOₓ/moisture histories, with prospective (not retrospective) predictive accuracy demonstrated.
why: It replaces fresh-sorbent capacity assumptions with chemically informed lifetime prediction, so capture performance can be forecast over an adsorbent's actual aging history rather than assumed from its initial state.
key_works: H. Goettsche et al. (2024), “Effects of moisture and aging upon decomposition of methyl iodide by reduced silver mordenite,” [DOI: 10.1007/s10450-024-00473-8](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10450-024-00473-8); A. I. Wiechert et al. (2020), “Capture of Iodine from Nuclear-Fuel-Reprocessing Off-Gas: Influence of Aging on a Reduced Silver Mordenite Adsorbent after Exposure to NO/NO2,” [DOI: 10.1021/acsami.0c15456](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsami.0c15456).

title: Origin of humidity inhibition in methyl-iodide decomposition on silver mordenite
open: Is the humidity inhibition of methyl-iodide decomposition on silver mordenite caused by water blocking reactant adsorption, or by product species that remain on the catalyst and limit the rate? If retained products control the rate, they should be identified and their desorption kinetics measured.
status: 2024 experiments found approximately 30% slower apparent decomposition under humid conditions (H. Goettsche et al. 2024, DOI: 10.1007/s10450-024-00473-8). Goettsche's 2025 dissertation leaves the rate-limiting step and practical working capacity unresolved because catalytic conversion can obscure iodine retention.
solved_when: The rate-limiting step under humid conditions is experimentally identified, and either adsorption blocking is confirmed or the retained product species are identified with measured desorption kinetics.
why: Without knowing the limiting step, disappearance of CH₃I cannot be interpreted as a measure of true conversion versus iodine capture, since catalytic conversion can obscure iodine retention.
key_works: H. Goettsche et al. (2024), “Effects of moisture and aging upon decomposition of methyl iodide by reduced silver mordenite,” [DOI: 10.1007/s10450-024-00473-8](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10450-024-00473-8); H. Goettsche (2025), “Investigations into methyl iodide adsorption and decomposition on reduced silver mordenite,” [doctoral dissertation](https://verso.uidaho.edu/esploro/outputs/doctoral/Investigations-into-methyl-iodide-adsorption-and/996825066201851).

title: The nickel hydride behind additive-switched silylene–Ni hydrosilylation
open: What is the active nickel species that nBuLi generates from the bis(silylene)-pincer Ni(II) chloride precursor, and is it a nickel hydride? In particular, does an intact pincer-bound Ni–H account for the Markovnikov selectivity observed under those conditions?
status: A 2026 paper reports opposite regioselectivity with nBuLi versus KOtBu and suggests a nickel hydride as the active catalyst under the former conditions, without establishing its structure or abundance (Z. Yang et al. (2026), "Additive-controlled selective hydrosilylation of aryl alkenes catalyzed by bis(silylene) pincer nickel(II) chloride," [DOI: 10.1039/D5NJ03998C](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5NJ03998C)).
solved_when: The catalyst arising under nBuLi conditions is identified with its structure and relative abundance established experimentally, and the origin of the Markovnikov selectivity is attributed (or not) to an intact pincer-bound Ni–H species.
why: It distinguishes ligand-controlled selectivity from additive-induced catalyst reconstruction, determining whether the pincer ligand or the additive is the true selectivity switch.
key_works: Z. Yang et al. (2026), “Additive-controlled selective hydrosilylation of aryl alkenes catalyzed by bis(silylene) pincer nickel(II) chloride,” [DOI: 10.1039/D5NJ03998C](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5NJ03998C).

title: Solution-phase N₂ capture by a designed silylene–borole frustrated Lewis pair
open: Can a computationally designed silylene–borole frustrated Lewis pair be synthesized and made to bind and activate dinitrogen in solution? The goal is to realize the predicted pair experimentally and establish its structural identity, reaction rate, and equilibrium constant for N₂ binding.
status: The 2025 computational designs of Dong, Wang, and Zhu predict barriers of 16.9–22.5 kcal/mol and reaction free energies of −32.3 to −36.7 kcal/mol for the designed pair. N₂ cleavage by SiH₂ in a cryogenic matrix was demonstrated by Cai et al. in 2024, but the designed solution chemistry remains untested.
solved_when: The predicted silylene–borole pair has been synthesized and shown to bind and activate N₂ in solution, with structural identity, reaction rate, and equilibrium constant determined — testing the 2025 computational predictions of barriers of 16.9–22.5 kcal/mol and reaction free energies of −32.3 to −36.7 kcal/mol.
why: It tests whether aromaticity-driven cooperativity — the design principle behind the prediction — survives actual synthesis and solvent effects, rather than only in silico.
key_works: S. Dong, W. Wang, and J. Zhu (2025), “Design of Borole- and Silylene-Based Frustrated Lewis Pairs for Dinitrogen Activation Promoted by Aromaticity: A Combined DFT and Machine Learning Study,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c02343](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c02343); L. Cai et al. (2024), “N2 cleavage by silylene and formation of H2Si(μ-N)2SiH2,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-48064-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-48064-z).

title: A bottleable triplet phosphinidene that avoids intramolecular arene addition
open: Can a free, monocoordinate triplet phosphinidene be isolated in a hydrindacene-type environment without it attacking its own aryl framework? The goal is a bottleable species whose spin state, identity, and solution persistence can all be established.
status: The 2024 attempt instead produced singlet phosphanorcaradiene through intramolecular dearomatization. This failed triplet isolation is still discussed in 2026 primary literature; isolated singlet phosphinidenes and precursor equivalents do not fulfill this specific target (Y. Chen, P. Su, D. Wang, Z. Ke, and G. Tan (2024), "Molecular-strain induced phosphinidene reactivity of a phosphanorcaradiene," [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-49042-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-49042-1)).
solved_when: A free, monocoordinate triplet phosphinidene in a hydrindacene-type environment is isolated and shown to avoid intramolecular arene addition, with its spin state, identity, and solution persistence experimentally established.
why: It would expose genuine phosphorus-centered triplet chemistry directly, without the precursor-release equilibria that complicate existing phosphinidene equivalents.
key_works: Y. Chen, P. Su, D. Wang, Z. Ke, and G. Tan (2024), “Molecular-strain induced phosphinidene reactivity of a phosphanorcaradiene,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-024-49042-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-49042-1).

title: The fleeting Sb(III) hydride in disulfide hydroboration
open: Does the hydridostibine proposed as an intermediate in disulfide hydroboration actually exist as a separately populated species, and if so, how long does it live and in what concentration? Concretely, can experiment measure its population and lifetime between the borane metathesis step and Sb(I) regeneration, and provide kinetic evidence that distinguishes this stepwise hydride from a concerted alternative?
status: The 2024 paper (M. Huang, K. Li, Z. Zhang, and J. Zhou, “Antimony Redox Catalysis: Hydroboration of Disulfides through Unique Sb(I)/Sb(III) Redox Cycling,” [DOI: 10.1021/jacs.4c05905](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.4c05905)) establishes Sb(I)/Sb(III) disulfide-hydroboration turnover and proposes the reaction sequence; direct hydride-population measurements remain a proposed mechanistic test of that account. A related difficulty is bounding species lifetimes that fall below instrumental resolution.
solved_when: Direct measurements quantify the population and lifetime of the proposed hydridostibine formed between borane metathesis and Sb(I) regeneration, and the kinetic data discriminate between a separately populated hydride intermediate and a concerted mechanism.
why: It tests the elementary event — Sb–H formation followed by elimination — that the proposed catalytic cycle assigns as the key turnover step, so resolving it either confirms the Sb(I)/Sb(III) redox account or forces its revision.
key_works: M. Huang, K. Li, Z. Zhang, and J. Zhou (2024), “Antimony Redox Catalysis: Hydroboration of Disulfides through Unique Sb(I)/Sb(III) Redox Cycling,” [DOI: 10.1021/jacs.4c05905](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.4c05905).

title: One-electron versus two-electron flux in antimonate–NHPI aerobic coupling
open: How does the antimonate–NHPI aerobic coupling reaction actually proceed — through single-electron oxidation at antimony, hydrogen abstraction by PINO, a distinct two-electron antimonate pathway, or some combination, and in what proportions? A quantitative accounting of the flux through each route, together with identification of the antimony oxidation states populated during turnover, would settle the mechanism.
status: The 2013 report (Tanoue, Yoo, and Kobayashi, DOI: 10.1002/adsc.201200999) explicitly left the roles of antimonate and NHPI unclear. Coupling persisted at 21% yield in the presence of a radical inhibitor, motivating a proposed alternative two-electron pathway, but neither its structure nor its flux was established.
solved_when: The relative contributions of Sb-centered single-electron oxidation, PINO-mediated hydrogen abstraction, and the proposed two-electron antimonate pathway are quantified under the reaction conditions, and the antimony oxidation states populated during turnover are experimentally identified.
why: It determines whether a catalytic counteranion operates through one mechanism or several, which in turn dictates how such aerobic coupling catalysts can be rationally designed and improved.
key_works: A. Tanoue, W.-J. Yoo, and S. Kobayashi (2013), “Antimony/N-Hydroxyphthalimide as a Catalyst System for Cross-Dehydrogenative Coupling Reactions under Aerobic Conditions,” [DOI: 10.1002/adsc.201200999](https://doi.org/10.1002/adsc.201200999).

title: A free phosphatetrazolate [PN₄]⁻ ring
open: Can the aromatic [PN₄]⁻ ring be liberated from its metal coordination environment and isolated as a free, metal-free species without losing nitrogen or fragmenting P–N bonds? Alongside isolation, what counterions stabilize it, and how fast does it decompose?
status: An osmium-bound PN₄ ring was formed in 2025 through phosphorus-mononitride chemistry (S. Edin et al., "Unleashing phosphorus mononitride," DOI: 10.1038/s41467-025-60669-6). Metal-free isolation remains a proposed next target; HCPN₃⁻ and P₂N₃⁻ are different compositions.
solved_when: A metal-free [PN₄]⁻ salt is isolated and characterized, with nitrogen loss and P–N fragmentation ruled out, and its counterion dependence and decomposition kinetics determined.
why: Isolation would test whether aromatic stabilization alone sustains this nitrogen-rich phosphorus heterocycle, independent of metal coordination.
key_works: S. Edin et al. (2025), “Unleashing phosphorus mononitride,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-025-60669-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-60669-6).

title: The hydridophosphorane in trialkylphosphine-catalysed C–F cleavage
open: Can the proposed phosphorus hydride intermediate be caught in the act during pentafluoropyridine hydrodefluorination — that is, directly observed forming and decaying under catalytic conditions? In particular, does hydride transfer to phosphorus generate a hydridophosphorane, and does its decay rate match the rate at which the C–H product forms?
status: The 2024 work of S. Bonfelle, C. Lorber, J. M. Lynam, A. Simonneau, and J. M. Slattery ("Metallomimetic C–F Activation Catalysis by Simple Phosphines," [DOI: 10.1021/jacs.3c10614](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.3c10614)) observes phosphonium intermediates and computationally supports fluorosilicate-mediated hydride delivery followed by reductive elimination; the proposed phosphorus hydride still lacks a direct kinetic assignment during turnover.
solved_when: Hydride transfer to phosphorus and the resulting hydridophosphorane are directly observed during pentafluoropyridine hydrodefluorination, with a kinetic assignment during turnover showing that the intermediate's decay supplies the C–H product at the catalytic rate.
why: It tests the central bond-making step of the simple-phosphine redox cycle, anchoring the mechanistic proposal in directly observed intermediates rather than computation alone.
key_works: S. Bonfante, C. Lorber, J. M. Lynam, A. Simonneau, and J. M. Slattery (2024), “Metallomimetic C–F Activation Catalysis by Simple Phosphines,” [DOI: 10.1021/jacs.3c10614](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.3c10614).

title: Chloride-versus-sulfate pathway flux in cinnabar blackening
open: When cinnabar paint blackens under museum light, how much of the mercury sulfide converts through chloride-assisted chemistry and how much through a chloride-free, sulfate-mediated route? The goal is a quantitative apportionment of these pathway fluxes that closes the mercury balance across pigment, binder, secondary salts, and vapor phase.
status: Metallic mercury was directly demonstrated in photoaged cinnabar tempera in 2021 (Elert, Pérez Mendoza, and Cardell, [DOI: 10.1038/s42004-021-00610-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42004-021-00610-2)), including a chloride-free pathway. Relative pathway fluxes under ordinary display conditions remain unmeasured and are the proposed narrower target.
solved_when: A measurement (or set of measurements) under ordinary display illumination yields separate flux estimates for the chloride-assisted and sulfate-mediated pathways, with the mercury balance closed across pigment, binder, secondary salts, and vapor.
why: Knowing which pathway dominates in a given paint tells conservators which environmental intervention — chloride control or otherwise — will actually slow that object's darkening.
key_works: K. Elert, M. Pérez Mendoza, and C. Cardell (2021), “Direct evidence for metallic mercury causing photo-induced darkening of red cinnabar tempera paints,” [DOI: 10.1038/s42004-021-00610-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42004-021-00610-2).

title: Molecular identity of emerald-green photo-oxidation products
open: What are the emerald-green photo-oxidation products that form when emerald green pigments are illuminated — specifically, what are their stoichiometry, coordination environment, hydration, and connectivity? The answer should distinguish among copper arsenates, mixed-cation products, and arsenate associated with organic paint components, even though the products are predominantly amorphous.
status: A 2025 study (S. Carboni Marri et al., "Discovering the dual degradation pathway of emerald green in oil paints: The effects of light and humidity," [DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.ady1807](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.ady1807)) separated light-driven surface oxidation from humidity-driven arsenolite formation, but explicitly left the structure and stoichiometry of the predominantly amorphous As(V) products unresolved.
solved_when: The amorphous As(V)-rich products formed during illumination are structurally and stoichiometrically characterized, with their coordination, hydration, and connectivity determined and their assignment among copper arsenates, mixed-cation products, and organically associated arsenate resolved.
why: The molecular identity of the products determines whether arsenic remains immobilized in the paint layer or is released and migrates.
key_works: S. Carboni Marri et al. (2025), “Discovering the dual degradation pathway of emerald green in oil paints: The effects of light and humidity,” [DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.ady1807](https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.ady1807).

title: Sulfur mass balance during orpiment deterioration
open: Where does the sulfur go when orpiment (As₂S₃) deteriorates in a painting? A complete mass balance is needed that quantifies sulfur released as H₂S, as dissolved reduced sulfur, as oxidized sulfur species, and as fractions retained in the binder, with each sulfur pathway tied to its corresponding arsenic transformation.
status: Broers and colleagues established two arsenic-degradation pathways in 2023 but explicitly excluded sulfur fate from their study (F. T. H. Broers et al., 2023, “Two Pathways for the Degradation of Orpiment Pigment (As2S3) Found in Paintings,” DOI: 10.1021/jacs.2c12271). Earlier suggestions of H₂S release do not establish its yield or the competing sulfur sinks.
solved_when: A closed sulfur mass balance over the deteriorating As₂S₃ system is reported, accounting quantitatively for H₂S, dissolved reduced sulfur, oxidized sulfur, and binder-retained species, and each pathway is correlated with a known arsenic transformation product.
why: Mobile sulfur products can migrate and alter neighboring pigments, so knowing which sulfur species form and in what proportions is what determines the risk to surrounding paint.
key_works: F. T. H. Broers et al. (2023), “Two Pathways for the Degradation of Orpiment Pigment (As2S3) Found in Paintings,” [DOI: 10.1021/jacs.2c12271](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.2c12271).

title: Ultramarine sites initiating binder photoradicals
open: Which specific sulfur center, framework defect, or surface state in ultramarine is responsible for generating the radicals that degrade its paint binder? A satisfactory answer ties the site assignment to a measured action spectrum and demonstrates that selectively suppressing that site halts the damage.
status: The 2017 work (E. R. de la Rie et al., DOI: 10.1016/j.polymdegradstab.2017.08.002) demonstrated light-induced binder deterioration while the pigment itself remained intact, establishing a route to ultramarine disease, but it did not assign the initiating active site.
solved_when: The radical-initiating site in ultramarine is identified and the assignment is validated by an action spectrum matching its absorption and by selective suppression of the site stopping light-induced binder deterioration.
why: It would enable targeted passivation that preserves both the pigment's color and the binder's integrity in affected paintings.
key_works: E. R. de la Rie et al. (2017), “Photo-catalytic degradation of binding media of ultramarine blue containing paint layers: A new perspective on the phenomenon of ‘ultramarine disease’ in paintings,” [DOI: 10.1016/j.polymdegradstab.2017.08.002](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.polymdegradstab.2017.08.002).

title: Water’s catalytic step in zinc-soap crystallization
open: Through what elementary, coordination-changing step does trace water accelerate the crystallization of zinc carboxylates in cured oil? The goal is to identify the mechanism and measure the relevant intermediate, its water dependence, and whether water is regenerated (true catalytic turnover).
status: In 2023, swelling alone did not cause the acceleration, while water-containing solvent induced crystallization; stabilization of transient charged states was proposed without direct observation of the intermediate (J. Hermans, K. Helwig, S. Woutersen, and K. Keune, "Traces of water catalyze zinc soap crystallization in solvent-exposed oil paints," [DOI: 10.1039/D2CP04861B](https://doi.org/10.1039/D2CP04861B)).
solved_when: The coordination-changing intermediate is directly observed, its rate of formation is quantified as a function of water concentration, and it is established whether water is consumed or catalytically regenerated in the crystallization of zinc carboxylates.
why: It would explain why small water impurities in treatment solvents reorganize metal soaps, which is decisive for the conservation and cleaning of oil paintings.
key_works: J. Hermans, K. Helwig, S. Woutersen, and K. Keune (2023), “Traces of water catalyze zinc soap crystallization in solvent-exposed oil paints,” [DOI: 10.1039/D2CP04861B](https://doi.org/10.1039/D2CP04861B).

title: Ambient aluminium catalysis in alum-treated archaeological wood
open: How much of the chemical degradation in alum-treated archaeological wood is driven by aluminium species rather than by acid alone under normal storage conditions? A resolution would identify the aluminium species active at ambient temperature and quantify their catalytic contribution at matched acidity and moisture against proton-catalyzed damage.
status: Oseberg conservation research and a 2021 collection comparison (J. J. Łucejko et al. (2021), "Comparative chemical investigations of alum treated archaeological wood from various museum collections") show that acidity alone does not explain the observed damage patterns; aluminium's additional ambient catalytic contribution remains insufficiently quantified (S. Braovac et al. (2018), "Navigating conservation strategies: linking material research on alum-treated wood from the Oseberg collection to conservation decisions").
solved_when: The active aluminium species are identified, and their contribution to degradation is quantified at matched acidity and moisture at storage temperatures, cleanly separating aluminium-mediated catalysis from proton-catalyzed damage.
why: If aluminium catalysis is a significant pathway, neutralization treatments alone would leave a degradation route active, and the wood would continue to deteriorate despite de-acidification.
key_works: J. J. Łucejko et al. (2021), “Comparative chemical investigations of alum treated archaeological wood from various museum collections,” [publisher article](https://www.nature.com/articles/s40494-021-00517-0); S. Braovac et al. (2018), “Navigating conservation strategies: linking material research on alum-treated wood from the Oseberg collection to conservation decisions,” [DOI: 10.1186/s40494-018-0241-y](https://doi.org/10.1186/s40494-018-0241-y).

title: Native structures of latent copper–sulfhydryl complexes in wine
open: What are the native copper complexes in wine that store releasable hydrogen sulfide — their copper oxidation states, nuclearity, sulfide content, and glutathione coordination — and how can they be measured before analytical reagents shift their equilibria?
status: Allison and Sacks showed in 2021 that brine release depends on halide chemistry and glutathione; their assay defines a releasable pool but does not uniquely identify its native molecular constituents.
solved_when: The copper complexes constituting the releasable H₂S pool are identified with their oxidation state, nuclearity, sulfide content, and glutathione coordination, and are measured under conditions that do not perturb their native equilibria.
why: Knowing the native structures tells winemakers whether copper treatment permanently removes sulfur off-odors or only temporarily conceals them behind latent complexes that can re-release H₂S.
key_works: R. B. Allison and G. L. Sacks (2021), “Brine-Releasable Hydrogen Sulfide in Wine: Mechanism of Release from Copper Complexes and Effects of Glutathione,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.jafc.1c04885](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jafc.1c04885).

title: Electron donors sustaining sulfide regeneration in anoxic wine
open: Which constituents of anoxic wine supply the electrons that reduce Cu(II) and convert sulfur at oxidation state −I into H₂S sulfur at −II? A complete answer should identify the donors and balance their oxidized organic products against the volatile sulfur regenerated.
status: The 2024 remediation study of Sánchez-Gimeno, Vela, Ferreira, and Ontañón [DOI: 10.20870/oeno-one.2024.58.4.7655](https://doi.org/10.20870/oeno-one.2024.58.4.7655) explicitly identifies these electron donors as missing; experiments with copper treatment, filtration, and adjuvants did not resolve the recurring-sulfide mechanism.
solved_when: The electron donor(s) are identified, and the oxidized organic products they generate account, by electron balance, for the quantity of regenerated volatile sulfur (H₂S) observed after oxygen depletion.
why: It exposes the chemical driver behind the recurrence of reductive sulfur off-odors after oxygen depletion, which current treatments fail to control.
key_works: D. Sánchez-Gimeno, E. Vela, V. Ferreira, and I. Ontañón (2024), “Alternative strategies for eliminating hydrogen sulfide and methanethiol from wine: results and learnings,” [DOI: 10.20870/oeno-one.2024.58.4.7655](https://doi.org/10.20870/oeno-one.2024.58.4.7655).

title: Non-methionine methanethiol precursors in aged wine
open: What chemical species in aged wine supplies the methanethiol that continues to form after the measured free methanethionine pool has been exhausted? The task is to identify these non-methionine precursors and characterize their sulfur yields and temperature-dependent conversion kinetics.
status: A 2025 study by Ainsa-Zazurca, Ontañón, and Ferreira followed twelve wines for up to eighteen months at 35 °C and shorter periods at higher temperatures, and found that methanethiol production persisted without closure of the measured precursor balance (DOI: 10.1021/acs.jafc.5c04010).
solved_when: The precursor pool responsible is chemically identified, with quantitative sulfur yields and temperature-dependent conversion kinetics determined, so that observed methanethiol production under accelerated aging (up to eighteen months at 35 °C and shorter periods at higher temperatures) can be fully accounted for by the identified precursors.
why: Without identifying this pool, sulfur faults can emerge late in a wine's life and go undetected by volatile measurements made at bottling; knowing the precursors enables prevention of these delayed faults.
key_works: S. Ainsa-Zazurca, I. Ontañón, and V. Ferreira (2025), “Kinetic Studies on the Ability of Wines to Produce Hydrogen Sulfide (H2S) and Methanethiol (MeSH),” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.jafc.5c04010](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jafc.5c04010).

title: IRC7-independent thiol release in brewing yeast
open: Which enzymes and substrates account for the aroma-thiol release that persists in brewing yeast after IRC7 is deleted, and can this alternative route be pinned down genetically and reconstituted enzymatically?
status: A 2025 comparison found an IRC7 knockout with thiol release resembling its parent (R. Samia, A. Shayevitz, T. Fischborn, and T. H. Shellhammer (2025), "Wort Nitrogen and Yeast Strain Drive Thiol Release, Flavor Expression, and Fermentation Performance in Beer," [DOI: 10.1080/03610470.2025.2530859](https://doi.org/10.1080/03610470.2025.2530859)), implicating alternative routes without identifying the compensating enzyme system.
solved_when: The compensating enzyme system and its substrates are identified, with necessity shown by genetic perturbation and sufficiency shown by enzyme reconstitution reproducing the thiol release observed in an IRC7 knockout.
why: It makes strain aroma performance predictable in cases where targeting the commonly manipulated β-lyase gene IRC7 is insufficient.
key_works: R. Samia, A. Shayevitz, T. Fischborn, and T. H. Shellhammer (2025), “Wort Nitrogen and Yeast Strain Drive Thiol Release, Flavor Expression, and Fermentation Performance in Beer,” [DOI: 10.1080/03610470.2025.2530859](https://doi.org/10.1080/03610470.2025.2530859).

title: Chemical identity of sake fraction DMTS-P2
open: What is the actual molecule (or set of molecules) hiding in the sake fraction known as DMTS-P2, and how does it give rise to dimethyl trisulfide? In particular, does its activity depend on an interaction between compounds that purification pulls apart?
status: The 2009 work by Isogai et al. identified DMTS-P1 but left another active fraction unresolved; Isogai's doctoral thesis subsequently investigated DMTS-P2 and its interaction with a neutral fraction, but without converting those operational fractions into molecular structures.
solved_when: The active constituent or constituents of DMTS-P2 are identified as molecular structures, the mechanism by which they generate dimethyl trisulfide is established, and it is determined whether activity requires interacting compounds separated during purification.
why: It would resolve a source of stale-sake sulfur aroma beyond the already-identified P1 pathway, which matters for understanding and controlling off-flavor formation in aged sake.
key_works: A. Isogai et al. (2009), “Screening and Identification of Precursor Compounds of Dimethyl Trisulfide (DMTS) in Japanese Sake,” [DOI: 10.1021/jf802582p](https://doi.org/10.1021/jf802582p); A. Isogai (2009), “清酒の熟成に関与する香気成分およびその生成機構に関する研究,” [doctoral thesis](https://ir.lib.hiroshima-u.ac.jp/31097/files/19891).

title: Grape-derived dimethyl-trisulfide precursors in wine
open: Which grape-derived compounds give rise to substantial dimethyl trisulfide (DMTS) formation as wine ages? The goal is to identify these precursor structures and establish their contribution independently of methanethiol and the known sake-derived precursor DMTS-P1.
status: A 2017 study found that dead yeast in synthetic must did not reproduce grape-juice behavior, and known precursors explained only a minor contribution; the operative grape-derived structures remain unidentified [N. Nishibori, A. Kuroda, O. Yamada, and N. Goto-Yamamoto (2017), "Factors Affecting Dimethyl Trisulfide Formation in Wine," DOI: 10.3136/fstr.23.241].
solved_when: The grape-derived precursor structures responsible for substantial DMTS formation during aging are identified, and their contribution is demonstrated to be independent of methanethiol and DMTS-P1.
why: It would connect grape and must composition to delayed sulfur defects in wine, allowing vineyard and processing decisions to target the source of off-flavors rather than their late-stage symptoms.
key_works: N. Nishibori, A. Kuroda, O. Yamada, and N. Goto-Yamamoto (2017), “Factors Affecting Dimethyl Trisulfide Formation in Wine,” [DOI: 10.3136/fstr.23.241](https://doi.org/10.3136/fstr.23.241).

title: Chromophore responsible for Sauvignon-blanc pinking
open: What chemical species turns some Sauvignon-blanc wines pink? The goal is to identify the responsible chromophore, distinguish trace anthocyanins from alternative oxidized phenolic products, and reproduce the pinking behavior at native concentrations.
status: Anthocyanins were established as a cause of pinking in Síria wines in 2014 (J. Andrea-Silva et al., [DOI: 10.1021/jf500825h](https://doi.org/10.1021/jf500825h)). The 2022 Sauvignon-blanc study (A. P. Nel, W. J. du Toit, and F. P. van Jaarsveld, [DOI: 10.21548/43-1-4812](https://doi.org/10.21548/43-1-4812)) remained inconclusive: its 1 mg/L detection limit exceeded the 0.3 mg/L visibility threshold reported for Síria, so absence of a signal could not be distinguished from concentrations below detection.
solved_when: The chromophore is identified and its pinking behavior is reproduced at native concentrations; method sensitivity must reach below the 0.3 mg/L visibility threshold reported for Síria, improving on the 1 mg/L detection limit of the 2022 study.
why: A definitive identification enables susceptibility testing of wines before pinking occurs and targeted prevention measures rather than guesswork.
key_works: A. P. Nel, W. J. du Toit, and F. P. van Jaarsveld (2022), “Attempted Identification of Causal Constituents of Pink Discolouration in White Wines,” [DOI: 10.21548/43-1-4812](https://doi.org/10.21548/43-1-4812); J. Andrea-Silva et al. (2014), “Origin of the pinking phenomenon of white wines,” [DOI: 10.1021/jf500825h](https://doi.org/10.1021/jf500825h).

title: Fluoride tunneling between two germanium centers of a molecular receptor
open: Can the proposed double-germanium fluoride receptor be synthesized and shown to exhibit low-temperature intersite fluoride transfer with a genuine tunneling signature — that is, exchange cleanly distinguished from static disorder and from thermal hopping?
status: The ping-pong process was predicted in 2018 (Nandi, Sucher, and Kozuch, DOI: 10.1002/chem.201802782). The 2025 experimental fluorine-tunneling paper (Müller et al., DOI: 10.1038/s41467-025-59008-6) still describes this receptor as hypothetical; its observed polyfluoride system is chemically distinct.
solved_when: The receptor is realized experimentally and low-temperature intersite fluoride transfer is detected with a tunneling signature demonstrably distinct from static disorder and thermal hopping.
why: It would test whether tunneling of a relatively heavy nucleus can be deliberately controlled through molecular geometry.
key_works: A. Nandi, A. Sucher, and S. Kozuch (2018), “Ping-Pong Tunneling Reactions: Can Fluoride Jump at Absolute Zero?” [DOI: 10.1002/chem.201802782](https://doi.org/10.1002/chem.201802782); C. Müller et al. (2025), “Experimental observation of quantum mechanical fluorine tunnelling,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-025-59008-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-59008-6).

title: Experimental verification of tunneling-driven XeF₆ pseudorotation
open: Can an experiment cleanly attribute the low-temperature pseudorotation of XeF₆ to quantum tunneling rather than residual thermal motion, in a well-characterized environment? Concretely, this means detecting the predicted tunneling splittings, or an isotope-sensitive exchange signature, that only the tunneling mechanism produces.
status: Sedgi and Kozuch (2020) predicted rapid near-zero-temperature fluorine tunneling on the XeF₆ pseudorotation path (DOI: 10.1039/D0CP03205K). As of the 2025 polyfluoride study on experimental observation of quantum mechanical fluorine tunnelling (DOI: 10.1038/s41467-025-59008-6), XeF₆ remains a computational prediction, with no experimental confirmation reported.
solved_when: XeF₆ is studied in a characterized environment at low temperature, and the observed pseudorotation dynamics — specifically the predicted splittings or isotope-sensitive exchange — are shown to arise from near-zero-temperature fluorine tunneling, excluding residual thermal motion as the explanation.
why: It would elevate a computationally predicted phenomenon to observation, directly testing quantum dynamics in a classic fluxional hypervalent molecule.
key_works: I. Sedgi and S. Kozuch (2020), “Heavy atom tunnelling on XeF6 pseudorotation,” [DOI: 10.1039/D0CP03205K](https://doi.org/10.1039/D0CP03205K); C. Müller et al. (2025), “Experimental observation of quantum mechanical fluorine tunnelling,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41467-025-59008-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-59008-6).

title: Testing hyperconjugation as the cause of solvent-enhanced carbon tunneling
open: Does coordination-dependent geminal hyperconjugation actually cause the observed changes in carbon tunneling rates in the benzene oxide/oxepin system? A decisive experiment must independently constrain the coordination populations and separate barrier narrowing from purely energetic stabilization.
status: The 2025 calculations of Laconsay, Jain, Schleif, Karney, and Wu connect coordination motifs to C–C bond shortening and enhanced tunneling. Solvent-controlled tunneling already has experimental precedents; what remains open is testing this proposed electronic cause and its quantitative prediction.
solved_when: The hyperconjugation mechanism is either confirmed or refuted by measurements that independently determine coordination populations and quantitatively distinguish tunneling-rate enhancement due to barrier narrowing from that due to energetic stabilization, matching the mechanism's quantitative prediction.
why: Confirmation would make solvent selection a rational tool for controlling heavy-atom tunneling, rather than an empirical curiosity.
key_works: C. J. Laconsay, I. Jain, T. Schleif, W. L. Karney, and J. I. Wu (2025), “Geminal hyperconjugation as a driving force for C–C bond shortening in heavy-atom tunnelling,” [DOI: 10.1039/D5SC02914G](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5SC02914G).

title: General sequencing of branched native glycans
open: Can we sequence any branched native glycan — reading out monosaccharide identity, linkage positions, anomeric configurations, and branching — even when it occurs in a mixture, with the residual structural ambiguity quantified and calibrated?
status: A longstanding structural problem. Enzymatic nanopore decoding in 2025 and fragment reassembly in 2026 (Xia et al. (2026), *Nanopore-Based Glycan Sequencing via a Fragmentation-Reassembly Strategy*, [DOI:10.1021/jacs.5c22760](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.5c22760)) established partial routes; universal sequencing remains open.
solved_when: A method exists that determines monosaccharide identity, linkage position, anomeric configuration, and branching for arbitrary glycans in mixtures, with calibrated structural ambiguity attached to each assignment.
why: It would allow complete characterization of glycoproteins and of cell-surface recognition chemistry, where incomplete glycan structure currently limits interpretation.
key_works: Xia et al. (2026), *Nanopore-Based Glycan Sequencing via a Fragmentation-Reassembly Strategy*, [DOI:10.1021/jacs.5c22760](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.5c22760).

title: Individually addressable carborane vertices
open: Can any chosen non-equivalent boron vertex of a carborane cage be functionalized at will, including sequential substitutions with different groups at different vertices, with full control over both cage and substituent stereochemistry?
status: This is a longstanding cluster-synthesis problem. A 2025 rhodium-carbene method achieved site- and enantioselective B–H insertion for selected carboranes (Lee et al. (2025), *Site- and enantioselective B−H functionalization of carboranes*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-59410-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-59410-0)), but complete vertex addressability remains unavailable.
solved_when: A general method exists that selectively functionalizes any targeted non-equivalent boron vertex of a carborane cage, permits sequential different substitutions, and controls cage and substituent stereochemistry.
why: Vertex-level control would expand access to three-dimensional pharmacophores, ligands, and electronically unusual materials built on the carborane scaffold.
key_works: Lee et al. (2025), *Site- and enantioselective B−H functionalization of carboranes*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-59410-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-59410-0).

title: Molecular parity-violating enantiomer energy difference
open: Can we experimentally detect the tiny parity-violating energy difference between left- and right-handed molecular enantiomers? Specifically, this means measuring the electroweak energy or transition-frequency difference between enantiomers with systematic errors brought below the predicted signal.
status: The effect has been predicted for decades but remains experimentally undetected; a July 2026 proposal (D. Martínez-Gil, P. Bargueño and S. Miret-Artés, *Ultracold amplification proposal for parity violation in chiral molecules*, [DOI:10.1103/54yp-6397](https://doi.org/10.1103/54yp-6397); [arXiv:2606.08717](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08717)) still describes molecular parity violation as unobserved and identifies heavy chiral species and ultracold amplification as possible experimental routes.
solved_when: A measurement of the electroweak energy or transition-frequency difference between molecular enantiomers is reported in which the systematic errors are smaller than the predicted parity-violating signal.
why: Detection would directly test the weak interaction in molecular matter and constrain microscopic sources of chiral bias, connecting precision Standard Model tests with the open question of biological homochirality.
key_works: D. Martínez-Gil, P. Bargueño and S. Miret-Artés (2026), *Ultracold amplification proposal for parity violation in chiral molecules*, [DOI:10.1103/54yp-6397](https://doi.org/10.1103/54yp-6397); [arXiv:2606.08717](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.08717).

title: Indefinite nonenzymatic RNA replication
open: Can enzyme-free RNA replication be made to sustain itself indefinitely, cycling through copying, strand separation, and fresh substrate supply for arbitrary mixed sequences without an external reset after each generation? Formally, the challenge is to integrate template-directed copying, duplex separation, and monomer replenishment into a single autonomous chemical system that repeats indefinitely.
status: Chemical copying has advanced for decades. Virtual-circular-genome experiments in 2023 (Ding et al., *Experimental Tests of the Virtual Circular Genome Model for Nonenzymatic RNA Replication*, DOI:10.1021/jacs.3c00612) tested a route around duplex trapping without establishing indefinite autonomous replication.
solved_when: *see above*
why: *see above*
key_works: Ding et al. (2023), *Experimental Tests of the Virtual Circular Genome Model for Nonenzymatic RNA Replication*, [DOI:10.1021/jacs.3c00612](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.3c00612).

title: Carrier and charge state of the 8621 Å diffuse interstellar band
open: What molecule, and in what charge state, causes the diffuse interstellar band at 862.1 nm? An answer requires laboratory spectra matched to the astronomical feature together with a photoionization/recombination model consistent with its behavior across clouds.
status: A 2026 study of 12 clouds (H. Zhao and L. Li (2026), *A cationic carrier for the diffuse interstellar band at 862.1 nm: Evidence of the skin effect in nearby diffuse to translucent clouds*, [DOI:10.1051/0004-6361/202557833](https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202557833); [arXiv:2603.05631](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05631)) finds spatial behavior supporting a cation; ionization-energy constraints remain model-dependent and do not identify the molecule.
solved_when: The 862.1 nm band is assigned to a specific molecule and charge state, with laboratory spectra reproducing the feature and a photoionization/recombination model consistent with its observed spatial behavior (e.g., across the 12 clouds studied in 2026).
why: It would give Gaia's extensive measurements of this DIB a chemical identity, turning a mapping tool into a probe of specific interstellar chemistry.
key_works: H. Zhao and L. Li (2026), *A cationic carrier for the diffuse interstellar band at 862.1 nm: Evidence of the skin effect in nearby diffuse to translucent clouds*, [DOI:10.1051/0004-6361/202557833](https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-6361/202557833); [arXiv:2603.05631](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.05631).

title: Substrate-oxygen assignment in photosystem II
open: Which two oxygen atoms in the oxygen-evolving complex of photosystem II couple to form the O₂ molecule during catalysis — the O5–O6 pair or the competing O3–O6 pair?
status: A 2026 calculation proposed O3–O6 coupling, while new structural measurements located the additional S₃-state oxygen without directly identifying the reacting pair. The remaining target is an experimentally discriminating atom assignment.
solved_when: An experimental determination directly identifies the two oxygen atoms that form O₂, discriminating between O5–O6 and O3–O6 coupling.

title: Proton-and-electron-only recycling of triphenylphosphine oxide
open: Can ordinary triphenylphosphine oxide — the stoichiometric waste product of countless Wittig, Appel, and Staudinger reactions — be reduced back to triphenylphosphine using only electricity and a proton source, with no stoichiometric silanes, hydrides, or halogenating activators?
status: A 2026 study by A. Laverny et al. (*Proton-coupled electrochemical reduction of a phosphine oxide*, [DOI:10.1016/j.chempr.2026.102946](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chempr.2026.102946)) achieved 90% yield for the proton-coupled electrochemical reduction of a specially designed fused dipyridyl phosphine oxide; extending this chemistry to commodity phosphine oxides such as triphenylphosphine oxide remains open.
solved_when: Triphenylphosphine oxide is converted to triphenylphosphine by proton-coupled electrochemical reduction, without any stoichiometric silane, hydride, or halogenating activator, at a yield comparable to the 90% benchmark set for the specially designed fused dipyridyl phosphine oxide.
why: It would close the phosphorus-reagent cycle for some of the most widely used reactions in organic synthesis, turning a stoichiometric waste stream back into the reagent that generated it.
key_works: A. Laverny et al. (2026), *Proton-coupled electrochemical reduction of a phosphine oxide*, [DOI:10.1016/j.chempr.2026.102946](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.chempr.2026.102946).

title: Causal product control by the initial electronic coherence
open: Can the initial electronic coherence of a molecule causally steer its chemistry — that is, if we change only the initial electronic relative phase while holding populations and deposited energy fixed, does the later product distribution change?
status: Full-dimensional ethylene simulations in 2025 (L. Fransén et al., *Attochemical Control of Nuclear Motion despite Fast Electronic Decoherence*, DOI:10.1021/acs.jpclett.5c01895) predict altered nuclear motion despite rapid electronic decoherence; the controlled experimental phase-to-product test remains open.
solved_when: An experiment demonstrates that varying the initial electronic relative phase at fixed populations and fixed deposited energy produces a measurable change in a subsequent product distribution.
why: It would establish whether attosecond coherent control can deliver genuine chemical selectivity, converting electronic coherence into a causal handle on reaction outcomes.
key_works: L. Fransén et al. (2025), *Attochemical Control of Nuclear Motion despite Fast Electronic Decoherence*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.jpclett.5c01895](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpclett.5c01895).

title: Equimolar oxidative cross-Kolbe coupling
open: Can two different free aliphatic carboxylic acids be coupled at approximately equimolar loading by oxidative decarboxylation with selectivity for the cross-product over the two homocoupled products, without preconverting either acid into an activated ester?
status: Reductive heterocoupling through activated esters is established; the 2023 waveform-controlled oxidative method (Y. Hioki et al., *Overcoming the limitations of Kolbe coupling with waveform-controlled electrosynthesis*, DOI:10.1126/science.adf4762) broadened direct scope but did not establish general nonstatistical cross-coupling of similar acids. Relatedly, B. Zhang et al. (2022), *Ni-electrocatalytic Csp3–Csp3 doubly decarboxylative coupling*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-022-04691-4, is a key work.
solved_when: A direct oxidative decarboxylative method achieves nonstatistical cross-coupling of two similar free aliphatic carboxylic acids at approximately equimolar loading, avoiding activated-ester intermediates.
why: It would make abundant carboxylic acids interchangeable coupling partners while eliminating the activation step and its attendant waste.
key_works: B. Zhang et al. (2022), *Ni-electrocatalytic Csp3–Csp3 doubly decarboxylative coupling*, [DOI:10.1038/s41586-022-04691-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-022-04691-4); Y. Hioki et al. (2023), *Overcoming the limitations of Kolbe coupling with waveform-controlled electrosynthesis*, [DOI:10.1126/science.adf4762](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adf4762).

title: Address-selective hydrocarboxylation of internal alkenes
open: Can we add CO₂ and hydrogen across either chosen carbon of an unactivated internal alkene, keeping the original double-bond position as the reaction site? Formally, this demands address-selective, nonmigratory hydrocarboxylation in which the carboxyl group is delivered to a predesignated carbon of the C=C bond.
status: Alternating-polarity hydrocarboxylation and migratory carboxylation advanced in 2025–2026, via Fors, Yap and Malapit (2025), *Effect of Alternating Polarity in Electrochemical Olefin Hydrocarboxylation*, [DOI:10.1002/anie.202424865](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202424865), and M. Dong et al. (2026), *Electrocatalytic Migratory Carboxylation of Unactivated Olefins or Halides with CO2*, [DOI:10.1002/anie.202518160](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202518160). Those methods leave independently selectable, nonmigratory internal-alkene regiochemistry unresolved.
solved_when: A catalytic method is demonstrated that hydrocarboxylates unactivated internal alkenes with CO₂ and hydrogen, delivering the carboxyl group to either chosen carbon of the original double bond at that position, without migration of the alkene.
why: It would convert inexpensive internal olefins into specific, position-defined carboxylic acid building blocks on demand.
key_works: Fors, Yap and Malapit (2025), *Effect of Alternating Polarity in Electrochemical Olefin Hydrocarboxylation*, [DOI:10.1002/anie.202424865](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202424865); M. Dong et al. (2026), *Electrocatalytic Migratory Carboxylation of Unactivated Olefins or Halides with CO2*, [DOI:10.1002/anie.202518160](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202518160).

title: Localizing three or more adjacent mucin O-glycans
open: Can we determine which glycan sits on which serine or threonine when three or more of these residues close together in a mucin peptide each carry an O-glycan? A solution requires assigning individual glycan compositions — not just a total — to each site with calibrated confidence, even when different arrangements share the same overall composition.
status: The 2026 DeepGPO framework handles singly and doubly glycosylated peptides; its authors (Y. Zong, Y. Wang and L. Qiao, 2026, *Deep Learning Prediction of O-Glycopeptide Tandem Mass Spectra Enhances O-Glycoproteomics*, DOI:10.1002/advs.76760) identify three-plus glycans as beyond current capability due to spectral complexity and scarce training data.
solved_when: A method assigns individual glycan compositions to three or more adjacent serine/threonine residues, distinguishes isomeric arrangements with identical total composition, and reports calibrated confidence for each localization.
why: Dense O-glycosylation patterns define mucin surfaces, so resolving which glycan occupies which site would reveal the fine structure that current methods collapse into a single aggregate.
key_works: Y. Zong, Y. Wang and L. Qiao (2026), *Deep Learning Prediction of O-Glycopeptide Tandem Mass Spectra Enhances O-Glycoproteomics*, [DOI:10.1002/advs.76760](https://doi.org/10.1002/advs.76760).

title: Complete intact-ganglioside structural assignment
open: Can we determine the full structure of a single, native ganglioside molecule at once — glycan sequence and linkages, ceramide chains, and the position and stereochemistry of every double bond? In other words, can complete structural assignment be achieved on the intact molecule rather than piecemeal?
status: A 2026 HILIC–nanoESI-MS/MS workflow (N. Troppmair et al., *Comprehensive Isomer-Resolved Ganglioside Profiling by HILIC-nanoESI-MS/MS*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.analchem.6c00380](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.analchem.6c00380)) quantified 80 species across 18 subclasses in ten mouse tissues, but molecular-species annotation still falls short of complete stereochemical structures.
solved_when: A workflow assigns, on the same native molecule, the glycan sequence and linkage pattern, the ceramide chains, the position of every double bond, and all relevant stereochemistry — going beyond the current state of annotation of 80 species across 18 subclasses in ten mouse tissues.
why: It would distinguish compositionally identical molecules that differ in membrane function, which current annotation cannot resolve.
key_works: N. Troppmair et al. (2026), *Comprehensive Isomer-Resolved Ganglioside Profiling by HILIC-nanoESI-MS/MS*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.analchem.6c00380](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.analchem.6c00380).

title: Secure detection of interstellar glycine
open: Can we establish a secure detection of glycine in the interstellar medium? A convincing detection would identify multiple unblended spectral transitions whose intensities are consistent with a single excitation temperature and abundance, with no strong predicted lines missing from the data and with explicit discrimination among glycine's conformers.
status: The disputed early-2000s claim never became secure. A September 2026 preprint by Wurmel and Simmie still treats interstellar glycine as undetected and examines conformer kinetics as a search constraint [arXiv:2609.17243]. The earlier rigorous verification attempt is L. E. Snyder et al. (2005), *A Rigorous Attempt to Verify Interstellar Glycine* [NIST record](https://www.nist.gov/publications/rigorous-attempt-verify-interstellar-glycine).
solved_when: Glycine is reported detected in an astronomical source via multiple unblinded, unblended transitions showing consistent excitation and abundance, with no missing strong lines and explicit conformer discrimination.
why: A secure detection would anchor the observational link between interstellar chemistry and the amino-acid inventories delivered to planetary surfaces.
key_works: L. E. Snyder et al. (2005), *A Rigorous Attempt to Verify Interstellar Glycine*, [NIST record](https://www.nist.gov/publications/rigorous-attempt-verify-interstellar-glycine); J. Wurmel and J. M. Simmie (2026), *Glycine in the interstellar medium revisited: Resolving conformational complexity kinetically*, [arXiv:2609.17243](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.17243).

title: Motif-II structure of the hydrated electron in water clusters
open: Which atomic structure and electron-binding geometry underlies motif II in size-selected water-cluster anions? A convincing assignment must reconcile the photoelectron and absorption spectra recorded under identical source conditions with the candidate calculated structures.
status: An and Kim’s 2026 measurements expanded the experimentally distinguished motifs from four to five; the correspondence between motif II and calculated structures remains unresolved [S. An and S. K. Kim (2026), “Structure and isomer-specific femtosecond real-time relaxation dynamics of hydrated electron motifs in water cluster anions,” DOI: 10.1038/s42004-026-02006-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42004-026-02006-6).
solved_when: A structural assignment of motif II is established that explains the measured photoelectron and absorption data obtained under the same source conditions, resolving its correspondence with calculated structures.
why: A secure assignment would test how a small hydrogen-bond network stabilizes an excess electron, with implications for structural inversion from overlapping spectra and for understanding electron localization preceding molecular damage in radiation biology.
key_works: S. An and S. K. Kim (2026), “Structure and isomer-specific femtosecond real-time relaxation dynamics of hydrated electron motifs in water cluster anions,” [DOI: 10.1038/s42004-026-02006-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42004-026-02006-6).

title: Water evaporation versus electron loss in the 340-ps cluster-anion decay
open: When a vibrationally excited water-cluster anion relaxes, does it primarily shed a neutral water molecule or lose its excess electron, and how does that answer change with cluster size and electron-binding motif? A quantitative, channel-resolved measurement of the branching between water evaporation and electron autodetachment, resolved across sizes and motifs, is the goal.
status: An and Kim (2026) observed an approximately 340-ps ground-state decay component in hydrated electron cluster anions and provisionally attributed it to evaporation and/or autodetachment; channel-specific identification remains open.
solved_when: The approximately 340-ps ground-state decay component is assigned channel-specifically — i.e., the relative yields of neutral-water evaporation and electron autodetachment are measured as functions of cluster size and electron-binding motif, not merely inferred as a combined "evaporation and/or autodetachment" attribution.
why: It establishes how small hydrated electrons survive after optical excitation, which underpins any mechanistic picture of excess-electron relaxation in finite aqueous systems.
key_works: S. An and S. K. Kim (2026), “Structure and isomer-specific femtosecond real-time relaxation dynamics of hydrated electron motifs in water cluster anions,” [DOI: 10.1038/s42004-026-02006-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42004-026-02006-6).

title: Unknown side products that divert irradiated chromium recombination
open: What chemical species accumulate in molten LiCl–KCl eutectic under irradiation and divert Cr(I)/Cr(III) recombination away from clean second-order kinetics, and by what pathways are they formed?
status: Pulse-radiolysis measurements by K. Iwamatsu et al. (2026; first published 2025, "Kinetics of radiation-induced Cr(II) and Cr(III) redox chemistry in molten LiCl–KCl eutectic," [DOI: 10.1039/D4CP04190A](https://doi.org/10.1039/D4CP04190A)) resolved the primary reactions, but increasing accumulated dose introduced competing chemistry whose products remain unidentified.
solved_when: The accumulating side products generated by increasing dose are chemically identified, and their formation and reaction pathways are determined such that the departure of Cr(I)/Cr(III) recombination from second-order kinetics is explained.
why: It would reveal the point at which nominally reversible radiation chemistry produces persistent chemical change in a molten salt, which is essential for predicting cumulative-dose effects that invalidate independent-event models.
key_works: K. Iwamatsu et al. (2026; first published 2025), “Kinetics of radiation-induced Cr(II) and Cr(III) redox chemistry in molten LiCl–KCl eutectic,” [DOI: 10.1039/D4CP04190A](https://doi.org/10.1039/D4CP04190A).

title: Room-temperature Pr(V) persistence beyond the demonstrated protective ligand environment
open: Can a molecular praseodymium(V) complex be isolated that persists at room temperature without the heavily shielded imidophosphorane ligand environment currently required? More precisely, can such a complex be prepared, its decomposition kinetics measured, and its electronic-state assignment established?
status: Molecular formal Pr(V) was isolated at low temperature in 2025 (A. C. Boggiano et al., "Praseodymium in the formal +5 oxidation state," [DOI: 10.1038/s41557-025-01797-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-025-01797-w)). A 2026 ligand comparison (T.-R. Nero et al., "Ligand Design Criteria for the Stability of High Oxidation State Praseodymium Complexes," [DOI: 10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c05024](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c05024)) found modest redox-potential changes but major stability differences across ligands, with some Pr(V) states observable only electrochemically.
solved_when: A room-temperature-persistent molecular Pr(V) complex outside the demonstrated imidophosphorane environment is isolated, with measured decomposition kinetics and an established electronic-state assignment.
why: It would enable systematic study of high-valent lanthanide reactivity beyond specially protected examples, opening this unusual oxidation state to general synthetic and mechanistic use.
key_works: A. C. Boggiano et al. (2025), “Praseodymium in the formal +5 oxidation state,” [DOI: 10.1038/s41557-025-01797-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-025-01797-w); T.-R. Nero et al. (2026), “Ligand Design Criteria for the Stability of High Oxidation State Praseodymium Complexes,” [DOI: 10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c05024](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.inorgchem.5c05024).

title: High-turnover elemental-germanium bromoalkylation with a closed inventory
open: Develop mechanically activated elemental Ge for alkene bromoalkylation with measured recovery and losses. A proposed engineering milestone is at least 100 cumulative turnovers without continuous net consumption of the Ge inventory.
status: Guo and colleagues demonstrated activation and catalytic bromoalkylation in 2025, alongside separate Ge recycling experiments. The 100-turnover criterion with a complete inventory is a proposed assessment, not a reported record.
solved_when: At least 100 cumulative turnovers are achieved without continuous net consumption of the Ge inventory, with recovery and losses quantitatively measured.
why: Establishes whether elemental Ge can function as a reusable process material.
key_works: G. Guo et al. (2025), “Elemental Germanium Activation and Catalysis Enabled by Mechanical Force,” [DOI: 10.1002/anie.202421446](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202421446).

title: The transient silane–silylium ion in stibenium-catalysed Si–C redistribution
open: Can the proposed silane–silylium ion [Et₂HSi···H–SiEt₃]⁺ be directly detected, or at least kinetically discriminated, during silane redistribution catalysed by a structurally constrained stibenium? In formal terms, the question is whether this transient cation is the actual carrier of exchange between Et₃SiH and the redistribution products Et₂SiH₂/Et₄Si.
status: The 2026 work of Toami and Dobrovetsky demonstrates Si–C activation and identifies Sb(V) species consistent with the catalytic cycle, but the short-lived silane–silylium carrier remains only proposed.
solved_when: Either the [Et₂HSi···H–SiEt₃]⁺ intermediate is observed directly, or kinetic data conclusively establish (or rule out) its role in mediating exchange between Et₃SiH and Et₂SiH₂/Et₄Si under constrained-stibenium conditions.
why: Settling this determines whether Si–C redistribution proceeds at the antimony centre or instead propagates through a cationic silicon chain — mechanistic knowledge that directly guides catalyst design in this class.
key_works: D. Toami and R. Dobrovetsky (2026), “Structurally Constrained Stibenium: Metallomimetic C−Si Bond Activation,” [DOI: 10.1002/anie.3059944](https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.3059944).

title: An isolable molecular antimony-mononitride adduct
open: Can an intact antimony-mononitride (SbN) unit be stabilized within an isolable molecular adduct, and if so, what are its bonding and vibrational characteristics? A successful synthesis should be paired with a full structural and spectroscopic characterization, including an isotope-sensitive vibrational signature for the SbN unit.
status: SbN has been known in the gas phase since Coy and Sponer's 1940 emission spectroscopy experiments, but it has never been isolated in a molecular adduct; the 2026 work of Qian and colleagues, which reports an o-benzoquinone arsenic-mononitride (As≡N) complex, lists SbN among the heavier analogues detected but not isolated.
solved_when: An intact SbN-containing molecular adduct is synthesized and isolated as a characterizable sample, with its bonding established and its isotope-sensitive vibrational signature identified.
why: An isolable sample would directly test how coordination to a molecular framework stabilizes a heavy-element nitride, informing broader understanding of heavy-element multiple bonds.
key_works: N. H. Coy and H. Sponer (1940), “Emission Spectrum of Antimony Nitride,” [DOI: 10.1103/PhysRev.58.709](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRev.58.709); W. Qian et al. (2026), “Synthesis of an o-Benzoquinone Arsenic Mononitride (As≡N) Complex and Its Reaction to Singlet Arsinonitrene,” [DOI: 10.1021/jacs.5c20377](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.5c20377).

title: Carbon and electron sources of iron oxalate in gall-ink paper
open: Does the oxalate that accumulates in aged gall-ink paper draw its carbon from the cellulose substrate, from the polyphenols of the ink, or from some other component — and which species donates the electrons that reduce Fe(III) along the way? A decisive answer pairs isotopic or chemical tracing of the oxalate carbon source with identification of the coupled electron donor.
status: A 2026 ink/mockup study (M. Nunes et al., "From Ink to Mockup: An Integrated Study of Historical Gall Ink Formulations and Their Impact on Paper," DOI: 10.1002/cplu.202500369) observed ferrous oxalate emerging as ferric polyphenol complexes were depleted, but product detection alone did not establish the oxalate's carbon source or the complete redox balance.
solved_when: The carbon source of the oxalate in aged gall-ink paper (cellulose, ink polyphenols, or another component) is experimentally identified, and the electron donor coupled to Fe(III) reduction is determined, with the redox balance closed.
why: It settles whether iron oxalate formation is a diagnostic marker of cellulose destruction, of ink alteration, or of both — the distinction that conservators need to interpret the compound's presence in a document.
key_works: M. Nunes et al. (2026), “From Ink to Mockup: An Integrated Study of Historical Gall Ink Formulations and Their Impact on Paper,” [DOI: 10.1002/cplu.202500369](https://doi.org/10.1002/cplu.202500369).

title: The simultaneous DOE ultimate PEM electrolyser target
subfield: Water splitting, hydrogen production and fuel cells
open: Can a single practical PEM electrolysis stack meet the full set of DOE ultimate targets at once — high current density, low noble-metal loading, and long service life — rather than trading one against another? Formally, the goal is simultaneous achievement of 3 A cm⁻² at 1.6 V per cell, 0.125 mg cm⁻² total platinum-group metals, 80,000-hour lifetime, and the associated cost requirements, on one practical stack.
status: This is a combined target and no stack meets it. A 2025 study (Y. Chen et al., *Support-free iridium hydroxide for high-efficiency proton-exchange membrane water electrolysis*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-58019-7) achieved below 1.75 V at 4 A cm⁻² with 0.375 mg Ir cm⁻², advancing only some constraints. The targets come from the U.S. DOE official table, *Technical Targets for Proton Exchange Membrane Electrolysis*.
solved_when: One practical stack simultaneously demonstrates 3 A cm⁻² at 1.6 V per cell, 0.125 mg cm⁻² total platinum-group metals, 80,000-hour lifetime, and the DOE cost requirements.
why: It would sharply reduce renewable hydrogen's material and capital intensity, by cutting both the iridium/platinum inventory per unit of capacity and the capital cost of electrolysis plants.
key_works: U.S. DOE, *Technical Targets for Proton Exchange Membrane Electrolysis*, [official table, accessed 2026-10-06](https://www.energy.gov/cmei/fuels/technical-targets-proton-exchange-membrane-electrolysis); Y. Chen et al. (2025), *Support-free iridium hydroxide for high-efficiency proton-exchange membrane water electrolysis*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-58019-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-58019-7).

title: Transferable orbital-free kinetic-energy functional
open: Can we build an orbital-free kinetic-energy functional that stays accurate on molecules it was not trained on — reproducing optimized densities, forces and dissociation curves across unfamiliar molecules, charge states and bonding environments? Formally, the functional should retain its accuracy under distribution shift and, once training and density-optimization costs are counted, deliver a genuine scaling advantage over orbital-based methods.
status: The kinetic-energy closure has obstructed molecular orbital-free calculations for decades. Deep learning brought substantial molecular progress in 2024 (H. Zhang et al. (2024), *Overcoming the barrier of orbital-free density functional theory for molecular systems using deep learning*, [DOI:10.1038/s43588-024-00605-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43588-024-00605-8); [arXiv:2309.16578](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16578)), but broad chemical transferability remains unresolved.
solved_when: A single orbital-free kinetic-energy functional, trained on a defined set of systems, yields optimized densities, forces and dissociation curves of demonstrated accuracy on held-out molecules spanning unfamiliar charge states and bonding environments, and the total cost including training and density optimization shows a scaling advantage over orbital-based electronic-structure calculations.
why: It would push accurate electronic-structure simulation into size and timescale regimes for large reactive systems that orbital-based methods cannot reach.
key_works: H. Zhang et al. (2024), *Overcoming the barrier of orbital-free density functional theory for molecular systems using deep learning*, [DOI:10.1038/s43588-024-00605-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s43588-024-00605-8); [arXiv:2309.16578](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16578).

title: Reliable density-functional double excitations
open: Can density-functional theory be made to reliably predict states with substantial double-excitation character — their excitation energies, oscillator strengths and potential-energy surfaces — across diverse molecules, including where such states mix and near bond dissociation?
status: Ordinary adiabatic linear-response TDDFT has a longstanding limitation for double excitations. A 2025 ensemble-functional construction (T. Gould, S. G. Dale, L. Kronik and S. Pittalis, *State-Specific Density Functionals for Excited States via a Density-Driven Correlation Model*, [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.134.228001](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.134.228001)) resolved representative failures; broad validation and reliable dynamics remain open.
solved_when: A density-functional method delivers accurate excitation energies, oscillator strengths and potential-energy surfaces for states of substantial double-excitation character across diverse molecules, correctly treating state mixing and bond dissociation, with broad validation beyond representative cases and reliable dynamics.
why: Double excitations participate in photochemistry, relaxation and multiexciton generation, so reliable access to them underpins applications from optoelectronics such as efficient singlet fission to accurate many-body excitation spectra.
key_works: T. Gould, S. G. Dale, L. Kronik and S. Pittalis (2025), *State-Specific Density Functionals for Excited States via a Density-Driven Correlation Model*, [DOI:10.1103/PhysRevLett.134.228001](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevLett.134.228001).

title: Experimentally anchored spin-gap benchmark beyond SSE17
open: Can we build a reference set of spin splittings for multimetal and heavier-element complexes that carries the same experimental anchoring as today's benchmarks, with quantified corrections for vibrational, environmental, and measurement effects?
status: SSE17 assembled 17 experimentally grounded cases of transition-metal spin-state energetics in 2024 (M. Radoń et al. (2024), *Performance of quantum chemistry methods for a benchmark set of spin-state energetics derived from experimental data of 17 transition metal complexes (SSE17)*, [DOI:10.1039/D4SC05471G](https://doi.org/10.1039/D4SC05471G)); broader chemical coverage remains incomplete.
solved_when: A benchmark exists covering multimetal and heavier-element complexes beyond the 17 cases of SSE17, with each reference spin splitting accompanied by quantified vibrational, environmental, and measurement uncertainties.
why: Without trustworthy references, apparent gains in computational methods cannot be distinguished from noise, so genuine improvements stay hidden.
key_works: M. Radoń et al. (2024), *Performance of quantum chemistry methods for a benchmark set of spin-state energetics derived from experimental data of 17 transition metal complexes (SSE17)*, [DOI:10.1039/D4SC05471G](https://doi.org/10.1039/D4SC05471G).

title: Wavefunction foundation models across chemical regimes
open: Can a pretrained electronic wavefunction model carry its chemical knowledge into unfamiliar territory — new elements, charge states, geometries, and correlation regimes — without extensive retraining, while still reporting trustworthy accuracy diagnostics? In formal terms, the goal is a construction achieving reliable transfer across these distribution shifts, with validated forces and energy differences.
status: Orbformer, first posted in 2025 and revised in September 2026, learned from 22,000 structures and reported chemical accuracy on selected bond-breaking benchmarks [A. Foster et al., *An ab initio foundation model of wavefunctions that accurately describes chemical bond breaking*, arXiv:2506.19960, DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-76604-2]. Broad reliability under distribution shift remains open.
solved_when: A pretrained wavefunction foundation model demonstrates transfer to unseen elements, charges, geometries, and correlation regimes with limited retraining, provides reliable accuracy diagnostics, and validates forces and energy differences.
why: Reusing electronic knowledge across chemical regimes could substantially reduce the repeated wavefunction optimization currently required for each new system.
key_works: A. Foster et al. (2025/2026), *An ab initio foundation model of wavefunctions that accurately describes chemical bond breaking*, [arXiv:2506.19960](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.19960), DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-76604-2.

title: Ground-state preparation with predictable chemical scaling
open: Can we prepare ground states of chemically difficult instances so that quantum energy estimation succeeds with total cost growing favorably as system size increases — without assuming the exact ground-state energy or overlap is known in advance?
status: Fomichev and colleagues supplied an integrated preparation and energy-distribution framework in 2024 (S. Fomichev et al. (2024), *Initial State Preparation for Quantum Chemistry on Quantum Computers*, [DOI:10.1103/PRXQuantum.5.040339](https://doi.org/10.1103/PRXQuantum.5.040339); [arXiv:2310.18410](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.18410)); inexpensive preparation across strongly correlated molecular families remains unestablished.
solved_when: A preparation method exists whose total cost (preparation plus estimation) and success probability scale favorably with system size on strongly correlated molecular families, with overlap or energy distributions assessed without knowledge of the exact answer.
why: State preparation can dominate the cost of otherwise efficient quantum algorithms, so unpredictable preparation scaling would negate the advantage of fast energy estimation.
key_works: S. Fomichev et al. (2024), *Initial State Preparation for Quantum Chemistry on Quantum Computers*, [DOI:10.1103/PRXQuantum.5.040339](https://doi.org/10.1103/PRXQuantum.5.040339); [arXiv:2310.18410](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.18410).

title: End-to-end useful quantum advantage for molecular energies
open: Can a quantum computer perform a molecular-energy calculation that genuinely matters — beating the best applicable classical method once every cost is counted? Formally, the full end-to-end pipeline, including state preparation, error correction, measurements, and model errors, must yield an accuracy or cost advantage over the strongest available classical approach for a chemically consequential system.
