status: A 2026 preprint by S. Kanasugi, R. Toshio, K. Maruyama and H. Oshima (*Enabling Chemically Accurate Quantum Phase Estimation in the Early Fault-Tolerant Regime*, [arXiv:2603.22778](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.22778)) estimated selected 20–50-orbital calculations on roughly 100,000 physical qubits. These are architecture-dependent resource estimates; the requested experimental advantage remains open.
solved_when: An executed calculation demonstrates an end-to-end advantage over the best applicable classical methods on a consequential molecular-energy problem, with preparation, error-correction, measurement, and model errors all included; this goes beyond resource estimates such as the 2026 preprint's 20–50-orbital calculations on roughly 100,000 physical qubits.
why: It would establish when quantum computing actually changes the practical cost of chemical discovery, rather than merely promising to.
key_works: S. Kanasugi, R. Toshio, K. Maruyama and H. Oshima (2026), *Enabling Chemically Accurate Quantum Phase Estimation in the Early Fault-Tolerant Regime*, [arXiv:2603.22778](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.22778), preprint.

title: Uniformly reliable surface hopping
open: Can we build a trajectory-based surface-hopping method that is affordable, yet treats coherence, decoherence, state crossings, and equilibrium populations consistently across coupling regimes, with controlled errors against full quantum dynamics?
status: Surface hopping has developed over decades. Mannouch and Richardson's 2023 mapping approach (arXiv:2212.11773) supplied a principled alternative, while general reliability for realistic multistate dynamics remains unresolved.
solved_when: Such a method exists and its error against reference quantum dynamics is controlled and quantified uniformly across coupling regimes, at a cost that keeps it affordable for realistic multistate dynamics.
why: Photochemical branching depends on electronic transitions and nuclear motion evolving together, so a method that fails in any coupling regime or loses error control mispredicts product outcomes.
key_works: J. R. Mannouch and J. O. Richardson (2023), *A mapping approach to surface hopping*, [arXiv:2212.11773](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.11773).

title: Common molecular benchmarks for nonadiabatic dynamics
open: Can the nonadiabatic dynamics community agree on a set of public, common molecular benchmarks that allow methods to be compared on equal footing? The goal is benchmarks with shared initial conditions, reproducible Hamiltonians, converged reference observables, experimental comparisons, and quantified uncertainties.
status: A 2024 CECAM workshop and a 2025 community roadmap (L. E. Cigrang et al. (2025), *Roadmap for Molecular Benchmarks in Nonadiabatic Dynamics*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.jpca.5c02171](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpca.5c02171); [arXiv:2502.14569](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14569)) explicitly identified the shortage of comprehensive realistic benchmarks; existing individual comparisons provide only partial coverage.
solved_when: Publicly available benchmark sets exist that include shared initial conditions, reproducible Hamiltonians, converged reference observables, experimental comparisons, and quantified uncertainties for realistic nonadiabatic molecular systems.
why: Consistent reference data would make algorithm selection and claims of methodological progress genuinely assessable, replacing ad hoc pairwise comparisons with a common standard.
key_works: L. E. Cigrang et al. (2025), *Roadmap for Molecular Benchmarks in Nonadiabatic Dynamics*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.jpca.5c02171](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpca.5c02171); [arXiv:2502.14569](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.14569).

title: Predictive roaming-channel branching
open: Can roaming reactions — those that bypass a conventional transition state — be predicted quantitatively? The goal is a theory that yields roaming branching fractions, lifetimes, and correlated product-state distributions across excitation energies and isotopic substitutions, and that identifies the regimes where quantum resonances render classical trajectory descriptions invalid.
status: Roaming was first identified in formaldehyde in 2004, and the 2024 direct observation of a roaming intermediate by G. L. Abma et al. (*Direct Observation of a Roaming Intermediate and Its Dynamics*, DOI:10.1021/jacs.4c01543) strengthened the mechanistic evidence; a transferable quantitative rate theory nevertheless remains open.
solved_when: A transferable, quantitative rate theory reproduces roaming branching fractions, lifetimes, and correlated product states as functions of excitation energy and isotope, and delineates the conditions under which quantum resonances invalidate classical trajectory descriptions.
why: Roaming alters combustion and photolysis product distributions without following a conventional transition-state pathway, so without such a theory these product channels cannot be predicted from first principles.
key_works: G. L. Abma et al. (2024), *Direct Observation of a Roaming Intermediate and Its Dynamics*, [DOI:10.1021/jacs.4c01543](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.4c01543).

title: Complete state-to-state polyatomic reaction maps
open: Can we build complete reaction maps for polyatomic reactions that specify the correlated quantum-state distribution of every product channel, and how those distributions depend on the reactant's initial vibrational mode and collision geometry? Formally, the goal is to measure and predict full state-to-state correlations while quantifying channels that escape detection.
status: State-resolved work now extends beyond triatomics, but comprehensive coverage remains limited. A 2025 D + CH₄ study identified umbrella bending as a reporter of reaction dynamics (Y. Tan et al. 2025, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-61117-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-61117-1)); see also H. Pan et al. (2023), [DOI:10.1021/acs.jpclett.3c02853](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpclett.3c02853).
solved_when: A polyatomic reaction is characterized by measured and predicted correlated quantum-state distributions of all products, including their dependence on selected reactant vibrations and collision geometry, with undetected channels quantified.
why: Such maps reveal how energy placed in a particular vibrational mode controls chemical outcomes, turning mode-selective chemistry from case studies into a predictive framework.
key_works: H. Pan et al. (2023), *State-to-State Dynamics in Mode-Selective Polyatomic Reactions*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.jpclett.3c02853](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpclett.3c02853); Y. Tan et al. (2025), *Revealing umbrella bending as a reporter mode in the D+CH4 reaction*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-61117-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-61117-1).

title: Quantum tomography of a reacting polyatomic molecule
open: Can we perform full quantum-state tomography on a polyatomic molecule while it is reacting — reconstructing a molecular density matrix, including the coherences, in a way that stands up to experimental scrutiny? A satisfactory answer must state its identifiability assumptions and quantify what information the measurement scheme leaves undetermined.
status: A 2021 ultrafast diffraction experiment reconstructed rotational wavepackets (M. Zhang et al., *Quantum state tomography of molecules by ultrafast diffraction*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-021-25770-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-25770-6)). Extending tomography to coupled electronic and vibrational motion in reacting polyatomics remains substantially harder. Related work includes scalable state tomography in quantum information and identifiability analysis for inverse problems in applied mathematics.
solved_when: An experimental reconstruction of a density matrix for a reacting polyatomic molecule is demonstrated, capturing the relevant electronic and vibrational coherences, with an explicit statement of the identifiability assumptions and a quantification of the missing information.
why: Quantum-state information can distinguish reaction mechanisms that produce similar average structures, which average-observable measurements cannot separate.
key_works: M. Zhang et al. (2021), *Quantum state tomography of molecules by ultrafast diffraction*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-021-25770-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-021-25770-6).

title: Separating collective vibrational-cavity effects from heat transport
open: Once temperature, radiative energy transfer, and surface chemistry have been independently measured, do any residual rate changes remain that genuinely require collective quantum light–matter effects? Formally, the challenge is to predict those residual effects quantitatively rather than merely invoke them.
status: The field expanded after 2015. Brawley and colleagues showed in 2025 that radiative energy transfer explains a particular dehydration effect (Z. T. Brawley et al. (2025), *Vibrational weak and strong coupling modify a chemical reaction via cavity-mediated radiative energy transfer*, [DOI:10.1038/s41557-024-01723-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-024-01723-6)); other systems remain unsettled.
solved_when: A quantitative account of cavity-modified reaction rates is achieved in which temperature, radiative energy transfer, and surface chemistry are each measured independently, and any remaining rate changes are predicted quantitatively as collective effects.
why: Without such discrimination, cavity-controlled chemistry cannot be made predictable — apparent collective effects may simply mask ordinary thermal or radiative mechanisms.
key_works: Z. T. Brawley et al. (2025), *Vibrational weak and strong coupling modify a chemical reaction via cavity-mediated radiative energy transfer*, [DOI:10.1038/s41557-024-01723-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-024-01723-6).

title: Test of the vibrational-condensation hypothesis
open: Does macroscopic occupation of a collective vibrational state actually occur under experimental dark-cavity conditions, and can it quantitatively account for the observed chemical changes? In other words, is the proposed vibrational-condensation mechanism the correct explanation of vibrational strong coupling effects on reactions?
status: Mondal, Montillo Vega and Huo proposed the mechanism in July 2026 in *A macroscopic condensation theory for vibrational strong coupling effects* ([DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-75222-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-75222-2)); it remains a theoretical hypothesis awaiting discriminating experimental tests.
solved_when: A discriminating experimental test under dark-cavity conditions either observes or rules out macroscopic occupation of the collective vibrational state, and the measured chemical changes are quantitatively matched by the condensation theory.
why: Validation would establish a direct link between molecular-level coupling and macroscopic reaction-rate changes, grounding the interpretation of vibrational strong coupling experiments in a predictive microscopic mechanism.
key_works: M. E. Mondal, S. Montillo Vega and P. Huo (2026), *A macroscopic condensation theory for vibrational strong coupling effects*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-75222-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-75222-2).

title: Quantitative map of water’s liquid–liquid critical region
open: Can we produce an independent, quantitative map of the liquid–liquid critical region of deeply supercooled water — its coexistence curve, critical parameters, and scaling behavior — while cleanly distinguishing genuine equilibration from crystallization?
status: Experimental evidence for a liquid–liquid critical point in supercooled water was reported in March 2026 by You and colleagues (S. You et al. 2026, *Experimental evidence of a liquid-liquid critical point in supercooled water*, [DOI:10.1126/science.aec0018](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aec0018)), including critical-region behavior around 210 ± 8 K; independent quantitative phase mapping remains open.
solved_when: The coexistence curve, critical parameters, and critical scaling behavior of deeply supercooled water are independently determined, with equilibration demonstrably separated from crystallization, and the critical-region behavior around 210 ± 8 K is quantitatively confirmed or refuted.
why: Such a map would tightly constrain explanations of water’s thermodynamic and structural anomalies, anchoring the liquid–liquid critical point scenario in measured data rather than inference.
key_works: S. You et al. (2026), *Experimental evidence of a liquid-liquid critical point in supercooled water*, [DOI:10.1126/science.aec0018](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aec0018).

title: Controlled real-time nuclear quantum dynamics in liquids
open: Can we compute real-time correlation functions and reaction dynamics for quantum nuclei in condensed phases with errors that are controlled and systematically improvable, at scale? In particular, where exactly do current approximations fail for tunneling, coherence, and spectral line shapes in liquids?
status: Equilibrium path-integral methods are well established, but real-time dynamics remains substantially harder. DL_POLY Quantum 2.1 incorporated improved centroid and quasi-centroid methods in 2025, with selected demonstrations on vibrational spectra [N. London et al. (2025), *DL_POLY Quantum 2.1: A Suite of Real-Time Path Integral Methods for the Simulation of Dynamical Properties and Vibrational Spectra*, DOI:10.1021/acs.jpca.4c08644]. The core obstacle is the dynamical sign problem of quantum statistical mechanics.
solved_when: A scalable method exists that yields real-time correlation functions and reaction dynamics for quantum nuclei in the condensed phase with controlled, quantified errors, and the failure boundaries of the method are established for tunneling, coherence, and spectral line shapes.
why: Quantum motion of hydrogen nuclei directly shapes reaction rates, spectra, and transport in liquids, so reliable real-time methods would make these observables predictable rather than qualitatively estimated.
key_works: N. London et al. (2025), *DL_POLY Quantum 2.1: A Suite of Real-Time Path Integral Methods for the Simulation of Dynamical Properties and Vibrational Spectra*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.jpca.4c08644](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpca.4c08644).

title: Depth-resolved self-ion distribution at the air–water interface
open: How are hydronium and hydroxide ions distributed in depth at a clean, nominally neutral water surface? Specifically, can the predicted double-layer arrangement of separate hydronium and hydroxide layers be directly confirmed at the molecular depth scale, bringing spectroscopy, electrokinetics and simulation into agreement?
status: The acid–base character of the air–water interface has been disputed for decades. A 2024 simulation by P. Zhang, M. Feng and X. Xu (*Double-Layer Distribution of Hydronium and Hydroxide Ions in the Air–Water Interface*, [DOI:10.1021/acsphyschemau.3c00076](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsphyschemau.3c00076)) proposed separate hydronium and hydroxide layers; direct confirmation remains open.
solved_when: A measurement of the hydronium and hydroxide concentration profiles across an uncontaminated, nominally neutral air–water interface resolves the profiles with molecular depth resolution, and its findings are consistent with spectroscopic, electrokinetic and simulation evidence.
why: Local proton availability at the interface controls interfacial reaction pathways, so knowing the true depth profiles determines which chemistry actually proceeds at water surfaces.
key_works: P. Zhang, M. Feng and X. Xu (2024), *Double-Layer Distribution of Hydronium and Hydroxide Ions in the Air–Water Interface*, [DOI:10.1021/acsphyschemau.3c00076](https://doi.org/10.1021/acsphyschemau.3c00076).

title: Finite-temperature ideal glass transition in molecular liquids
open: Does a realistic three-dimensional molecular liquid truly reach an equilibrium ideal-glass transition at finite temperature, where its configurational entropy vanishes, or does some mechanism intervene to avoid this entropy crisis?
status: The entropy-crisis question dates to Kauzmann's 1948 analysis. Enhanced sampling has extended equilibrium entropy measurements, but extrapolation to a genuine singularity remains disputed; see L. Berthier et al. (2017), *Configurational entropy measurements in extremely supercooled liquids that break the glass ceiling*, [arXiv:1704.08257](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.08257).
solved_when: A determination, theoretical or experimental, of whether the equilibrium configurational entropy of a realistic three-dimensional molecular liquid vanishes at a finite temperature, or a demonstration of what mechanism prevents such a singularity.
why: A resolution would discriminate between the major competing explanations of glass formation, replacing extrapolation-based arguments with a settled verdict on the Kauzmann paradox.
key_works: L. Berthier et al. (2017), *Configurational entropy measurements in extremely supercooled liquids that break the glass ceiling*, [arXiv:1704.08257](https://arxiv.org/abs/1704.08257).

title: Molecular origin of secondary glass relaxation
open: Can we predict, from molecular structure, which motions give rise to secondary relaxation peaks and excess wings in glass formers, and how those motions couple to structural relaxation across chemically distinct systems?
status: These longstanding spectroscopic features are becoming accessible to simulations. Simon, Barrat and Berthier (2026) reached experimental-glass-transition conditions for a molecular model and visualized excess-wing motion [*Molecular Motion at the Experimental Glass Transition*, DOI:10.1103/4twk-33j7].
solved_when: A predictive account exists that identifies the molecular motions responsible for secondary relaxation peaks and excess wings, and correctly describes their coupling to structural relaxation across chemically distinct glass formers.
why: Secondary relaxation governs dielectric loss, mechanical response, and residual mobility, so a predictive account would connect molecular structure to key material properties of glasses.
key_works: R. Simon, J.-L. Barrat and L. Berthier (2026), *Molecular Motion at the Experimental Glass Transition*, [DOI:10.1103/4twk-33j7](https://doi.org/10.1103/4twk-33j7).

title: Hydrophobic attraction for heterogeneous molecular surfaces
open: Can we predict the water-mediated association free energy between chemically patterned, curved, and flexible molecular surfaces purely from measurable surface properties? In particular, under what conditions do critical-drying descriptions of hydrophobic attraction remain quantitatively accurate for such heterogeneous real surfaces?
status: A universal molecular description has remained elusive for decades. Wilding and Turci's 2025 theory explains the temperature-dependent attraction for model spherical solutes [DOI:10.1103/66lz-1yw9], but heterogeneous real surfaces remain open.
solved_when: A theory exists that predicts water-mediated association free energies for chemically patterned, curved, and flexible surfaces from measurable properties, and specifies when critical-drying descriptions remain quantitative for those surfaces.
why: Reliable predictions would make self-assembly and molecular recognition models genuinely predictive rather than fitted, replacing decades of case-by-case modeling.
key_works: N. B. Wilding and F. Turci (2025), *Origin of the inverse temperature dependence of hydrophobic attraction*, [DOI:10.1103/66lz-1yw9](https://doi.org/10.1103/66lz-1yw9).

title: Operational electric-field distributions at reactive aqueous surfaces
open: What electric fields do reacting solutes actually experience at aqueous surfaces — how strong are these fields, how long do they last, and how much do they quantitatively change reaction rates? A resolution requires locally resolved field distributions and lifetimes together with consistent mappings between spectroscopic observables and simulation outputs.
status: A 2025 study by J. C. Shirley et al. (*Reevaluating Anomalous Electric Fields at the Air–Water Interface: A Surface-Specific Spectroscopic Survey*, [DOI:10.1021/jacs.5c14541](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.5c14541); [arXiv:2508.15422](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.15422)) found no exceptionally strong or long-lived fields at pristine neutral air–water interfaces; charged and compositionally complex reactive interfaces remain to be measured separately.
solved_when: Local electric-field distributions and lifetimes at reactive aqueous interfaces are measured and/or computed with a validated spectroscopy–simulation mapping, and their quantitative contribution to interfacial rate changes is established.
why: It would replace qualitative electric-field explanations of interfacial reactivity with reaction models constrained by measured field data.
key_works: J. C. Shirley et al. (2025), *Reevaluating Anomalous Electric Fields at the Air–Water Interface: A Surface-Specific Spectroscopic Survey*, [DOI:10.1021/jacs.5c14541](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.5c14541); [arXiv:2508.15422](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.15422).

title: Transferable homogeneous ice-nucleation rates
open: Can we predict how fast supercooled water droplets freeze — the homogeneous ice-nucleation rate — in a way that transfers across temperature, droplet size, and cooling history, with quantified uncertainties that account for both the choice of microscopic model and the details of the measurement protocol? A complete answer would be a predictive framework whose rate predictions, with error bars, are validated against experiments outside the conditions used to fit it.
status: The problem has been studied for decades and remains open. A 2024 analysis by R. K. R. Addulla, I. de Almeida Ribeiro, V. Molinero and B. Peters (*Modeling homogeneous ice nucleation from drop-freezing experiments: impact of droplet volume dispersion and cooling rates*, [DOI:10.5194/acp-24-10833-2024](https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-24-10833-2024)) showed that dispersion in droplet sizes biases inferred nucleation barriers and supplied an improved analysis framework; transferable microscopic prediction remains unsolved.
solved_when: A model exists that predicts homogeneous ice-nucleation rates across varying temperature, droplet size, and cooling history, with uncertainty estimates spanning both microscopic-model choices and measurement protocols, and is demonstrably transferable to conditions beyond its calibration set.
why: Ice-formation rates govern cloud microphysics, cryopreservation, and industrial freezing, so a transferable prediction would directly inform climate and process modeling where direct measurement is impractical.
key_works: R. K. R. Addula, I. de Almeida Ribeiro, V. Molinero and B. Peters (2024), *Modeling homogeneous ice nucleation from drop-freezing experiments: impact of droplet volume dispersion and cooling rates*, [DOI:10.5194/acp-24-10833-2024](https://doi.org/10.5194/acp-24-10833-2024).

title: Absolute nucleation-rate prediction across solvents
open: Can we predict, from first principles, the absolute rate at which crystals nucleate — including how long a supersaturated solution waits before crystallizing — for a given solute–solvent pair? A complete theory must hold across solvents, supersaturation levels, and impurity conditions, accounting for desolvation and interfacial barriers.
status: A 2025 study by J. Zeglinski et al. (*Toward Predicting Nucleation Difficulty of Organic Compounds Crystallized from Different Solvents*, DOI:10.1021/acs.cgd.5c00176) connected computed activity coefficients with relative nucleation difficulty for three organic solutes. Universal prediction of absolute rates and polymorph branching remains unresolved.
solved_when: A validated model reproduces absolute nucleation rates and induction-time distributions across solvents, supersaturations, and impurity conditions, with desolvation and interfacial barriers treated explicitly.
why: It would replace largely empirical crystallization-process development with predictive design of solvent and conditions.
key_works: J. Zeglinski et al. (2025), *Toward Predicting Nucleation Difficulty of Organic Compounds Crystallized from Different Solvents*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.cgd.5c00176](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.cgd.5c00176).

title: Methane-hydrate nucleation under realistic interfaces
open: Can we predict how methane hydrates nucleate — which pathway they follow and how long induction takes — under the messy conditions of the real world, rather than idealized ones? Formally, the goal is a theory or validated simulation protocol that yields hydrate nucleation pathways and induction times across realistic methane concentrations, sediment environments, ice surfaces, and thermal histories.
status: A 2025 study (D. Kumar, L.-Y. Huang, D. T. Wu and S.-T. Lin, *Accelerated Methane Hydrate Nucleation near Ice: Free Energy Landscape and Kinetic Enhancement*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.jpcc.5c03969](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpcc.5c03969)) quantified ice-mediated acceleration using 200 trajectories at a single temperature, pressure, and concentration. Generalizing beyond such controlled simulations remains open.
solved_when: Predictions of nucleation pathway and induction time match experiment (or simulation ground truth) across varied methane concentrations, sediments, ice surfaces, and thermal histories — not just a single controlled condition (one temperature, one pressure, one concentration).
why: Reliable predictive kinetics would directly inform gas storage design, pipeline safety against hydrate plug formation, and modeling of seafloor hydrate processes.
key_works: D. Kumar, L.-Y. Huang, D. T. Wu and S.-T. Lin (2025), *Accelerated Methane Hydrate Nucleation near Ice: Free Energy Landscape and Kinetic Enhancement*, [DOI:10.1021/acs.jpcc.5c03969](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jpcc.5c03969).

title: Predicting which computed polymorphs can actually crystallize
open: Which of the many crystal structures predicted for a molecule can actually be made in the lab? Formally: given a computed crystal energy landscape together with processing conditions, determine which minima are accessible and through what synthetic routes, accounting for solvent-dependent strain and the costs of forming nucleation surfaces.
status: A 2025 conceptual framework by J. van de Streek et al. (*A Conceptual Framework for the Crystallizability of Organic Compounds*, [DOI:10.1021/jacs.5c08933](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.5c08933)) linked molecular strain with crystallization accessibility, but identified missing absolute, solvent-dependent nucleation criteria as an open gap.
solved_when: A framework exists that takes a crystal landscape and processing conditions as input and identifies the accessible minima and routes to them, including absolute, solvent-dependent nucleation criteria tied to molecular strain and nucleation-surface costs.
why: A predicted thermodynamically stable polymorph is useful only if the material can actually be crystallized and obtained; without accessibility prediction, computational crystal structure prediction cannot tell chemists what to synthesize.
key_works: J. van de Streek et al. (2025), *A Conceptual Framework for the Crystallizability of Organic Compounds*, [DOI:10.1021/jacs.5c08933](https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.5c08933).

title: Dense-cloud sulfur budget and phase partition
open: Where does interstellar sulfur actually hide in dense clouds? Determine the partition of sulfur among gas-phase molecules, salts, polysulfanes, elemental sulfur, and refractory grains along the same sightlines, and account for how the observed depletion evolves as clouds evolve.
status: The decades-old budget problem has plausible candidate reservoirs: 2025 experiments produced polysulfanes and S₈ in irradiated ice (A. Herath et al. 2025), and XRISM observations provide iron-sulfide evidence on other sightlines (L. Corrales et al. 2025), but this does not close every dense-cloud sulfur budget.
solved_when: A self-consistent sulfur budget is achieved for the same dense-cloud sightlines, quantifying the fraction of sulfur in each reservoir (gas, salts, polysulfanes, elemental sulfur, refractory grains) at a level that explains the observed depletion across cloud evolutionary stages.
why: The volatility of the dominant sulfur reservoir sets how much sulfur is delivered to forming planets, directly shaping planetary elemental inheritance from protoplanetary disks.
key_works: A. Herath et al. (2025), *Missing interstellar sulfur in inventories of polysulfanes and molecular octasulfur crowns*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-61259-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-61259-2); L. Corrales et al. (2025), *XRISM insights for interstellar sulfur*, [DOI:10.1093/pasj/psaf068](https://doi.org/10.1093/pasj/psaf068).

title: Distribution-resolved diffusion data for interstellar ices
open: How do atoms and radicals actually diffuse across realistic, evolving amorphous interstellar ices, and can we measure the full distribution of diffusion barriers — not a single effective value — together with its dependence on ice morphology and quantified uncertainties?
status: Grain-surface models have relied on incomplete diffusion inputs for decades. A 2025 assessment by N. F. W. Ligterink et al. (*Molecular mobility of extraterrestrial ices: surface diffusion in astrochemistry and planetary science*, [DOI:10.1039/D5CP02278A](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5CP02278A)) identifies low-temperature mobility and ice restructuring as continuing gaps.
solved_when: Diffusion-barrier distributions for atoms and radicals on realistic evolving amorphous ices are measured (experimentally or theoretically) with explicit morphology dependence and uncertainties at a fidelity suitable for direct use in astrochemical reaction networks.
why: Encounter rates on grain surfaces determine whether complex molecules can form before they desorb or are destroyed, so unreliable diffusion inputs propagate directly into predictions of interstellar molecular complexity.
key_works: N. F. W. Ligterink et al. (2025), *Molecular mobility of extraterrestrial ices: surface diffusion in astrochemistry and planetary science*, [DOI:10.1039/D5CP02278A](https://doi.org/10.1039/D5CP02278A).

title: Interstellar phosphorus inventory and controlling reactions
open: How is interstellar phosphorus actually distributed between gas and grain reservoirs, and which reactions set the observed abundances of PO and PN? A resolution requires partitioning phosphorus between gas and grains and measuring the reactions that control PO and PN, so that depletion assumptions can be cleanly separated from kinetic explanations.
status: Observations currently constrain only part of the phosphorus inventory. A 2025 sensitivity analysis by M. Fernández-Ruz et al. ([DOI:10.3389/fspas.2025.1570525](https://doi.org/10.3389/fspas.2025.1570525)) reduced a 14-rate model to three influential parameters, identifying concrete measurement targets.
solved_when: The gas/grain phosphorus partition is determined and the reactions controlling PO and PN abundances are measured, with depletion effects disentangled from chemical kinetics; the influential parameters identified by the reduction of the 14-rate model are quantified.
why: It determines how much chemically available phosphorus is supplied to forming planets, a direct input on prebiotic chemistry's raw materials.
key_works: M. Fernández-Ruz et al. (2025), *Strong parameter hierarchy in the interstellar phosphorus chemical network*, [DOI:10.3389/fspas.2025.1570525](https://doi.org/10.3389/fspas.2025.1570525).

title: Operationally predictive actinide covalency
open: Can we build a bonding model for the actinides whose orbital and spectroscopic descriptors actually predict chemistry — coordination preferences, reactivity, separability — across compounds rather than case by case? Formally, this means connecting specified spectroscopic observables and orbital descriptions to transferable predictions of actinide bonding and reactivity, and resolving the standing conflict between overlap-based and energy-matching interpretations of covalency.
status: The ambiguity in how to define and measure actinide covalency is longstanding, but it has recently become experimentally sharper: in 2025, B. Schacherl et al. used resonant inelastic X-ray scattering to probe 5f populations and bond covalency (*Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering tools to count 5f electrons of actinides and probe bond covalency*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-024-54574-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-54574-7)). No universal predictive descriptor has emerged from this work.
solved_when: A descriptor (or small set of descriptors) derived from measurable spectroscopic observables and well-defined orbital populations is shown to predict actinide bonding and reactivity across distinct compounds, and adjudicates between overlap-based and energy-matching pictures of covalency.
why: Reliable bonding models are the basis for selective actinide coordination and separation — for example in nuclear fuel cycles and waste partitioning, where small differences in bonding decide what binds and what does not.
key_works: B. Schacherl et al. (2025), *Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering tools to count 5 f electrons of actinides and probe bond covalency*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-024-54574-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-54574-7).

title: Chemically reproducible thorium-229 nuclear clocks
open: Can the host composition, dopant sites, and defect landscape of a solid-state thorium-229 nuclear clock be controlled well enough that independently prepared clocks agree, with systematic uncertainties that are fully budgeted and smaller than in current demonstrations?
status: Ooi and colleagues measured 220 Hz reproducibility, approximately \(1.1\times10^{-13}\) fractionally, across two differently doped CaF₂ crystals in 2026 [DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-09999-5]. Their temperature-insensitive operating point addresses one source of variation.
solved_when: Independently prepared solid-state Th-229 clocks, differing in host or doping chemistry, reproduce the nuclear transition frequency with a fractional spread below the 2026 benchmark of approximately \(1.1\times10^{-13}\) (220 Hz), each with a complete systematic uncertainty budget.
why: Without reproducible host chemistry, solid-state nuclear clocks cannot serve as deployable frequency standards; with it, they enable transportable ultra-precise clocks and tests of varying fundamental constants.
key_works: T. Ooi et al. (2026), *Frequency reproducibility of solid-state thorium-229 nuclear clocks*, [DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-09999-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09999-5).

title: Closed-loop, energy-competitive lithium-mediated ammonia synthesis
open: Can lithium-mediated electrochemical ammonia synthesis be run as a truly closed-loop process, in which the electrolyte, proton carrier, and lithium are continuously balanced and recycled during continuous ammonia production from nitrogen and hydrogen? The goal is to achieve this at a total energy cost competitive with Haber–Bosch powered by renewable hydrogen.
status: A longstanding efficiency and scale problem. Li et al. demonstrated 300 hours of continuous operation in a 25 cm² flow electrolyser in 2024 (S. Li et al., *Long-term continuous ammonia electrosynthesis*, [DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-07276-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07276-5)); however, Faradaic efficiency alone does not establish total energy competitiveness.
solved_when: Continuous lithium-mediated ammonia production from N₂ and H₂ operates with closed electrolyte, proton-carrier, and lithium balances, at a total energy cost competitive with renewable-hydrogen Haber–Bosch — not merely at high Faradaic efficiency.
why: It would enable distributed fertilizer production with recyclable process materials, removing the dependence on centralized Haber–Bosch infrastructure.
key_works: S. Li et al. (2024), *Long-term continuous ammonia electrosynthesis*, [DOI:10.1038/s41586-024-07276-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07276-5).

title: Predictive solid-electrolyte interphases for nitrogen reduction
open: Can we predict how selective a lithium-mediated nitrogen reduction system will be for ammonia — and how that selectivity ages — from the chemistry and transport properties of its solid-electrolyte interphase, measured independently of the electrolysis itself? Formally, the goal is a transferable model that takes electrolyte composition and current history as inputs and returns ammonia selectivity and its evolution over time.
status: Mechanistic understanding is developing. Herzog et al. (2026) resolved ethanol-driven lithium-alkoxide formation and interphase–conversion correlations using operando Raman spectroscopy ([DOI:10.1038/s41929-026-01562-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41929-026-01562-3)); transferable prediction remains open.
solved_when: A predictive framework, validated across multiple electrolyte compositions and current histories, correctly forecasts ammonia selectivity and its aging from independently measured interphase chemistry and transport parameters.
why: It would replace empirical electrolyte screening with systematic, mechanism-based design of electrolytes and operating protocols for electrochemical ammonia synthesis.
key_works: A. Herzog et al. (2026), *Unveiling solid electrolyte interphase dynamics in electrochemical lithium-mediated ammonia synthesis via operando Raman spectroscopy*, [DOI:10.1038/s41929-026-01562-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41929-026-01562-3).

title: Sustainable calcium-mediated nitrogen reduction
open: Can a calcium-mediated nitrogen reduction reactor be run as a sustainable closed loop, in which the mediator and its reactive interface regenerate continuously rather than degrading batch by batch?
status: Fu et al. established calcium-mediated electrosynthesis for electrochemical ammonia synthesis in work published online in 2023 and in a 2024 issue (DOI:10.1038/s41563-023-01702-1). Durable closed-loop operation remains unresolved.
solved_when: A continuously regenerating calcium-mediated ammonia reactor is demonstrated with controlled passivation and no net consumption of electrolyte or proton donor over sustained operation.
why: It would test whether an abundant mediator such as calcium can replace lithium in electrochemical ammonia synthesis while preserving selectivity, and durable closed-loop operation is the main barrier to that replacement being practical.
key_works: X. Fu et al. (2024), *Calcium-mediated nitrogen reduction for electrochemical ammonia synthesis*, [DOI:10.1038/s41563-023-01702-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-023-01702-1).

title: Energy-efficient plasma–electrochemical nitrogen fixation
open: Can the full plasma-driven chain — air to NOₓ, absorption, electroreduction, and ammonia recovery — be engineered so that, under consistent energy accounting, it beats competing distributed nitrogen-fixation routes?
status: A 2025 four-cell demonstration (W. Liu et al. (2025), *Full runner electrolyzer stack for industrial-current-density NOₓ⁻-mediated ammonia synthesis from air and water*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-61069-6) exceeded 91% ammonia Faradaic efficiency and 95% NOₓ conversion, with over 200 hours of electrolyser stability; integrated energy competitiveness remains open.
solved_when: The complete air-to-NOₓ-to-ammonia chain is optimized end-to-end and shown, under consistent energy accounting, to outperform competing distributed routes.
why: Success would enable small fertilizer plants that respond flexibly to renewable electricity.
key_works: W. Liu et al. (2025), *Full runner electrolyzer stack for industrial-current-density NOx−-mediated ammonia synthesis from air and water*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-61069-6](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-61069-6).

title: Vacancy catalysts for practical low-pressure ammonia synthesis
open: Can a catalyst keep its nitrogen-activating anion vacancies alive over long operating periods and through transients, while sustaining practically useful ammonia production from N2 and H2 using only abundant constituents?
status: Mild-condition alternatives to Haber–Bosch have been sought for a century. A 2025 study by Z. Zhang et al. demonstrated nitrogen activation on Ba–Si oxynitride-hydride vacancies (*Anion vacancies activate N2 to ammonia on Ba–Si orthosilicate oxynitride-hydride*, [DOI:10.1038/s41557-025-01737-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-025-01737-8)).
solved_when: A vacancy-based catalyst demonstrates sustained N2-to-ammonia conversion at useful production rates under low-pressure operation through prolonged runs and transient cycling, with vacancies remaining active and the catalyst made of abundant elements.
why: It would enable lower-pressure, smaller-scale ammonia plants than Haber–Bosch and free catalyst design from scarce or costly materials.
key_works: Z. Zhang et al. (2025), *Anion vacancies activate N2 to ammonia on Ba–Si orthosilicate oxynitride-hydride*, [DOI:10.1038/s41557-025-01737-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-025-01737-8).

title: Low-temperature, precious-metal-free ammonia cracking
open: Can ammonia be cracked to fuel-cell-grade hydrogen at low temperature using only inexpensive, precious-metal-free catalysts, with all thermal or optical energy input counted against the process? The goal is a system combining high conversion, very low residual ammonia, and sustained hydrogen productivity without noble metals or high heating demand.
status: This is a longstanding hydrogen-carrier bottleneck. Ni–CeO₂−x photothermal interfaces operated for over 50 hours in a 2025 demonstration (R. Tan et al., *Breakthrough photothermal ammonia decomposition via low-barrier Ni-CeO2-x interfaces on carbon nanotubes*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-66325-3), but long-duration product-purity performance remains unresolved.
solved_when: A precious-metal-free catalyst system achieves high ammonia conversion, very low residual ammonia, and sustained hydrogen productivity over long-duration operation, with all thermal or optical input included in the accounting.
why: It would deliver fuel-cell-grade hydrogen from ammonia at lower material and heating cost, removing a longstanding hydrogen-carrier bottleneck.
key_works: R. Tan et al. (2025), *Breakthrough photothermal ammonia decomposition via low-barrier Ni-CeO2-x interfaces on carbon nanotubes*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-66325-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-66325-3).

title: Direct methane-to-methanol with simultaneous selectivity and throughput
open: Can methane be converted directly to methanol in a single sustained process that achieves both high selectivity and substantial conversion? Formally, the target is continuous direct methane oxidation yielding recoverable methanol at meaningful throughput, with overoxidation suppressed and oxidant and energy inputs properly accounted for.
status: A decades-old problem. Li et al. achieved 83.5% methanol selectivity through time-dependent charge control in 2026; continuous high-conversion manufacture remains a separate target. Key work: Y. Li et al. (2026), *Spatiotemporal photon distribution control on active sites enables bio-inspired methane-to-methanol conversion*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-70134-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-70134-7).
solved_when: A sustained direct methane-to-methanol process is demonstrated that maintains high methanol selectivity at substantial conversion, avoids overoxidation to CO₂, and honestly accounts for oxidant consumption and energy input.
why: Success would open smaller-scale routes from methane (stranded gas, biogas) to transportable liquid feedstocks, bypassing the syngas detour of conventional methanol synthesis.
key_works: Y. Li et al. (2026), *Spatiotemporal photon distribution control on active sites enables bio-inspired methane-to-methanol conversion*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-70134-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-70134-7).

title: Abundant-metal electrochemical methane hydroxylation
open: Can methane be converted selectively to methanol at room temperature by electrochemical oxidation on an anode made only of earth-abundant metals, with the product accumulating over sustained operation and the oxygen source demonstrably regenerated?
status: The state of the art is the 2025 work of C. Kim et al., which achieved high-selectivity room-temperature partial oxidation of methane to methanol via electrochemical oxygen promotion on IrO₂ catalysts, using carbonate promotion and reaching approximately 11.1 mmol methanol g-catalyst⁻¹ h⁻¹ in continuous operation ([DOI:10.1038/s41929-025-01363-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41929-025-01363-0)). Replacing IrO₂ with an abundant metal remains open.
solved_when: A room-temperature electrochemical methane-to-methanol oxidation is demonstrated on an abundant-metal anode, with sustained methanol accumulation during continuous operation and verified regeneration of the oxygen source — matching, in kind, the benchmark set by IrO₂ (approximately 11.1 mmol methanol g-catalyst⁻¹ h⁻¹ under continuous operation).
why: Replacing scarce iridium with abundant metals would free electrically controlled methane activation from critical-resource constraints, enabling scalable electrified routes from stranded methane to liquid fuels and chemicals.
key_works: C. Kim et al. (2025), *High-selectivity room-temperature partial oxidation of methane to methanol enabled by electrochemical oxygen promotion on IrO2 catalysts*, [DOI:10.1038/s41929-025-01363-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41929-025-01363-0).

title: High-yield oxidative methane coupling without deep oxidation
open: Can methane be converted to C₂+ hydrocarbons by oxidative coupling in a single pass at high yield, without the coupling products being burned to COₓ and without uneconomically large energy input? Formally, the goal is a process combining substantial single-pass methane conversion, high C₂ selectivity, sustained catalyst activity, and low heating or photon input.
status: The problem has been pursued since the 1980s. Song et al. reported approximately 90% C₂+ selectivity and high photocatalytic productivity in 2025 [H. Song et al. (2025), *Integrating photochemical and photothermal effects for selective oxidative coupling of methane into C2+ hydrocarbons with multiple active sites*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-58101-0], but the combined conversion–selectivity–energy target remains open.
solved_when: A catalyst–process combination demonstrably meets the combined conversion–selectivity–energy target: substantial single-pass methane conversion together with high C₂ selectivity, sustained catalytic activity, and low heating or photon input, at or beyond the roughly 90% C₂+ selectivity with high productivity already shown photocatalytically.
why: Success would open alternative routes from natural gas to basic petrochemicals such as ethane and ethylene, decoupling their supply from petroleum cracking.
key_works: H. Song et al. (2025), *Integrating photochemical and photothermal effects for selective oxidative coupling of methane into C2+ hydrocarbons with multiple active sites*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-58101-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-58101-0).

title: Durable CO₂-rich methane reforming with complete energy accounting
open: Can CO₂-rich methane streams be converted to specified syngas compositions in a way that controls carbon deposition and preserves integrated electrochemical–thermal efficiency? In other words, can dry reforming be made both durable and energy-accountable over realistic operating lifetimes?
status: Dry reforming has long faced durability problems. Lv et al. (2025) demonstrated tandem electro-thermocatalytic super-dry reforming [*Super-dry reforming of methane using a tandem electro-thermocatalytic system*, DOI:10.1038/s41557-025-01768-1], but integrated lifetime and scale-up remain open.
solved_when: A reforming system operating on CO₂-rich methane feeds achieves the target syngas composition with controlled carbon deposition, while maintaining integrated electrochemical–thermal efficiency over an integrated lifetime at meaningful scale.
why: Success would broaden the range of usable gas feeds for reforming and enable flexible synthesis-gas production without sacrificing energy efficiency or catalyst lifetime.
key_works: H. Lv et al. (2025), *Super-dry reforming of methane using a tandem electro-thermocatalytic system*, [DOI:10.1038/s41557-025-01768-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-025-01768-1).

title: Predictive plasma–surface coupling in CO₂ hydrogenation
open: Can we predict, from first knowledge of the plasma excitation, the catalyst surface state, and the temperature, the rate and selectivity of methanol formation in plasma-driven CO₂ hydrogenation? Formally, the challenge is to build a transferable, quantitative account that separates genuinely nonequilibrium excitation effects from ordinary heating and mass-transfer limitations.
status: A 2026 operando study (S. Xu et al., *Unveiling active sites and the cooperative role of non-thermal plasma and copper–zinc catalysts in the hydrogenation of CO2 to methanol*, DOI:10.1038/s41929-025-01477-5) resolved site evolution and cooperative plasma effects for Cu–Zn/ZSM-5, but transferable mechanistic prediction remains developing.
solved_when: A predictive framework quantitatively reproduces methanol rates and selectivity as functions of plasma excitation conditions, surface state, and temperature, with the nonequilibrium contribution cleanly and quantitatively distinguished from thermal and mass-transfer effects, and demonstrated to be transferable across catalysts and conditions.
why: It would make electrically driven catalytic reactors reliably scalable, replacing empirical trial-and-error with mechanistic design rules.
key_works: S. Xu et al. (2026), *Unveiling active sites and the cooperative role of non-thermal plasma and copper–zinc catalysts in the hydrogenation of CO2 to methanol*, [DOI:10.1038/s41929-025-01477-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41929-025-01477-5).

title: Atom-resolved catalytic turnover assignments under operating conditions
open: Can we attribute individual catalytic turnovers to specific, evolving surface motifs while a catalyst operates under realistic pressures? The goal is an atom-resolved, operando account of which sites turn over, together with quantified observation-induced perturbations and reliable statistics on rare active sites.
status: Active-site debates date to the earliest days of heterogeneous catalysis. Jenkinson et al. (2026) tracked individual Pt atoms operando in single nanoparticles and observed the coexistence of Langmuir and Taylor active-site classes, but complete turnover attribution remains harder.
solved_when: Individual turnovers are assigned to identified surface motifs under operating conditions, with the measurement-induced changes and the contribution of rare active-site classes quantitatively characterized.
why: It would identify which structures actually perform catalysis during operation, resolving long-standing active-site debates in heterogeneous catalysis and guiding the rational design of catalyst surfaces.
key_works: K. Jenkinson et al. (2026), *Operando single-atom tracking in individual Pt nanoparticles detects the coexistence of Langmuir and Taylor active sites*, [DOI:10.1038/s41929-026-01612-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41929-026-01612-w).

title: Catalysis by complete fluxional cluster ensembles
open: Can we predict the catalytic activity and selectivity of a cluster catalyst from the full ensemble of interconverting structures it actually populates under working conditions, and experimentally verify which ensemble members contribute what?
status: Fluxionality has complicated cluster catalysis for decades. A 2025 multiscale study (J.-L. Chen et al., *Collectivity effect in cluster catalysis under operational conditions*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-64187-3) demonstrated collective contributions across sizes, isomers and sites, but transferable experimental validation remains incomplete.
solved_when: A predictive framework connects populated, fluxional cluster ensembles to measured activity and selectivity, with experimental validation attributing contributions to individual ensemble members (sizes, isomers, and sites).
why: Catalyst design fails if it ignores the structures that are actually populated under operating conditions; resolving this makes rational design of fluxional cluster catalysts possible.
key_works: J.-L. Chen et al. (2025), *Collectivity effect in cluster catalysis under operational conditions*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-64187-3](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-64187-3).

title: Low-voltage acidic CO₂-to-ethylene electrolysis at scale
open: Can an acid-fed CO₂ electrolyser maintain selective C–C coupling to ethylene at practical electrode areas while simultaneously achieving low full-cell voltage, suppressed hydrogen evolution, and long-term durability?
status: A 2025 demonstration (D. Chen et al., *Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to ethylene in an acid-fed membrane electrode assembly at 10 A*, DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-65831-8) achieved 10 A operation for over 300 hours, approximately 50% ethylene Faradaic efficiency and about 4.5 V. Efficient long-life manufacture remains open.
solved_when: A practical-area acid-fed electrolyser sustains ethylene-selective CO₂ reduction with, at minimum, the demonstrated performance envelope — roughly 10 A operation for over 300 hours at about 4.5 V full-cell voltage and approximately 50% ethylene Faradaic efficiency — while improving on voltage, hydrogen evolution, and degradation beyond that baseline.
why: It would make carbon-efficient acidic CO₂-to-ethylene electrolysis economically competitive as an efficient, long-life manufacturing route, which is what currently blocks scale-up.
key_works: D. Chen et al. (2025), *Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to ethylene in an acid-fed membrane electrode assembly at 10 A*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-65831-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-65831-8).

title: Low-energy carbonate recovery in CO₂ electrolysis
open: Can we recover, at minimal total energy cost, the CO₂ that gets diverted into carbonate during CO₂ electrolysis — accounting for membrane water dissociation, acidification, and gas separation — while simultaneously raising carbon utilization?
status: This is a persistent electrolyser problem. Acid-fed, bipolar and asymmetric membranes partially address carbon loss, but the 2025 10 A acid-fed membrane electrode assembly demonstration (D. Chen et al. (2025), *Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to ethylene in an acid-fed membrane electrode assembly at 10 A*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-65831-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-65831-8)) still showed limited single-pass ethylene carbon utilization.
solved_when: A recovery scheme is demonstrated that minimizes total energy across membrane water dissociation, acidification and gas separation, and increases single-pass carbon utilization beyond the limited levels of current acid-fed demonstrations.
why: It would make more of the captured or purchased CO₂ feed end up as product rather than being lost as carbonate, directly improving the economics of CO₂ electrolysis.
key_works: D. Chen et al. (2025), *Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction to ethylene in an acid-fed membrane electrode assembly at 10 A*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-65831-8](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-65831-8).

title: Salt- and flooding-resistant ethylene electrolysers over service lifetimes
open: Can a CO₂-to-ethylene electrolyser stack keep its gas access, ion transport, and ethylene selectivity through long continuous operation and repeated shutdown–restart cycles, without frequent maintenance? Formally, the goal is a device architecture that resists salt precipitation and flooding over a whole-device service lifetime, not just over a single extended run.
status: Fang et al. (2026), in work finalized in 2026, reported over 1,000 hours of operation at 200 mA cm⁻² with periodic membrane replacement and electrolyte refreshment, and demonstrated a five-cell stack [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-67719-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-67719-z). Whole-device service lifetime remains unresolved.
solved_when: An electrolyser stack sustains ethylene production at high current density over extended operation with only infrequent maintenance (no periodic membrane replacement or electrolyte refreshment as routine interventions), maintaining gas access, ion transport, and selectivity across repeated shutdowns.
why: It removes the principal obstacle between high-performing laboratory cathodes and continuous industrial ethylene production; without it, promising CO₂-to-ethylene devices remain confined to short-lived demonstrations.
key_works: M. Fang et al. (2026), *Thousand-hour salt precipitation-free CO2-to-ethylene electrosynthesis at high current densities*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-67719-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-67719-z).

title: Predicting active copper after reconstruction
open: Can we predict which copper sites are actually active during CO₂ reduction, given only the starting catalyst structure, the applied potential, and the gas history — accounting for the dissolution and redeposition that reshape the surface in operation? In other words, can a model map the initial structure and operating conditions to the working copper-site distribution and the resulting C₁-versus-C₂ product selectivity?
status: This is a longstanding problem in copper electrocatalysis. A 2025 study by Y. Yang et al. (*Operando probing dynamic migration of copper carbonyl during electrocatalytic CO2 Reduction*, [DOI:10.1038/s41929-025-01359-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41929-025-01359-w)) observed nanocube reconstruction and copper-carbonyl migration operando, demonstrating that static starting-facet descriptions are inadequate.
solved_when: A predictive framework exists that takes initial catalyst structure, potential, and gas history as inputs and outputs the in-operando copper-site distribution and C₁/C₂ selectivity, explicitly incorporating dissolution and redeposition dynamics.
why: It would let synthesis efforts target the catalyst structure that actually persists and operates under reaction conditions, rather than the structure that exists only before the reaction begins.
key_works: Y. Yang et al. (2025), *Operando probing dynamic migration of copper carbonyl during electrocatalytic CO2 reduction*, [DOI:10.1038/s41929-025-01359-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41929-025-01359-w).

title: Selective third-carbon addition in CO electroreduction
open: Can an electrocatalyst be made to favor adding a third carbon to C₂ intermediates over all competing pathways — ethylene, ethanol, and hydrogen evolution — during CO electroreduction? Formally, the goal is C₂-to-C₃ coupling that dominates those competing routes while sustaining high reaction rates and producing a concentrated propanol stream.
status: Selectivity beyond two carbons remains difficult. Strain-enhanced propanol electrosynthesis from CO on copper was demonstrated by M. Wang et al. (2026), *Strain boosts propanol electrosynthesis from CO on copper* ([DOI:10.1038/s41929-026-01501-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41929-026-01501-2)), but practical selective C₃ production remains open.
solved_when: A catalyst system demonstrates selective C₂-to-C₃ coupling dominating ethylene, ethanol, and hydrogen pathways at high rates, with concentrated propanol output.
why: It would extend renewable-carbon electrosynthesis beyond two-carbon products to higher alcohols such as propanol.
key_works: M. Wang et al. (2026), *Strain boosts propanol electrosynthesis from CO on copper*, [DOI:10.1038/s41929-026-01501-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41929-026-01501-2).

title: Stable direct CO₂-to-methanol electrosynthesis
open: Can direct electrochemical reduction of CO₂ to methanol be made to run stably at scale, combining a methanol-selective molecular catalyst that does not degrade or restructure with low full-cell energy consumption and a usefully concentrated methanol product stream?
status: Song et al. reached 132 mA cm⁻² methanol partial current and 62% selectivity near pH 1 in 2025 (Y. Song et al. (2025), *Efficient CO2-to-methanol electrocatalysis in acidic media via microenvironment-tuned cobalt phthalocyanine*, [DOI:10.1038/s41565-025-02059-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41565-025-02059-z)). Long-duration performance, including recovery, remains open.
solved_when: An electrosynthesis system achieves durable operation at or beyond 132 mA cm⁻² methanol partial current and 62% selectivity, with low full-cell energy use and useful methanol concentration, while sustaining that performance over long durations without catalyst loss or restructuring.
why: Success would supply a major liquid feedstock directly from CO₂ and electricity.
key_works: Y. Song et al. (2025), *Efficient CO2-to-methanol electrocatalysis in acidic media via microenvironment-tuned cobalt phthalocyanine*, [DOI:10.1038/s41565-025-02059-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41565-025-02059-z).

title: Organic-crossover-resistant electrolyser anodes
open: Can an electrolyser anode be designed that resists dissolution when organic crossover products reach it, while the membrane keeps its conductivity and the desired organic products are preserved? Formally, the goal is an anode–membrane architecture in which aldehyde-driven destabilization of the iridium-oxide lattice is mitigated across realistic product mixtures without sacrificing ion transport or product selectivity.
status: Ka et al. showed in 2025 that aldehyde oxidation can destabilize iridium-oxide lattices ([DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-63992-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-63992-0)); durable mitigation across product mixtures remains unresolved.
solved_when: A durable mitigation strategy is demonstrated that suppresses organic-crossover-accelerated anode dissolution across the relevant product mixtures while retaining membrane conductivity and preserving the desired organic products.
why: It would preserve scarce iridium catalyst and improve integrated product yield in CO2 electrolysers.
key_works: S. Ka et al. (2025), *Accelerated dissolution of iridium anode in the presence of organic compounds*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-63992-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-63992-0).

title: Pure-water anion-exchange electrolysis with industrial durability
subfield: Water splitting, hydrogen production and fuel cells
open: Can an electrolyzer running on pure water, rather than a circulated alkaline electrolyte, sustain industrially relevant current densities using only abundant-metal electrodes for tens of thousands of hours? Formally, the challenge is to preserve membrane and ionomer conductivity — through aging, shutdowns, and current interruptions — while operating at high current density with a pure-water feed.
status: A 2026 local-alkalinity design achieved 3 A cm⁻² at 2.08 V and approximately 1,400 hours at 1 A cm⁻² (J. Guo et al. (2026), *Local alkalinity enables high-performance pure water anion exchange membrane electrolysis*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-69053-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-69053-4)). Simultaneous high-current efficiency and service-life durability remain open.
solved_when: High-current electrolysis is sustained with abundant-metal electrodes and a pure-water feed while membrane and ionomer conductivity is preserved through aging and interruptions, going beyond the current state of the art of 3 A cm⁻² at 2.08 V and roughly 1,400 hours at 1 A cm⁻².
why: It would combine inexpensive, abundant-metal catalysts with simpler liquid-feed handling, removing the cost and complexity of circulating caustic electrolyte.
key_works: J. Guo et al. (2026), *Local alkalinity enables high-performance pure water anion exchange membrane electrolysis*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-69053-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-69053-4).

title: Preventing iridium filaments across PEM electrolyser membranes
subfield: Water splitting, hydrogen production and fuel cells
open: How does dissolved iridium migrate and assemble into conducting filaments that bridge a PEM electrolyser membrane, and can materials choices or operating controls suppress these cross-membrane paths and the parasitic currents they carry?
status: Heume et al. identified this degradation route in 2026 after 5,000 hours of industry-oriented operation, showing that affected cells can continue functioning while losing efficiency (C. Heume et al. (2026), *Cross-plane iridium-based filaments sap efficiency in proton exchange membrane electrolyzers*, [DOI:10.1016/j.joule.2025.102238](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joule.2025.102238)).
solved_when: A mechanistic account of iridium filament formation is established, and a materials or operating intervention is demonstrated that prevents conducting cross-membrane paths and eliminates the associated parasitic currents over long-term operation.
why: Cells can keep running while silently losing efficiency to these hidden shunts, so a fix removes efficiency losses that simple operability tests miss.
key_works: C. Heume et al. (2026), *Cross-plane iridium-based filaments sap efficiency in proton exchange membrane electrolyzers*, [DOI:10.1016/j.joule.2025.102238](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joule.2025.102238).

title: Durable cooperative oxygen evolution beyond single-site scaling
subfield: Water splitting, hydrogen production and fuel cells
open: Can a cooperative, multi-site oxygen evolution mechanism be made to run durably at practical current densities, escaping the overpotential floor imposed by single-site scaling relations? Formally: establish transferable low-overpotential OER catalysis through cooperative sites while preserving the proposed mechanism and the active species inventory under operating conditions.
status: Scaling-relation limits on oxygen evolution are longstanding. Kuai et al. (2025) showed that dissolved iron participates in a cooperative solid–molecular NiFe mechanism for the OER on NiFe-based catalysts ([DOI:10.1038/s41929-025-01342-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41929-025-01342-5)); however, a stable general implementation of this cooperative mechanism remains unresolved.
solved_when: A cooperative-site oxygen evolution catalyst is demonstrated that maintains its mechanism and active inventory at practical currents with durable, low-overpotential operation, and the approach is transferable beyond a single catalyst system.
why: It would cut water-splitting losses beyond what conventional single-site catalyst optimization can reach, since single-site designs are bounded by scaling-relation limits.
key_works: C. Kuai et al. (2025), *Dissolved Fe species enable a cooperative solid–molecular mechanism for the oxygen evolution reaction on NiFe-based catalysts*, [DOI:10.1038/s41929-025-01342-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41929-025-01342-5).

title: Efficient scalable photocatalytic water splitting with separated gases
subfield: Water splitting, hydrogen production and fuel cells
open: Can a photocatalytic water-splitting system be built that simultaneously achieves efficient use of unconcentrated sunlight, keeps the hydrogen and oxygen product streams separated, and runs durably over large areas with low mediator losses?
status: Pursued since the 1970s. A 2025 system (H. Fu et al., *A scalable solar-driven photocatalytic system for separated H2 and O2 production from water*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-56314-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-56314-x)) achieved 2.47% solar-to-hydrogen efficiency and 1.21% outdoors in a 692.5 cm², week-long test. Related challenges include large-area light management (optical engineering) and mediator crossover and gas purification (process engineering).
solved_when: A system demonstrates efficient unconcentrated-sunlight operation with separated H2 and O2 streams, durable large-area operation, and low mediator losses — measurably surpassing the current benchmark of 2.47% solar-to-hydrogen efficiency (1.21% outdoors) sustained over a week-long test on a 692.5 cm² area.
why: It would provide direct solar fuel while simplifying gas separation, since separated product streams eliminate the energy cost and safety issues of separating mixed gases after splitting.
key_works: H. Fu et al. (2025), *A scalable solar-driven photocatalytic system for separated H2 and O2 production from water*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-56314-x](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-56314-x).

title: Durable organic passivation of neutral-pH silicon photocathodes
subfield: Water splitting, hydrogen production and fuel cells
open: Can an organic passivation layer on a silicon photocathode keep charge extraction and hydrogen evolution working while blocking corrosion through monolayer defects, catalyst boundaries, and aging in neutral-pH electrolyte?
status: Amze et al. reported six-hour stability for Pt-island/octadecyl-passivated silicon in work published online in 2025 and finalized in 2026 (DOI:10.1038/s41598-025-30589-y); long-life passivation remains open.
solved_when: A silicon photocathode with an organic passivation layer is demonstrated that sustains hydrogen evolution at neutral pH with charge extraction preserved, and resists corrosion through defects, catalyst boundaries, and aging over a lifetime substantially exceeding the six-hour stability reported by Amze et al.
why: It would enable simple semiconductor protection in mild electrolytes, removing the need for harsh conditions or elaborate protective schemes for durable solar hydrogen production.
key_works: M. Amze et al. (2026), *Hybrid island-and-sea approach for corrosion protection of Si photocathode in neutral-pH water splitting*, [DOI:10.1038/s41598-025-30589-y](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-025-30589-y).

title: Untreated-seawater electrolysis without chlorine or precipitation
subfield: Water splitting, hydrogen production and fuel cells
open: Can a complete electrolyser run directly on variable natural seawater for practical durations while suppressing chlorine chemistry, calcium/magnesium precipitation, and corrosion with minimal conditioning?
status: A longstanding paired-electrode challenge. Separate 2026 advances include 1,500-hour simulated-seawater anode tests (L.-l. Ma et al., 2026, *Breaking the activity-stability trade-off via dual-mechanism induced by rare earths for lasting seawater electrolysis*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-75978-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-75978-7)) and natural-seawater cathode antifouling (Z. Li et al., 2026, *Cation-inhibitor and metal–support synergy for efficient and durable hydrogen evolution in natural seawater*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-72268-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-72268-0)); the full integrated target remains open.
solved_when: A fully integrated electrolyser operates on untreated, variable natural seawater — not simulated seawater or a single electrode — while suppressing chlorine evolution, Ca/Mg precipitation, and corrosion with little conditioning.
why: It would establish whether direct saline-water use offers a practical system advantage for hydrogen production, avoiding costly pretreatment or desalination.
key_works: L.-l. Ma et al. (2026), *Breaking the activity-stability trade-off via dual-mechanism induced by rare earths for lasting seawater electrolysis*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-75978-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-75978-7); Z. Li et al. (2026), *Cation-inhibitor and metal–support synergy for efficient and durable hydrogen evolution in natural seawater*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-72268-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-72268-0).

title: Platinum-free fuel-cell cathodes with service-life stability
subfield: Water splitting, hydrogen production and fuel cells
open: Can an iron–nitrogen–carbon cathode sustain fuel-cell power under realistic air, humidity and load cycling over a full service life? Formally, the problem is to suppress demetallation, carbon corrosion and reactive-oxygen damage while maintaining high Fe–N–C cathode performance in operating conditions.
status: A decades-old target. A 2026 study by Y. Zeng et al. (*Regulating in situ gaseous deposition to construct highly durable Fe–N–C oxygen-reduction fuel cell catalysts*, DOI:10.1038/s41929-026-01482-2) reported strong accelerated-cycling durability, including H₂–air membrane-electrode assemblies; field service lifetime remains unresolved.
solved_when: An Fe–N–C cathode demonstrates power retention under realistic air, humidity and load cycling for a demonstrated field service lifetime, not merely accelerated-cycling durability tests.
why: It would cut platinum requirements for fuel cells while preserving power output, removing a major cost barrier to deployment.
key_works: Y. Zeng et al. (2026), *Regulating in situ gaseous deposition to construct highly durable Fe–N–C oxygen-reduction fuel cell catalysts*, [DOI:10.1038/s41929-026-01482-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41929-026-01482-2).

title: Retaining beneficial platinum strain without dissolution
subfield: Water splitting, hydrogen production and fuel cells
open: Can we keep platinum catalysts in the surface-strain regime that boosts their activity — without the strain relaxing or the platinum dissolving — over the full operating life of a fuel cell, while using supports that do not demand excessive scarce metals?
status: A 2026 study by Z. Zeng et al. identified a critical surface strain regime for stable and active epitaxial platinum oxygen reduction electrocatalysts and demonstrated Pt-on-Ir films with under 10% loss after 30,000 cycles (DOI:10.1038/s41560-026-02108-4). Broad implementation with lower scarce-metal demand remains open.
solved_when: A supported platinum electrocatalyst retains the critical strain regime and accessible surface area through fuel-cell operation with under 10% loss after 30,000 cycles, using materially less scarce metal than Pt-on-Ir epitaxial films.
why: It would let the activity gains from engineered strain survive for a useful device lifetime instead of decaying, making strained-platinum catalysts practical rather than laboratory-scale curiosities.
key_works: Z. Zeng et al. (2026), *Critical surface strain regime for stable and active epitaxial platinum oxygen reduction electrocatalysts*, [DOI:10.1038/s41560-026-02108-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-026-02108-4).

title: Unified chemical–mechanical prediction of lithium dendrite penetration
open: Can we predict where and when a lithium dendrite will penetrate a given solid electrolyte? A satisfactory answer would take the form of a unified model coupling electrochemical decomposition, stress, microstructure, and transport, validated across materials rather than tuned to a single system.
status: Dendrite penetration of solid electrolytes is a longstanding battery problem. Fincher et al. (2026) showed that dendrites can propagate at stresses up to 75% below mechanical-fracture expectations because electrochemical corrosion accompanies growth (*Electrochemical corrosion accompanies dendrite growth in solid electrolytes*, DOI:10.1038/s41586-026-10279-z), underscoring that mechanics alone is insufficient.
solved_when: A predictive framework exists that forecasts dendrite penetration location and timing in solid electrolytes from coupled chemistry, mechanics, microstructure, and transport, and its predictions are validated across multiple electrolyte materials.
why: It would turn dendrite avoidance from an empirical screening exercise into a predictive design task, allowing electrolytes and operating protocols to be engineered against penetration before failure.
key_works: C. D. Fincher et al. (2026), *Electrochemical corrosion accompanies dendrite growth in solid electrolytes*, [DOI:10.1038/s41586-026-10279-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10279-z).

title: Void-free lithium stripping at useful areal capacity
open: Can an anode be designed that keeps electrolyte contact during deep lithium stripping at practical current density, areal capacity, and low stack pressure, without at the same time becoming vulnerable to plating-induced short circuits? Formally, the goal is simultaneous suppression of void formation during stripping and dendrite/short suppression during plating under realistic operating conditions.
status: Contact loss during stripping is a longstanding problem. An August 2026 study by X. Ji et al. linked void suppression to the product of current and stripping capacity and demonstrated improved alloy behavior; however, simultaneous control of voids and dendrites remains open.
solved_when: A cell demonstrates void-free stripping at practical current and areal capacity under low pressure while also avoiding plating-induced shorts across cycling.
why: It would permit full lithium utilization with lighter pressure hardware, reducing the burden of stack-pressure components in practical cells.
key_works: X. Ji et al. (2026), *Void suppressive lithium anodes for all-solid-state batteries*, [DOI:10.1038/s41563-026-02729-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-026-02729-w).

title: Stable high-voltage sulfide-solid-electrolyte interfaces
open: Can sulfide solid electrolytes be made to resist ongoing oxidation and reduction at both electrodes while maintaining low-resistance ion transport and mechanical contact throughout high-voltage cycling?
status: The problem has been recognized since sulfide electrolytes became prominent. A 2025 electrophile-reduction strategy (W. Zhang et al., *Revitalizing interphase in all-solid-state Li metal batteries by electrophile reduction*, [DOI:10.1038/s41563-024-02064-y](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-024-02064-y)) suppressed decomposition and dendrites, but lifetime and manufacturing tolerance remain unresolved.
solved_when: An interface or interphase strategy demonstrates suppression of sulfide decomposition at both electrodes, with preserved ionic transport and mechanical integrity, over high-voltage cycling at industrially relevant lifetimes and manufacturing tolerances.
why: It would translate the high ionic conductivity of sulfide electrolytes into durable, high-energy all-solid-state cells.
key_works: W. Zhang et al. (2025), *Revitalizing interphase in all-solid-state Li metal batteries by electrophile reduction*, [DOI:10.1038/s41563-024-02064-y](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-024-02064-y).

title: Long-life 500 Wh/kg-class anode-free cells
open: Can an anode-free lithium battery hold above 500 Wh/kg at the cell level while surviving deep cycling over a useful lifetime under realistic constraints — lean electrolyte, a finite lithium inventory, and manufacturable stack pressure?
status: Liu et al. demonstrated 508 Wh/kg, 2.7 Ah pouch cells in 2026 that reached 100 full-depth cycles, or 250 cycles at 80% depth-of-discharge, both to 80% capacity retention (L. Liu et al. (2026), *Planar Li deposition and dissolution enable practical anode-free pouch cells*, [DOI:10.1038/s41586-026-10402-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10402-0)).
solved_when: A cell retains energy density above 500 Wh/kg while substantially exceeding the current benchmark of 100 full-depth cycles (or 250 cycles at 80% depth-of-discharge) to 80% capacity retention, all with lean electrolyte, finite lithium inventory, and manufacturable pressure requirements.
why: Without extended life, the energy-density advantage of anode-free designs evaporates over a product's service life; solving it makes the 500 Wh/kg-class gain actually usable in practical devices.
key_works: L. Liu et al. (2026), *Planar Li deposition and dissolution enable practical anode-free pouch cells*, [DOI:10.1038/s41586-026-10402-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10402-0).

title: Fast charging combined with slow discharge in lithium-metal cells
