open: Can a high-loading, lean-electrolyte lithium-metal cell retain high lithium reversibility when it is charged fast and discharged slowly — the duty cycle that real devices actually impose — including under cold operation and after calendar aging? More precisely, the question is whether cycling protocols of fast charge/slow discharge can sustain lithium reversibility in such cells across these practical conditions.
status: Many laboratory gains used the opposite (slow-charge/fast-discharge-style) protocol. Kim et al. addressed this degradation mode with an electrolyte diluent in 2026 (*Electrolyte diluent with large electrostatic potential difference for fast charging and slow discharging lithium metal batteries*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-69870-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-69870-7)); broad practical operating envelopes remain open.
solved_when: A high-loading, lean-electrolyte lithium-metal cell sustains lithium reversibility under a fast-charge/slow-discharge protocol, including during cold operation and after calendar exposure, across a broad practical operating envelope.
why: It would align lithium-metal chemistry with how electric vehicles and mobile devices are actually used, whereas most laboratory gains so far came from the opposite protocol and so may not transfer to real duty cycles.
key_works: M. Kim et al. (2026), *Electrolyte diluent with large electrostatic potential difference for fast charging and slow discharging lithium metal batteries*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-69870-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-69870-7).

title: Practical lean-electrolyte lithium–sulfur lifetime
open: Can a lithium–sulfur full cell simultaneously achieve a lean electrolyte, high sulfur loading, and limited lithium excess while sustaining long cycle life? Formally, the challenge is to combine low electrolyte-to-sulfur ratio and high areal sulfur loading with constrained lithium excess in a full cell that endures hundreds of cycles, with packaging included in the energy-density accounting.
status: This has been a commercialization barrier for decades. A 2025 study (H. Cho et al., *Interconvertible and rejuvenated Lewis acidic electrolyte additive for lean electrolyte lithium sulfur batteries*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-62169-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-62169-z)) reported 493 Wh/kg excluding external packaging at 2.4 μL electrolyte/mg sulfur, with 70% retention after 220 cycles.
solved_when: A full cell is demonstrated at a low electrolyte-to-sulfur ratio (at or below the current benchmark of 2.4 μL electrolyte/mg sulfur), with high sulfur loading and limited lithium excess, achieving long full-cell life (matching or exceeding 70% capacity retention after 220 cycles) at an energy density at or above 493 Wh/kg including external packaging.
why: It would convert sulfur's inexpensive capacity into durable lightweight storage, clearing a decades-old barrier to commercialization.
key_works: H. Cho et al. (2025), *Interconvertible and rejuvenated Lewis acidic electrolyte additive for lean electrolyte lithium sulfur batteries*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-025-62169-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-62169-z).

title: Predictive Li₂S deposition in concentrated polysulfide electrolytes
open: Can we predict where, in what morphology, and how reversibly Li₂S deposits in a concentrated polysulfide electrolyte, given only the concentration profile and operating history — including how surface and solution pathways compete under lean-electrolyte conditions?
status: Long unresolved. Zhou et al. directly imaged concentration-driven interfacial segregation in 2026 and connected it with competing Li₂S deposition routes (S. Zhou et al. (2026), *Revealing competitive interfacial reactions in high-energy Li–S batteries*, [DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-09473-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09473-2)).
solved_when: A predictive theory exists that, from concentration and operating history alone, determines deposition location, morphology, and reversibility, correctly resolving the competition between surface and solution deposition routes under lean conditions.
why: It would guide electrode designs that avoid premature passivation and inaccessible sulfur, directly extending the practical energy density of Li–S batteries.
key_works: S. Zhou et al. (2026), *Revealing competitive interfacial reactions in high-energy Li–S batteries*, [DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-09473-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09473-2).

title: Suppressing parasitic oxygen chemistry in rechargeable Li–O₂ cells
open: Can a rechargeable Li–O₂ cell be cycled so that oxygen reduction and evolution proceed with complete oxygen and charge balances while singlet oxygen is prevented from attacking the electrolyte, carbon, and binder? Formally, the goal is simultaneous quantitative O₂/charge balance and suppression of parasitic singlet-oxygen chemistry over repeated cycles.
status: Rechargeability has been problematic since early nonaqueous Li–O₂ research. A 2025 study by S. Mondal et al. (2025), *Marcus kinetics control singlet and triplet oxygen evolving from superoxide* ([DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-09587-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09587-7)), established Marcus-kinetic control of singlet/triplet oxygen production from superoxide, providing a possible intervention.
solved_when: A rechargeable Li–O₂ cell demonstrates cycling of oxygen reduction and evolution with complete oxygen and charge balances and no singlet-oxygen-induced degradation of electrolyte, carbon, or binder.
why: It would open a practical path to the high theoretical specific energy of Li–O₂ chemistry, which parasitic oxygen reactions currently squander.
key_works: S. Mondal et al. (2025), *Marcus kinetics control singlet and triplet oxygen evolving from superoxide*, [DOI:10.1038/s41586-025-09587-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09587-7).

title: Reversible magnesium–sulfur conversion with practical loading
open: Can a magnesium–sulfur battery sustain reversible MgS formation and oxidation under practically relevant conditions — high sulfur loading and low electrolyte content — while limiting magnesium trapping and anode consumption?
status: This is a persistent multivalent-conversion problem. A 2026 solvation strategy by J. Li et al. (*Solvating magnesium polysulfides enables low–barrier speciation for magnesium sulfur batteries*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-70598-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-70598-7)) achieved 120 laboratory cycles and an initial pouch-cell demonstration.
solved_when: A cell demonstrates reversible MgS conversion at high sulfur loading and low electrolyte content, with magnesium trapping and anode consumption held to limited levels.
why: It would pair abundant, low-cost constituents with high storage capacity in a single electrochemical system.
key_works: J. Li et al. (2026), *Solvating magnesium polysulfides enables low–barrier speciation for magnesium sulfur batteries*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-70598-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-70598-7).

title: Long-lived room-temperature calcium-metal full cells
open: Can a rechargeable calcium-metal full cell be built that survives practical room-temperature cycling by combining reversible calcium plating with a useful high-voltage positive electrode?
status: Calcium reversibility remains an active barrier. A 2026 organoborate-solvation study made progress (S. Li et al. (2026), *Strongly-coordinating organoborates with eccentric solvation structure enable secondary calcium metal battery*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-73484-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-73484-4)), while a broadly durable anode–electrolyte–cathode combination remains unavailable.
solved_when: A room-temperature calcium-metal full cell demonstrates reversible calcium plating alongside a functioning high-voltage cathode, maintaining electrolyte compatibility and calcium inventory through cycling.
why: Success would diversify electrochemical energy storage beyond lithium and monovalent-ion chemistry, opening a cheaper, multivalent storage platform.
key_works: S. Li et al. (2026), *Strongly-coordinating organoborates with eccentric solvation structure enable secondary calcium metal battery*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-73484-4](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-73484-4).

title: Zinc-metal reversibility without excess zinc or electrolyte
open: Can an aqueous zinc-metal cell cycle reversibly with only a thin zinc anode and a lean electrolyte inventory, keeping hydrogen evolution, corrosion, and morphology under control both during cycling and at rest? Formally, this asks for simultaneous control of the corrosion–deposition competition and calendar aging under finite zinc and electrolyte budgets.
status: A longstanding problem. A 2026 low-surface-tension electrolyte controlled zinc nucleation (H. Wang et al. (2026), *Regulating zinc nucleation and growth with low-surface-tension electrolytes for practical aqueous zinc metal batteries*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-68393-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-68393-5)), but shelf life and finite-inventory cycling remain joint constraints.
solved_when: An aqueous cell sustains cycling with thin zinc and lean electrolyte while hydrogen evolution, corrosion, and morphology remain controlled during both cycling and idle periods, meeting shelf-life and finite-inventory constraints jointly.
why: It would raise the complete-system lifetime of inexpensive zinc storage, since excess zinc and electrolyte — the usual workarounds — erode the cost advantage.
key_works: H. Wang et al. (2026), *Regulating zinc nucleation and growth with low-surface-tension electrolytes for practical aqueous zinc metal batteries*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-68393-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-68393-5).

title: Wide-voltage aqueous batteries without concentrated-salt penalties
open: Can an aqueous battery operate at high full-cell voltage while retaining good conductivity and low electrolyte cost? The goal is a wide-voltage aqueous full cell that avoids concentrated-salt strategies, with water decomposition measured directly rather than inferred.
status: Water-in-salt approaches expanded apparent electrochemical windows in the 2010s. A 2026 study (G. Li et al., *Hydrophobic liquid electrolyte interphases for efficient aqueous zinc batteries*, [DOI:10.1038/s41565-026-02187-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41565-026-02187-0)) demonstrated hydrophobic interphases in 3-molal zinc electrolyte; transferable low-cost full-cell stability remains open.
solved_when: A transferable, low-cost aqueous full cell demonstrates high-voltage stable operation with good electrolyte conductivity, and direct measurement confirms suppressed water decomposition.
why: It would combine the inherent safety of aqueous chemistry with higher usable energy density, without paying the cost and conductivity penalties of highly concentrated electrolytes.
key_works: G. Li et al. (2026), *Hydrophobic liquid electrolyte interphases for efficient aqueous zinc batteries*, [DOI:10.1038/s41565-026-02187-0](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41565-026-02187-0).

title: Hard-carbon sodium storage with low irreversible inventory loss
open: Can the desolvation of sodium ions and the formation of the solid–electrolyte interphase on hard carbon be controlled so that a single electrode simultaneously retains its sodium inventory, its rate capability, and its cycle lifetime — regardless of which precursor batch the carbon came from? Formally, this asks for precursor-independent control of interphase chemistry and ion transport in hard-carbon anodes.
status: The problem has been studied since around 2000. A 2026 MOF-glass coating (J. Zhao et al., *Metal–organic framework glass enables durable sodium-ion storage for hard carbon negative electrodes*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-75060-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-75060-2)) improved transport and interphase stability, but precursor-independent control remains unresolved.
solved_when: A hard-carbon sodium-ion anode is demonstrated that retains sodium inventory, rate capability, and lifetime simultaneously, with performance independent of the precursor batch used to produce the carbon.
why: It would raise the usable energy utilization of sodium-ion cells and make hard-carbon anode manufacturing consistent across feedstock variation, which is what currently blocks reproducible production.
key_works: J. Zhao et al. (2026), *Metal–organic framework glass enables durable sodium-ion storage for hard carbon negative electrodes*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-75060-2](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-75060-2).

title: Manufacturing-tolerant high-nickel cathode chemomechanics
open: Can a high-nickel cathode be designed so that oxygen loss, pore evolution and mechanical damage are suppressed across realistic loading, voltage, temperature and manufacturing variation, without sacrificing energy density?
status: A longstanding tradeoff between capacity and chemomechanical stability exists. A 2026 uniform-pore architecture (D. Eum et al. (2026), *Uniform pore structure enables negligible degradation in undoped and uncoated Ni-rich cathodes*, [DOI:10.1038/s41560-026-01988-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-026-01988-w)) showed negligible degradation under the studied conditions, but robustness to industrial heterogeneity remains open.
solved_when: A cathode architecture demonstrates negligible degradation while retaining high capacity under realistic ranges of loading, voltage, temperature and manufacturing heterogeneity, not merely under idealized laboratory conditions.
why: It would let high-nickel cathodes keep high capacity without continually adding inactive protective material such as coatings and dopants.
key_works: D. Eum et al. (2026), *Uniform pore structure enables negligible degradation in undoped and uncoated Ni-rich cathodes*, [DOI:10.1038/s41560-026-01988-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-026-01988-w).

title: Reversible oxygen redox without interfacial destruction
open: Can the oxygen-redox capacity of lithium-rich manganese oxide cathodes be cycled reversibly over many charge–discharge cycles without voltage decay, oxygen escape, or oxidative damage to an adjacent sulfide electrolyte?
status: Irreversibility of oxygen redox has persisted for decades. A 2026 study by Y. Wu et al. investigated and mitigated the coupled lattice-oxygen and interface changes in Li-rich positive electrodes in sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries ([DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-74601-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-74601-z)), but simultaneous retention of voltage, capacity, and interfaces remains open.
solved_when: A lithium-rich manganese oxide electrode demonstrates sustained use of lattice-oxygen redox capacity with simultaneous retention of voltage, capacity, and interfacial integrity (no voltage decay, no oxygen escape, no sulfide electrolyte oxidation) across repeated cycles.
why: It would raise cathode capacity beyond what transition-metal redox alone provides while keeping degradation mechanisms under control.
key_works: Y. Wu et al. (2026), *Interplay between oxygen redox and interfacial stability of Li-rich positive electrodes in sulfide-based all-solid-state batteries*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-74601-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-74601-z).

title: Transferable electrolyte design rules for preventing cell thermal runaway
open: Can we formulate design rules for electrolytes that predict when a full cell will undergo thermal runaway driven by reactions with its charged electrodes? A complete answer must account for gas generation, cell aging, and evolving internal contact, not just fresh-cell flammability.
status: This remains a longstanding safety gap. The state of the art is a 2026 thermally polymerizing, non-flammable electrolyte (J. Zhang et al., *Thermal runaway-free ampere-hour-level Na-ion battery via polymerizable non-flammable electrolyte*, DOI:10.1038/s41560-026-02032-7) that enabled runaway-free ampere-hour-level sodium-ion cells under tested conditions; whether the approach transfers across chemistries and abuse modes is open.
solved_when: A predictive framework exists whose predictions of runaway onset (or its absence) transfer across cell chemistries and abuse modes — not merely under the specific tested conditions of a single design — and which prescribes electrolyte modifications that prevent runaway in full cells.
why: It would turn electrolyte safety from an empirical, per-design trial-and-error exercise into a predictable chemistry, so that safety improvements carry over across cell designs rather than needing to be re-validated each time.
key_works: J. Zhang et al. (2026), *Thermal runaway-free ampere-hour-level Na-ion battery via polymerizable non-flammable electrolyte*, [DOI:10.1038/s41560-026-02032-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-026-02032-7).

title: Predicting reversible versus destructive water attack on MOFs
open: Can we predict, from a metal–organic framework's structure and composition, whether water attack on its coordination bonds will heal reversibly or trigger permanent structural collapse? A complete theory would account for defect formation, repeated hydration–dehydration cycling, and competition among mixed guest molecules.
status: Framework stability has been a central concern since MOFs emerged. A 2026 study (Y. Fu et al., *Water-generated dangling linkers in a metal-organic framework*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-70247-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-70247-z)) demonstrated reversible water-stabilized dangling carboxylates even in the water-stable framework UiO-66.
solved_when: A predictive criterion (or validated model) exists that correctly classifies, before exposure, whether a given MOF–water system undergoes reversible water-induced coordination changes versus permanent framework damage, including behavior under defect formation, cycling, and mixed-guest conditions.
why: It would make porous materials dependable under wet operating conditions, where irreversible degradation currently limits deployment.
key_works: Y. Fu et al. (2026), *Water-generated dangling linkers in a metal-organic framework*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-70247-z](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-70247-z).

title: Predicting zeolitic imidazolate framework topology from synthesis conditions
open: Can we predict, from the metal, linker, solvent, and synthesis protocol alone, which zeolitic imidazolate framework topology will form — including when a dense phase will win instead?
status: Reticular synthesis remains partly empirical. An automated iterative strategy published online in 2025 and in a 2026 issue doubled the discovery rate over random exploration; transferable topology selection remains open (Z. Rong et al. (2026), *Algorithmic iterative reticular synthesis of zeolitic imidazolate framework crystals*, [DOI:10.1038/s44160-025-00939-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44160-025-00939-9)).
solved_when: A model or theory that, given specified synthesis conditions (metal, linker, solvent, protocol), correctly predicts the resulting ZIF topology, accounting for competition with dense phases; success is measured by predictive accuracy on syntheses not used in training.
why: Targeted pore networks would become accessible by design rather than trial and error, dramatically reducing the number of experiments needed to reach a desired framework.
key_works: Z. Rong et al. (2026), *Algorithmic iterative reticular synthesis of zeolitic imidazolate framework crystals*, [DOI:10.1038/s44160-025-00939-9](https://doi.org/10.1038/s44160-025-00939-9).

title: Macroscopic ordered two-dimensional covalent organic frameworks
open: Can two-dimensional covalent organic frameworks be grown as processable, macroscopic or large-area crystals whose stacking is controlled, whose porosity remains accessible, and whose order survives activation and cycling?
status: A challenge since the 2000s. Three single-crystal 2D COF isomers were resolved by electron diffraction in 2026 (B. Yu et al., *Single-crystal 2D covalent organic frameworks for high-capacity methane storage*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-69614-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-69614-7)); scalable ordered material remains a further target.
solved_when: A scalable route exists to macroscopic or large-area 2D COF crystals exhibiting controlled stacking, accessible porosity after activation, and preserved crystalline order through cycling.
why: It would connect designed molecular pores to practical adsorption and electronic applications.
key_works: B. Yu et al. (2026), *Single-crystal 2D covalent organic frameworks for high-capacity methane storage*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-69614-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-69614-7).

title: Suppressing illumination-driven mixed-halide segregation over lifetime
open: Can a wide-bandgap mixed-halide perovskite be made to keep its homogeneous halide distribution under simultaneous illumination, bias, and thermal cycling, without degrading its transport properties or the stability of its additives? Formally, the goal is a composition and device architecture in which illumination-driven halide demixing is suppressed over the full operational lifetime.
status: Recognized since the mid-2010s. Zhu et al. reported suppressed segregation on 1 October 2026 (X. Zhu et al. (2026), *Wide-bandgap perovskite with homogeneous crystallization and suppressed halogen segregation for efficient perovskite-organic tandem solar cells*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-78267-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78267-5)); broad composition coverage and complete operational lifetime remain unresolved.
solved_when: A wide-bandgap mixed-halide composition retains homogeneous halide distribution under light, bias, and thermal cycling across the complete operational lifetime, with broad composition coverage and with transport and additive stability preserved.
why: It would preserve the bandgap and voltage required for tandem photovoltaics.
key_works: X. Zhu et al. (2026), *Wide-bandgap perovskite with homogeneous crystallization and suppressed halogen segregation for efficient perovskite-organic tandem solar cells*, [DOI:10.1038/s41467-026-78267-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78267-5).

title: Chemically robust perovskite tandems under reverse bias
open: Can a perovskite tandem solar cell be made to withstand repeated partial-shading reverse-bias events without triggering irreversible chemical degradation of the perovskite and its interfaces — all while preserving efficiency and manufacturability? Formally, the goal is a device architecture or materials strategy that suppresses reverse-bias-driven chemical change under recurring current mismatch.
status: This is a contemporary tandem-deployment problem. Graded dielectric layers improved reverse-bias resistance in 2026 (L. Wang et al., *Improving the stability of monolithic perovskite/silicon tandems against reverse-bias stress using graded dielectric layers*, [DOI:10.1038/s41560-026-02067-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-026-02067-w)), but robustness across defects and outdoor stress histories remains open.
solved_when: A tandem design is demonstrated that survives repeated partial-shading reverse-bias events with no irreversible perovskite or interface chemistry, while maintaining its power-conversion efficiency and remaining compatible with scalable manufacturing, with robustness shown across realistic defects and outdoor stress histories.
why: It would prevent permanent damage from ordinary shading and current mismatch, which are unavoidable in real deployment and currently degrade tandem performance irreversibly.
key_works: L. Wang et al. (2026), *Improving the stability of monolithic perovskite/silicon tandems against reverse-bias stress using graded dielectric layers*, [DOI:10.1038/s41560-026-02067-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41560-026-02067-w).

title: Oxidation-stable lead-free tin-halide semiconductor interfaces
open: Can tin-halide semiconductors keep the intended tin oxidation state at their surfaces and grain boundaries over sustained device operation, rather than degrading through uncontrolled self-doping? Formally, this asks for an interface-control strategy that stabilizes the tin redox state and suppresses defect-mediated doping under operating conditions.
status: This is a persistent barrier for lead-free perovskites. A 2026 demonstration showed that volatile-coordination surface reconstruction improved tin-halide transistor stability (G. Park et al., *Tin perovskite transistors stabilized through volatile coordination*, [DOI:10.1038/s41586-026-10714-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10714-1)), but a transferable, long-life redox control strategy remains open.
solved_when: Lead-free tin-halide devices maintain the required tin oxidation state with self-doping suppressed at surfaces and grain boundaries during sustained operation, with redox-control strategies transferable across devices rather than single demonstrations.
why: It would enable less-lead-dependent optoelectronics — tin-halide transistors, photovoltaics, and related devices — that retain stable performance over device lifetimes instead of degrading at their interfaces.
key_works: G. Park et al. (2026), *Tin perovskite transistors stabilized through volatile coordination*, [DOI:10.1038/s41586-026-10714-1](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10714-1).

title: Predicting inorganic synthesis products from transport kinetics
subfield: Inorganic solid-state synthesis and corrosion chemistry
open: Can we predict what a multicomponent powder reaction will actually produce — intermediates, phase fractions, and final products — given only the precursor mixture and its thermal history, accounting for correlated diffusion and metastability along the way?
status: The gap between phase thermodynamics and synthesis outcomes is longstanding. A 2026 Ba–Ti–O study (V. Karan et al., *Ion correlations explain kinetic selectivity in diffusion-limited solid-state synthesis reactions*, [DOI:10.1038/s41563-026-02596-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-026-02596-5)) incorporated correlated transport, but transferring the approach across chemical systems remains open.
solved_when: A predictive framework exists whose predictions of intermediates, phase fractions, and final products from precursor and thermal history are validated across multiple chemical systems, including correlated diffusion effects and metastable phases.
why: It would close the gap between knowing a functional material is thermodynamically possible and actually making it, reducing failed synthesis attempts for predicted functional materials.
key_works: V. Karan et al. (2026), *Ion correlations explain kinetic selectivity in diffusion-limited solid-state synthesis reactions*, [DOI:10.1038/s41563-026-02596-5](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-026-02596-5).

title: Predicting chloride-pit initiation from real surface microstructure
subfield: Inorganic solid-state synthesis and corrosion chemistry
open: Can we predict where and when chloride pits will initiate on a real metal surface, given its actual microstructure — inclusions, passive-film chemistry, and processing history? More formally, can a transferable law be derived that yields the distributions of pit-initiation potentials and times, and hence corrosion resistance, under variable chloride exposure?
status: The problem has been studied for over a century. A 2026 study (S. Wang, M. Nishimoto and I. Muto, *Grinding-induced degradation in the pitting corrosion resistance of stainless steel: insights into passive film and MnS*, [DOI:10.1038/s41529-026-00750-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41529-026-00750-7)) resolved how grinding and MnS inclusions affect stainless-steel pitting, but a transferable initiation law remains absent.
solved_when: A predictive, transferable law exists that takes as input surface microstructural features (inclusion populations, passive-film chemistry, processing history) and outputs distributions of pit-initiation potentials and times matching experiment under variable chloride exposure.
why: It would connect surface processing directly to reliable infrastructure lifetime prediction, replacing empirical testing with microstructure-based design of corrosion-resistant surfaces.
key_works: S. Wang, M. Nishimoto and I. Muto (2026), *Grinding-induced degradation in the pitting corrosion resistance of stainless steel: insights into passive film and MnS*, [DOI:10.1038/s41529-026-00750-7](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41529-026-00750-7).

title: Predictive high-temperature hydrogen embrittlement chemistry
subfield: Inorganic solid-state synthesis and corrosion chemistry
open: Can damage from high-temperature hydrogen embrittlement be predicted from first principles when hydrogen trapping, carbide decomposition, methane formation, and deformation all interact? A successful theory would forecast embrittlement damage across alloy compositions and thermal histories rather than for a single material under fixed conditions.
status: Hydrogen embrittlement has been studied for a century, but predictive understanding at high temperature remains open. A 2026 study by S. Kong et al. (2026), *Hydrogen-induced damage in Ni-based superalloys at elevated temperatures* ([DOI:10.1038/s41563-026-02680-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-026-02680-w)), identified vacancy-mediated carbide reactions and localized methane formation in nickel superalloys, yet transferable high-temperature prediction remains open.
solved_when: A transferable predictive framework exists that captures the coupled hydrogen-trapping, carbide-decomposition, methane-formation, and deformation chemistry and predicts damage across varying alloy compositions and thermal histories.
why: It would let engineers set materials choices and operating limits for hydrogen-containing high-temperature fuels, such as hydrogen-compatible turbines and structural alloys.
key_works: S. Kong et al. (2026), *Hydrogen-induced damage in Ni-based superalloys at elevated temperatures*, [DOI:10.1038/s41563-026-02680-w](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41563-026-02680-w).
